MAgent Theory 2.0

      Gauge-Covariant Agents
     and Inherited Organization

           Robert C. Dennis

              Independent Researcher

                     October 2026
Abstract

An agent holds beliefs and generative models, receives records, makes predictions, and changes
its laws. We formulate these objects on associated statistical bundles, with independent directed
interactions that may depend on the current belief and model laws. On regular statistical families, the
joint-law Fisher metric and a connection induce a covariant pullback tensor on the contextual base.
A collective least-squares construction selects a connection class from declared comparison data.
Exact identities distinguish information lost under a channel from changes caused by incompatible
connections, and characterize when a parent retention preserves the collective connection.

Interacting agents admit three objectives, which we keep separate. In a global free energy all
agents are parts of one normalized joint, and local updates are coordinate descent of one functional.
In per-agent free energies each agent's generative model treats its peers' communicated laws
as competing sources of prior information. A reciprocal law potential generates coupled Fisher
dynamics in which sources also move toward their receivers; we prove that it is not the free energy
of any fixed normalized model whose recognition laws are the agent laws. Conditional-information
identities describe communication, common recovery, and the cost of discarding record history.
Parent dynamics and boundary responses must descend through the retained configuration.

A two-agent conditional-prediction experiment gives an exact interacting record model before
posterior projection. Each speaker samples its result prediction from private evidence and a shared
transcript; the receiver conditions on that actual mechanism. The joint private-record posterior
evolves with a fixed reconstruction of represented states, preserving correlated model/content
beliefs and the declared future communication laws. An affine Gaussian specialization closes
exactly, while finite Gaussian-mixture closure and retention of local beliefs alone can fail. The
common preparation and protocol are supplied, and the resulting fixed-history inference is distinct
from the population flows.

A formation standard requires selection, inheritance, compression, interaction necessity checked
against a null flow, and a second stage that depends on the first. Under the reciprocal potential, a
profile construction preserves coupled identity-channel dynamics and a declared response interface
through arbitrary finite binary depth on a supplied family; it is an equivariant symmetry reduction. A
four-agent Wishart construction selects two parents and then their union with exact original-time
inheritance, but its membership schedule is the centroid dendrogram of the prepared initial shapes
and is the same at zero coupling. A six-agent construction admits a full open set of positive bit-circle
laws, with preferential pairs, a later parent join, inherited moving-representative dynamics, adaptive
response histories, and nonflat rank-two contextual geometry on a declared finite window. Its
orientation loss is relative to the supplied interface, and in the proof regime the null flow reproduces
its membership history. A nonsmooth extension gives finite-time fusion whose grouping requires
the interaction, but fused parents compress nothing.

For the normalized per-agent free energies, a separate construction proves persistent interaction-
dependent grouping against conflicting records. An angular extension admits a physically nonin-
jective parent preserving the original-time port dynamics, every admitted finite adaptive response-

                                                                i
                                                                                                                    MAgent Theory 2.0

record history, and the actual collective connection and contextual tensor on a nonflat finite-window
family. Its phase-insensitive interface is available before grouping; no new second compressive
handoff is established. These results are single-stage or two-stage selections with exact inheritance
at their stated scopes. A construction meeting every clause of the formation standard remains
open.

A collective phase quotient preserves fixed relative probes and admits exact local two-jet evolution
with finite reference memory. A finite preparation generator gives another conditional realization.
A causal local phase accumulator obeys the original-time native dynamics and preserves every
admitted history; actual geometric inheritance additionally requires initial collective-phase coherence
across context. Scoped obstructions exclude rotation-invariant local value-path memory and
smooth bounded-jet causal memories on the rich open preparation class. The unrestricted causal-
local-parent question remains inconclusive; neither interaction-created invisibility nor a second
compressive handoff is proved.

A separate contextual extension couples neighboring laws through an auxiliary alignment energy.
On finite graphs, a regular minimizing branch gives an explicit Fisher force and local uniqueness.
On a supplied flat torus, a free proper isometric action reduces the contextual cost to a quotient
Dirichlet energy. The resulting shape PDE and frame and source-row ODEs have a local Sobolev
solution with exact total-energy dissipation. These results retain fixed-reference forces that need not
descend to the quotient. They establish no global regularity, singular-orbit passage, independent
row or link diffusion, or graph-refinement limit.

A separate geometric construction derives base transport from regular contextual law, interface,
and directed-link data. A spanning message matrix gives displacement identity, affine connection
covariance, and an explicit curvature formula; local alignment also gives a curved example built
only from reciprocal rotation links. A single marked square frame instead gives flat local transport.
Comparison metrics remain constitutive, continuous invisible gauge sectors obstruct a link-only
selector, and no new evolution or inheritance result is asserted.

Selective communication introduces a further distinction between the transmitted code and the
invertible dictionary used to interpret it. Conditional-information identities quantify reconstruction
loss for general laws. Grounded messages identify dictionaries modulo code stabilizers, while
an anchored loop prior couples their unread directions. A Gaussian tangent model gives exact
recognition formulas and separates global, receiver-owned, and reciprocal link dynamics. Inte-
grating out Gaussian contents produces an affine cost on coded reinterpretations. Its relation to
directed holonomy requires explicit cycle hypotheses. Supplied rigid clusters admit a restricted
parent description under normalization and connectivity conditions; this reduction supplies no new
formation theorem.

Reading the construction

The mathematical objects are introduced in the order in which they are needed: agent laws,
generative models and records, interactions, statistical and contextual geometry, free energies
and dynamics, predictive compression, inherited organization, a contextual-coupling extension,
and base transport derived from contextual agent data. The final three technical chapters develop
selective communication, latent dictionary learning, and curvature costs in supplied hierarchies.

                                                                ii
                                                                                                                    MAgent Theory 2.0
The main results include their decisive proofs. The appendices give the internal history construction,
conditional prediction and generative memory, exact interaction between conditional predictors,
directional links and base connections, an optional determinant-metric and circle example, and
notation. Secondary calculations are collected in a separate supplement.
Definitions specify the model's objects; constitutive choices specify how those objects interact.
A theorem states a consequence of explicit hypotheses. An open problem identifies a further
construction that is not supplied by those hypotheses. General probability measures are used
whenever measurability suffices. Finite alphabets, smooth statistical families, and vector fibers
enter only where an example or a differential calculation requires them. The general definitions
assume no Gaussian closure; the fusion example states its lognormal restriction explicitly.

                                             vii
Chapter 1

Agents, Possibilities, and Records

The program behind this theory asks whether interacting agents can produce further agents. This
text supplies the objects needed to pose that question exactly, the conditions under which a parent
description inherits the dynamics of its children, and constructions measured against a formation
standard (definition 6.31); a construction meeting every clause of that standard remains open
(open problem 6.32). The first distinction is between an agent's probability law and the possibilities
represented by that law. The second is between comparing two descriptions and specifying an
interaction that changes them. A parent construction must preserve enough of both to continue the
dynamics.

1.1 Statistical sections

Let C be a second-countable smooth base of contexts and let P  C be a principal G-bundle, with
G a second-countable Lie group. A context labels where a description applies; it is not identified
with physical position or time. For each agent i let Ki and Mi be standard Borel spaces with jointly
Borel actions G × Ki  Ki and G × Mi  Mi. Their elements k and m represent state contents
and model presentations. The actions may be different representations of the same group. They
act on probability measures by pushforward. When no agent index is needed we write K, M.

Throughout, one structure group acts on both sectors. A gauge transformation of an agent is a
single element of G, acting on state contents and on model presentations through the two actions;
there is no separate belief group and model group. The represented contents form two associated
bundles over the same principal bundle,

                      Eq = P ×G K, Es = P ×G M,          (1.1)

which in a linear realization are vector bundles P ×q Vq and P ×s Vs for representations q : G 
GL(Vq) and s : G  GL(Vs), of ranks K = dim Vq and K~ = dim Vs. The statistical bundle defined

next carries laws over the fiber product of Eq and Es, on which G acts diagonally.

Definition 1.1 (Statistical agent section). Set Yi = Ki × Mi, with the product action, and give

P(Yi) the sigma-algebra generated by evaluation on measurable sets. The associated statistical

bundle of agent i is

                      Bi = P ×G P(Yi), (ug, )  (u, g#).  (1.2)

The statistical component of agent i is a Borel section i of Bi over an open domain Ui  C. Smooth
sections are defined only into admitted smooth subbundles. The full state of the agent also includes
the internal variables and access mechanisms read by its update rule.

                          1
1. Agents, Possibilities, and Records     MAgent Theory 2.0

The associated-bundle construction is that of Kobayashi and Nomizu [87, Section I.5]. Its measur-
able form needs the joint measurability of the action. If each g acts bimeasurably but (g, y)  gy is
not jointly Borel, for example a translation of R by a discontinuous additive function of g  R, the
Borel class of a section can depend on the trivialization in which it is written.

Lemma 1.2 (Measurable structure of the statistical bundle). Under the stated hypotheses,
(g, )  g# is Borel on G × P(Yi), and Bi carries a standard Borel structure, independent of the
atlas, for which every local trivialization is a Borel isomorphism onto its image. Transition maps
preserve fiberwise mixtures, null sets, mutual absolute continuity, and relative entropy.

Proof. For a Borel set A, (g#)(A) = 1A(gy)(dy). The integrand is Borel in (g, y) by joint
measurability, and the integral of a bounded jointly Borel function against  is Borel in (g, ): this
holds for products f (g)h(y) and extends by the monotone class theorem. Since C is second
countable, countably many trivializing patches cover it, and their transition functions are Borel. The
gluing maps (c, )  (c, g(c)#) are therefore Borel bijections with Borel inverses. The space
P(Yi) is standard Borel [84], so Bi is a countable Borel union of standard Borel pieces glued by
Borel isomorphisms; a second atlas yields the same structure because its transitions to the first are
Borel by the same argument. Pushforward is affine and preserves null sets and absolute continuity,
and proposition 1.5 gives invariance of relative entropy.

At a fixed context, disintegration gives

i(dk, dm) = qi(dk | m)si(dm), qi(dk) = qi(dk | m)si(dm).  (1.3)

Here qi is the state marginal and si is the law over model presentations. Regular conditional
laws exist on the stated spaces, with versions defined up to the appropriate marginal null sets
[82]. Disintegration commutes with the product action: the conditional law of g#i given m
is g#qi(· | g-1m) for g#si-almost every m, so eq. (1.3) descends to bundle points. A model
presentation acquires predictive content through a normalized kernel; its name or coordinate value
alone supplies no prediction (section 1.4).

The product restriction i = qi  si removes dependence between the two sectors within an agent.
A product over agents makes a further restriction on represented contents. Neither restriction
prevents the update of one law from depending on other laws. Coupling is a property of the
dynamics; factorization is a property of a chosen probability description. The coupled population
flows developed below impose the product restriction. The general joint law enters through its
Fisher metric in chapter 3 and through the local conditional-prediction construction of section 5.2
and appendix B. The restriction is not neutral, as chapter 4 shows: it changes the local optimum of
a belief, and the joint-law flow does not preserve it.

Smoothness is an additional hypothesis. When derivatives of laws are required, use a declared
regular statistical family stable under the relevant coordinate changes. The whole space P(Yi) is
not assigned a smooth manifold structure by notation. Chapter 3 equips an admitted family with
the Fisher metric of the full joint law and pulls that metric back to contextual directions through a
covariant derivative. The product restriction has a simpler metric, but marginal metrics alone do not
measure changes of dependence in a general joint family. A collection of pointwise marginals also

                                       2
1. Agents, Possibilities, and Records                         MAgent Theory 2.0

does not determine a probability law on fields over C; section 1.5 supplies such a law as a separate
object.

The population at a context consists of the agents whose domains contain that context. Most
of the dynamics below is formulated at a common c. This retains the ambient bundle and local
sections without requiring parallel transport between distinct base points. Independent interactions
between agents at c are defined in chapter 2. Contextual statistical geometry is developed in
chapter 3; appendix D records the transformation law of connection data in a moving presentation.
Chapter 17 constructs such data from regular contextual laws, interfaces, and links with declared
comparison rules; selection of those rules and continuation through singular regions remain open.
The potentials of chapter 4 contain no coupling between contexts. The formation constructions
retain these context-local flows and compute connections as diagnostics. The separate extension
in chapter 16 adds an aligned contextual energy and derives its neighboring-context Fisher force
on declared regular families.

Parents in later chapters are maps between statistical descriptions of different agents. The following
definition supplies the corresponding morphism of bundles.

Definition 1.3 (Morphism of statistical bundles). Let f~ : P  P¯ be a principal bundle map
covering f : C  C¯ with homomorphism  : G  G¯, so that f~(ug) = f~(u)(g). Let  : Y  Y¯ be a
Markov kernel with (gy, ·) = (g)#(y, ·). The induced morphism is

                                       f~,[u, ] = [f~(u), ].  (1.4)

Proposition 1.4 (Statistical bundle morphisms). The map eq. (1.4) is well defined, fiberwise
affine, and contracts relative entropy within each fiber. In a linear realization, let A : Vq  V¯q and
A~ : Vs  V¯s be linear maps with Aq(g) = ¯q((g))A and A~s(g) = ¯s((g))A~ for all g  G. Then

the same principal map induces well-defined morphisms of the content bundles,

[u, k] = [f~(u), Ak], ~ [u, m] = [f~(u), A~m],                (1.5)

and the deterministic kernel ((k, m), ·) = (Ak,A~m) induces the corresponding statistical morphism.

Proof. Equivariance of  gives (g#) = (g)#(). Hence [u, g#]  [f~(u), (g)#()] =
[f~(u)(g), ], which is the image of the equivalent representative [ug, ]. The map    is affine,
and DKL()  DKL() is the data-processing inequality [35]. For the content morphisms,
the representative [ug, q(g)-1k] is sent to [f~(u)(g), Aq(g)-1k] = [f~(u)(g), ¯q((g))-1Ak] =
[f~(u), Ak], and likewise for ~ . The deterministic kernel is equivariant by the two intertwining
relations.

The belief and model morphisms share the principal map f~. A pair of sector morphisms covering
different principal maps would act with independent groups in the two sectors, and is not admitted.

A parent is an agent of a declared type when its retained state is again a section of such a bundle,
carries an admitted family, a register with a covariant readout, and an evaluator, and interacts with
exterior agents through channels of definition 2.1. Proving that a retention is closed in this sense is
part of the formation problem of chapter 6, not a consequence of the definition.

1.2 Presentation and probability

Fix c and a reference point   Pc. A frame of agent i is a point ui  Pc, and ui = Ui-1 defines
Ui  G. The point ui identifies the fiber of Bi at c with P(Yi), and the law displayed by agent i is the

coordinate expression of its bundle point in that frame. In a linear realization Ki = Vq and Mi = Vs
carry linear representations q, s of G, the sector frames are Uiq = q(Ui) and Uis = s(Ui), and
Eiq, Eis denote agent i's coordinate copies of Vq, Vs. Laws written on Eia, as in chapter 2, are the
displayed laws. The reference laws are

q¯i = ((Uiq)-1)#qi,                              s¯i = ((Uis)-1)#si.       (1.6)

They are the coordinate expressions in the reference frame , since [Ui-1, ] = [, (Ui-1)#]. A
passive change sends ui to uigi-1, hence qi to (giq)#qi and Uiq to giqUiq, with the corresponding
model-sector rule. The reference laws are unchanged. This is a change of description, not an
inference step. One frame induces both sector frames, and a passive change is one element gi
with giq = q(gi) and gis = s(gi). Independent sector changes would require the product group
Gq × Gs; the theory does not use them.

Because every frame-dependent object can be written through its reference law, covariance under
independent passive changes at each agent holds for any rule expressed in reference laws and
constrains nothing by itself. The frames act here as a dressing field in the sense of Fournel et al. [58].
A substantive symmetry requirement is a statement about the reference rules themselves, such
as equivariance of an interaction under a common change of reference at one context. Chapter 2
states it as eq. (2.13), and a result uses it only where it says so.

An active transformation changes the reference laws at fixed frames, for example q¯i  a#q¯i for a
bimeasurable bijection a of Ki. Whether two configurations related in this way are distinguishable
depends on a declared observable algebra: the rows, channels, and record kernels of the agents,
together with any declared external response protocol. A distinction is called gauge relative to such
an algebra when no element of the algebra separates the configurations. When only an external
protocol separates them, the text names that protocol rather than calling the distinction physical
without qualification.

For probability measures µ,  on one measurable space, relative entropy is

                                                 dµ                        (1.7)
                                       DKL(µ) =  log dµ,
                                                     d

when µ  , and is + otherwise. In this formula and below, a displayed integral is understood
with its declared measure; no common Lebesgue density is required. Relative entropy compares
distinguishability of laws [89].

Proposition 1.5 (Coordinate invariance). For an injective Borel map f between standard Borel
spaces, in particular a bimeasurable bijection, including divergences with value +,

                                       DKL(f#µf#) = DKL(µ).                (1.8)

1. Agents, Possibilities, and Records                           MAgent Theory 2.0

Proof. By the Lusin­Souslin theorem [84, Theorem 15.1] the image of f is Borel and f is a Borel
isomorphism onto it, so it suffices to treat a bimeasurable bijection onto a Borel set carrying both
pushforwards. Absolute continuity is preserved in both directions. If h = dµ/d, the transformed
density is h  f -1. Integrating its logarithm against f#µ gives the original integral. If absolute
continuity fails, a set of zero -measure and positive µ-measure is carried to a set with the same
property.

Definition 1.6 (Normalized channel). A Markov kernel K : X  Y assigns a probability measure
K(x, ·) to each x, measurably in x. Its action on a law is

                                       (µK)(A) = K(x, A)µ(dx).  (1.9)

A deterministic measurable map f : X  Y is represented by Kf (x, ·) = f(x). Then µKf = f#µ.

An invertible frame change preserves all distinctions. A channel that discards information or adds
noise need not. Both are well-defined operations on general probability laws, but their roles in an
agent interaction differ.

1.3 Internal records

At a fixed context, let Si be the admitted internal-state space of agent i, and let S be the complete
configuration space. It contains the statistical laws, the source rows defined in chapter 4, interfaces,
and memory variables that the dynamics reads. Write pri : S  Si for the local state projection.
For the measurable constructions, take these spaces to be standard Borel. A finite collection
of probability-law spaces and finite or Euclidean memory spaces supplies such a realization. A
flow, retention, or response used in a measurable construction must be Borel for these structures.
Smoothness in a Banach chart of log densities does not by itself ensure this, because the norm-
Borel sigma-algebra of L() for nonatomic  is strictly finer than the trace of the evaluation
sigma-algebra; where such flows are used, their measurability is a stated hypothesis.

Definition 1.7 (Record and readout). A record readout is a measurable map

                                       i : Si - Oi,             (1.10)

where Oi is a standard Borel alphabet of internally distinguishable outcomes. If an interaction with
source j produces configuration Zt+1, its record variable is

                                       Oij,t = i(pri Zt+1).     (1.11)

For stochastic dynamics this is a measurable function from the probability space of realizations to
Oi. A realized value is denoted oij,t. The source label is part of the record only when the internal
state retains it.

A record can be transient. Persistence means that the distinction remains accessible through a
specified later readout. A list kept outside the agent does not supply this accessibility. A memory

                                       5
1. Agents, Possibilities, and Records                                    MAgent Theory 2.0

coordinate is therefore an explicit part of the model unless the required distinction is already
represented in its state.

Proposition 1.8 (Induced record law). Let ij : S  S be a normalized interaction transition.

Then

      Rij(x, A) = ij x, {x : i(pri x)  A} ,                              (1.12)

is a normalized record kernel. If ij(x, ·) = Fij(x), the record is the deterministic function i pri Fij.

Proof. The right side is the pushforward of a probability measure through the measurable map

i  pri. Its total mass is one, and measurability in x follows from the defining property of a kernel.
The deterministic case follows by evaluating a Dirac measure.

A readout that reads frame-dependent coordinates can change under a mere change of description.
For example, a readout of the first coordinate of the displayed mean of qi returns 1 for the law
N (e1, I) in one frame and 0 after a passive rotation by /2, although the configuration is the
same. Records therefore carry a covariance requirement. A passive change  acts on S by a
Borel automorphism, on laws by pushforward, on frames by left multiplication, and on interface
data by their declared rule, with pri  = i  pri. A readout is invariant if i  i = i, and
equivariant if i  i = i()  i for a declared measurable action i on Oi. A transition is covariant if
ij(x, B) = ij(x, B) for all measurable B. Every readout, record kernel, and response kernel of
this text is required to be invariant or declared equivariant, and every interaction transition covariant.

Proposition 1.9 (Covariant record laws). If ij is covariant and i is equivariant with action i,
then Rij(x, A) = Rij(x, i()-1A). For an invariant readout, Rij(x, A) = Rij(x, A).

Proof. Write BA = {x : i(pri x)  A}. Covariance gives Rij(x, A) = ij(x, -1BA), and
-1BA = {x : i()i(pri x)  A} = Bi()-1A.

This definition introduces no observing agent outside the population. It specifies where an outcome
is available and how it can enter later dynamics. It does not derive the transition ij or decide
whether its stochasticity represents objective chance. Those are further modeling choices. A
response protocol queried from outside the population, as in chapter 13, is a separate declared
device and is named wherever it is the only element of the observable algebra that resolves a
distinction.

For example, a vector comparison can be represented by

      rij : Eiq × Ejq × Rr  Rr,        rij(ki, kj, ) = Aiki - Bijkj + .  (1.13)

Under passive changes ki  giki and kj  gjkj the comparison matrices transform as Ai  Aigi-1
and Bij  Bijgj-1, so the comparison value is invariant. A noise law turns this map into a record
kernel on represented contents. A joint content law determines its predicted outcomes. A transition
on agent states must still specify how an outcome is registered and how the agent changes. A
predictive likelihood and an internal update thus have different domains.

1.4 Beliefs and generative models

An agent holds beliefs and generative models. The joint law i describes the first; the second is the
mechanism that gives a model presentation predictive content.

Definition 1.10 (Generative model of an agent). At a fixed context, a generative model of agent i
consists of a proper reference law ri on Mi, a normalized evaluator Gi : Mi  Ki, and a normalized
record kernel i : Ki × Mi  Oi. They define the normalized joint

Pi(dm, dk, do) = ri(dm)Gi(m, dk)i(k, m; do).                    (1.14)

Each presentation m indexes the generative model Gi(m, dk)i(k, m; do): a prior over represented
contents together with a likelihood for records. The reference ri is the prior over presentations.
When i does not depend on m, it is the record kernel Hi of chapter 5.

Given a record value o at which a declared density of i yields 0 < Pi(o) < , the recognition law
i is a candidate for the posterior Pi(dm, dk | o), and

Fi(i; o) = DKL (iPi(· | o)) - log Pi(o)                         (1.15)

is its variational free energy [18, 59]. In this reading qi is the agent's belief about represented
contents, its perception, and si is its belief over generative models. The model law alone predicts
nothing: by eq. (1.14), prediction requires the evaluator and the record kernel. An evaluator that
does not depend on m makes the model sector predictively inert. Without records, the unique
minimizer of DKL(iriGi) is the reference joint itself, whose belief conditional qi(dk | m) equals
the evaluator Gi(m, dk); the conditional in eq. (1.3) is the agent's current departure from that prior.

Definition 1.11 (Shared generative model). Agents i and j share a generative model up to frame
if Mi = Mj, Ki = Kj, Oi = Oj, and there are bimeasurable bijections  of Mi and  of Ki with

rj = #ri, Gj((m), ·) = #Gi(m, ·), j((k), (m); ·) = i(k, m; ·).  (1.16)

A population whose members pairwise share a generative model is called a species.

Sharing a generative model is a statement about mechanisms. Agreement of beliefs over models,
DKL(sj#si) = 0, is a statement about states. The two are independent. Agents with a shared
model can hold different beliefs, and equal beliefs over presentations predict equal records only
when the evaluators and record kernels agree as in eq. (1.16) and the agents condition on the same
information. A record registered by one agent changes its posterior, and therefore its predictions,
without changing those of an agent that did not register it.

The free energy eq. (1.15) is a single-agent object. Interactions add a further choice. In one choice
all agents are parts of one normalized joint over their contents and records. In another each agent's
generative model treats the communicated laws of its peers as data. Chapter 4 develops both
choices and a third, a direct interaction potential between laws, and proves that the third is not the
free energy of any fixed normalized model in which the agent laws are recognition laws.

1. Agents, Possibilities, and Records                MAgent Theory 2.0

1.5 Content laws on fields

The global choice needs a joint law over the contents of all agents and, where contexts are
compared, over contents at different contexts. Write Ei = P ×G Yi for the associated sample
bundle. A point [u, ] of Bi at c is identified with the law (y  [u, y])# on the fiber of Ei at c; this
identification does not depend on the representative.

Definition 1.12 (Content law on fields). A content model consists of a standard Borel coefficient

space Z, a proper prior P0 on Z, and jointly measurable sample-section maps fi : Z × Ui  Ei with

fi(z, c) in the fiber over c. For a recognition law Q on Z, the agent sections and finite-design laws

are

     iQ(c) = (fi,c)#Q,                 QD = (FD)#Q,  FD(z) = fi(z, c) (i,c)D,  (1.17)

where fi,c = fi(·, c) and D is a finite set of pairs with c  Ui. A record mechanism is a normalized
kernel Ka(doa | z) that may read field evaluations, model presentations, communication maps,
and parallel transports along declared paths. A record kernel must be specified through bundle
points, equivalently it must transform with every fiber datum it reads. With conditionally independent
records, P(dz, do) = P0(dz) a Ka(doa | z).

Proposition 1.13 (Consistency and projected free energy). For D  D let rDD delete the
added coordinates. Then (rDD)#QD = QD, and the marginal of QD at (i, c) is iQ(c). For a record

value with likelihood o and posterior o as in eq. (4.18), and whenever the free energy is finite,

   F (Q; o) = DKL(QD(FD)#o) - log Zo + DKL Q(dz | FD = w)o(dz | FD = w) QD(dw).
                                                                                                                          (1.18)

Proof. Since FD = rDD  FD, pushforwards compose, which gives consistency, and the marginal
statement is the case of one pair. The second identity is the chain rule for relative entropy applied
to Q and o disintegrated along the measurable map FD, which is the deterministic-kernel case of
theorem 5.1, combined with F (Q; o) = DKL(Qo) - log Zo.

The last term of eq. (1.18) is the exact cost of the information that a finite description omits. It need
not vanish even when D contains every evaluation the records read, because recognition can have
the wrong conditional law in unobserved directions. The law-valued configuration of the agents at
the contexts in D is the list of marginals of QD; it does not determine QD. The reciprocal potential
of chapter 4 is a separate constitutive object defined on such lists, and proposition 4.21 shows that
it is not F(Q; o) for any fixed normalized model with these marginals as recognition laws.

1.6 What correlations describe

Suppose two represented bits have the independent uniform law. Register the event that they
agree. Their conditional joint law assigns probability 1/2 to each of (0, 0) and (1, 1). Each marginal
remains uniform, while the conditional expectation of their product changes from 1/4 to 1/2. An
exact joint posterior has acquired dependence that its two marginals cannot report.

                                       8
1. Agents, Possibilities, and Records     MAgent Theory 2.0

This example identifies a concrete need for a joint law: predicting an observable that reads both bits
after the shared record. It does not imply that every admissible agent dynamics must propagate
that posterior. A coupled product-family dynamics is another precise model, provided it is declared,
but it does not preserve the marginal symmetry. Against the hard agreement record, a product
recognition law has finite free energy only when it is a point mass on (0, 0) or on (1, 1), at relative
entropy log 2 from the posterior. For a soft record   eJ12 in spin variables, the symmetric
product optimum has magnetization solving m = tanh(Jm), which is zero for J  1 and nonzero
for J > 1. Similarly, two routes that inspect the same source must share its identity; replacing it by
independent redraws specifies a different experiment.

The same distinction governs what a comparison of laws can detect along a loop of routes.

Proposition 1.14 (Law comparisons and shared samples). Let H, H be bimeasurable bijections
of a standard Borel space E, for example two loop transports, and let   P(E).

   (i) If H# = H# , every functional of the pair of laws (, H#) takes the same value for H and
       H. In particular DKL(H#) = 0 exactly when H preserves .

   (ii) The law (id, H)# of the shared-sample pair (Y, HY ), Y  , determines H up to -null sets.

Proof. Part (i) is immediate because the pair of laws is the same. For (ii), suppose (id, H)# =
(id, H)#. The complement of the graph of H is a Borel set B. Its measure under the first law is
{H = H} and under the second law is zero.

Every interaction cost of chapters 2 and 4 compares laws, so the dynamics defined there cannot
respond to a loop transport that lies in the stabilizer of the transported law. A rotation by a fixed
angle, for instance, leaves an isotropic Gaussian law unchanged. A record that is sensitive to
such a transport must read a coupling of the same sample along the routes, as the route mark
of the supplement does; under a frame change g at the base point the pair transforms diagonally,
(Y, HY )  (gY, gHg-1gY ), so invariant records are diagonal-invariant functions of the pair. Such
records require a content law in the sense of definition 1.12.

The configuration x of law-valued agents, a sample tuple (ki, mi)i used in a probabilistic model,
and an ensemble of possible configurations are three different objects. A deterministic dynamics
on x needs no probability law over configurations. A preparation ensemble can be introduced to
assess predictions or compression, but it is then stated explicitly. These distinctions will matter
when a parent retains a law over contents while discarding information needed to evolve that law.

Chapter 2

Law-Dependent Interactions

An interaction compares or transmits information between agents. Its law may depend on the
agents' current statistical states. The general object is a normalized Markov channel between
represented spaces; exponential links of matrix generators are one constitutive example of such a
channel, not the definition of an interaction. Gauge covariance specifies how this dependence is
represented when coordinates change; it does not require the interaction to be a frame identification
or select a unique mechanism. We first construct these interactions at one context. Transport
between different contexts is a separate datum, whose transformation law is recorded in appendix D.

2.1 Two sectors and their comparison spaces

Fix a context c and a finite set of agents defined there. Write

                 iq = qi,      is = si,                                             (2.1)

for the belief and model marginals of agent i. The sector index a takes values in {q, s}. These laws
live on standard Borel spaces Eia. No product assumption between the two sectors, or between
different agents, is required to define an interaction between their marginals. Such a product is a
separate choice when a joint recognition law is needed.

In a vector realization choose reference spaces Vq, Vs and invertible presentation maps

Uia : Va - Eia,  q¯i = (Uiq)#-1qi,                               s¯i = (Uis)-#1si.  (2.2)

We also write ¯ia = (Uia)-#1ia and ¯a = (¯ia)i for the tuple of reference laws in sector a. Here Eia is
agent i's displayed coordinate copy of Va. At a common context all agents' statistical sections take
values in one fiber of the bundle of eq. (1.2); the per-agent presentations are points of the frame

torsor at that context, used to display each agent's law, and are not separate fibers. One structure

group G acts through the representations q, s of eq. (1.1), so a passive change at agent i is a
single element gi, with gia = a(gi). Independent sector changes would require the product group
Gq × Gs, which the theory does not use; the collective connection of proposition 3.9 depends on
this choice, because the group enters its normal equation. The two presentations do not identify

the belief and model interaction maps. Their domains, parameters, and dependence on the laws

remain separately specified.

A passive re-expression yi = giayi sends ia to (gia)#ia and Uia to giaUia. Therefore the reference
laws in eq. (2.2) are unchanged. A common reference change Uia  Uiaha instead sends every
reference law to (h-a 1)#¯ia. The first operation changes an agent's displayed coordinates; the
second changes the common coordinates in which interaction parameters are written.

                           10
2. Law-Dependent Interactions                                       MAgent Theory 2.0

Definition 2.1 (Normalized interaction channel). Let S be the standard Borel configuration space
of chapter 1. A sector channel from source j to receiver i is a Markov kernel

                               Kiaj : S × Eja  Eia,                 (2.3)

that is, (x, y)  Kiaj[x](y, A) is jointly measurable for every measurable A and is a probability
measure in A. At configuration x it sends a law to (jaKiaj[x])(A) = Kiaj[x](y, A)ja(dy). When the

channel does not depend on the configuration we omit x. Covariance requires

                               Kiaj(gjay, A) = Kiaj(y, (gia)-1A).   (2.4)

Composition of sending, transmission, and receiving kernels produces another normalized channel
by iterated integration. Invertibility is not required. Alternatively, two channels can send the receiver
and source laws into a common message space, where their communicated predictions are
compared. The primitive self channel Kiai is constitutive data. The identity channel is one choice;
later constructions may declare a nonidentity self channel, and they state which.

Joint measurability makes x  jaKiaj[x] a measurable map into P(Eia) by a monotone-class
argument, so the divergences, rows, and potentials built from these channels in chapter 4 are
measurable functions of the configuration.

Proposition 2.2 (Covariant law comparison). Under eq. (2.4), the divergence

                               Diaj = DKL(iajaKiaj ),               (2.5)

is unchanged by passive bimeasurable coordinate changes, including when its value is infinite.

Proof. Changing the integration variable in the kernel gives jaKiaj = (gia)#(jaKiaj). For any
bimeasurable bijection g, absolute continuity is preserved and the transformed Radon­Nikodym
derivative is (dµ/d)  g-1. Its logarithmic integral is therefore unchanged. Failure of absolute

continuity is also preserved, giving infinity on both sides.

This is the coordinate invariance of relative entropy [89]. It makes the comparison intrinsic without
asserting that either law is a posterior under a fixed population model.

2.2 Reference consistency

Per-agent covariance is automatic for any rule written in reference coordinates. If a channel is

specified by a reference kernel K¯iaj : Va  Va and displayed as Kiaj(y, A) = K¯iaj((Uja)-1y, (Uia)-1A),
then eq. (2.4) holds identically, and proposition 1.5 with f = (Uia)-1 gives

                               DKL(iajaKiaj ) = DKL(¯ia¯jaK¯iaj ).  (2.6)

The frames therefore act as a dressing field, as stated after eq. (1.6): per-agent covariance
constrains no reference rule. The substantive symmetry requirement concerns the common
reference change.

                               11
2. Law-Dependent Interactions                                        MAgent Theory 2.0

Hypothesis 2.3 (Reference consistency). A reference rule is reference consistent if, for every
common reference change ha in the declared structure group, re-expressing all reference laws and
supplied interface data leaves the displayed channel unchanged. For a reference kernel this means

        K¯iaj (ha-1)#¯a (h-a 1v, h-a 1B) = K¯iaj[¯a](v, B),                               (2.7)

and for the exponential generators below it is eq. (2.13). Without it, a displayed interaction depends
on the choice of reference point in the frame torsor and is not a function of the bundle data; on a
nontrivial principal bundle no global choice of that point exists. Every result below whose conclusion
concerns bundle data, rather than one fixed reference presentation, assumes reference consistency
and says so.

2.3 Exponential links: one constitutive example

Choose a message space Ha and reference interfaces

                               Tja : Va - Ha,        Oia : Ha - Va.                       (2.8)

Their direct content map is Miaj = UiaOiaTja(Uja)-1. A deterministic channel can push the entire law
through this map even when the image is lower dimensional. A density formula for a nonsingular law

cannot then be used on the original ambient space without accounting for that change of support.

Definition 2.4 (Law-dependent reference generator). Let Laij be a measurable function of the
tuple of reference laws ¯a, and of any explicitly declared interface data, with values in End(Va).

Define

        Liaj = Liaj (¯a),      aij = Uia exp(Liaj )(Uja)-1.                               (2.9)

Dependence on the two endpoint laws alone is the special case Liaj(¯ia, ¯ja). For a receiving­
sending factorization, Laij = Oia(¯a)Tja(¯a), provided both maps refer to the same Ha and Va. The
associated deterministic channel is Kiaj(y, ·) = aijy, which is an instance of definition 2.1. For
exponential links the primitive self link is the identity, Liai = 0.

The exponential is taken on the reference endomorphism, not on a map with different domain and

codomain. Its values lie in exp(gl(Va)), which is contained in the identity component GL+(Va) and,

for dim Va  2, is a proper subset of it: the matrix  -1 1   has determinant one and no real
                                                      0 -1

logarithm, because its single Jordan block for a negative eigenvalue occurs an odd number of times

[39]. Orientation-reversing and discrete interactions are therefore not exponential links, although

they are channels in the sense of definition 2.1. A smaller group acting on the frames can still

re-express exponential links covariantly. Interpreting them as parallel transports of a connection for

that smaller group would additionally require generators in its represented Lie algebra.

Definition 2.5 (Group-valued links). Let g be the Lie algebra of G, and identify frames with
elements Ui  G as in eq. (1.6). Group-valued links assign to each directed edge j  i a belief
generator ij  g and a model generator ~ij  g, either of which may depend on the laws as in

definition 2.4, and set

ij = Ui exp(ij)Uj-1,           ~ij = Ui exp(~ij)Uj-1,  iqj = q(ij ),        sij = s(~ij). (2.10)

The reference generators of eq. (2.9) are then Liqj = dq(ij) and Lsij = ds(~ij). The links are tied
when ij = ~ij, that is, when one G-valued link acts on both sectors through the two representations.

Opposite edges remain independent: ji is not required to equal i-j1, in either sector.

Proposition 2.6 (The sector mismatch is covariant). Under a passive change Ui  giUi at

Proof. The reference generators are unchanged by a passive change, so ij = giUi exp(ij)Uj-1gj-1 =
giijgj-1, and likewise for ~ij. Then ij = gi~ijgj-1gji-j1gi-1 = giijgi-1.

The general theory keeps both link fields. Results that use one G-valued link for both sectors state
the tied hypothesis ij = e. Because ij is covariant, a nonzero mismatch is a frame-independent
property of the interaction: the belief and model transports along the edge disagree.

                               iaj = giaiaj (gja)-1,                        (2.12)

Proposition 2.8 (Low-rank generator and invertible transport). For finite matrices O : H  V
and T : V  H, the map OT has rank at most dim H, whereas eOT is invertible. Moreover,

                         eOT v = v (v  ker T ), im(eOT - I)  im O.          (2.14)

                               13
2. Law-Dependent Interactions                                                  MAgent Theory 2.0

Proof. The rank statement follows from factorization. The exponential series and eOT e-OT = I
prove invertibility. Every positive power of OT vanishes on ker T , and every such power has image
in im O. Summing the convergent series proves the remaining assertions.

Thus the exponential link retains an identity action in unread directions. It is a different operation
from sending only the selective content OT v. Because the link is invertible, proposition 1.5 gives
DKL(i(ij)#j) = DKL((-ij1)#ij): an exponential link of a low-rank generator compares
complete laws and discards nothing. Information-discarding, or selective, channels are noninvertible
kernels of definition 2.1. The identity self-link also differs from a coarse internal loop: a parent may
retain nonidentity loop information inherited from several child interactions.

2.4 An explicit constitutive family for general laws

The preceding definition does not select the functional L. The following choice shows that noncon-
stant, reference-consistent generators can depend directly on laws without restricting them to a
Gaussian family.

Definition 2.9 (Moment-dependent receiving and sending). For each sector let Va = Rda and

           Laij = aij OiaTja,  Oia(t) = µai t,  Tja(v) = (µja)T (ja)-1v.                   (2.15)

coefficient is constitutive data, not a consequence of covariance.

Proof. Under Uia  Uiaha, the moments become µai  = ha-1µia and aj  = h-a 1aj ha-T . Consequently

                               (µja)T (aj )-1 = (µaj )T (ja)-1ha.                          (2.16)

No fixed Euclidean metric was inserted into this comparison: the source covariance supplies the
inverse bilinear form and transforms with the law. Finite moments and invertible covariance are
assumptions of this example alone. Centered laws give zero generators in this family, so it does not
encode all distinctions between laws.

For a non-Gaussian example in two dimensions, take independent centered Laplace coordinates
of variance one and translate their joint law to means e1 and e2 for two agents. Both covariances
equal I. With identity frames and unit edge coefficients,

2.5 Loops, reciprocity, and what a law-level cost can see

Opposite attending edges are independent constitutive choices. In particular, ji need not equal
-ij1, as eq. (2.17) demonstrates. Geometric reversal of the same transport is instead its inverse.
Endpoint covariance and conjugation of loop products are the familiar transformation laws of lattice
link variables [144], here holding in display coordinates only; neither imposes an inverse relation
between two independently modeled interactions. Directed non-inverse links at one context form a
representation of the interaction quiver. Under independent changes at each vertex its polynomial
invariants are generated by traces of products along oriented cycles [94]. Under the common
reference change alone, the group is one copy of GL(Va) acting by simultaneous conjugation on all
reference links, and the invariants include traces of arbitrary words in those links [123], for example
tr(eL12eL34), which is not a path product.

Proposition 2.11 (Reciprocal and backtrack parts of a directed pair). Let ij and ji be
invertible links of one sector, and suppose the backtrack loop Nj = jiij at j has no eigenvalue
in (-, 0]. With the principal square root, put

                               ij = ij Nj-1/2,      ij = ij Nj1/2.                   (2.18)

Then ji = i-j1, and under passive endpoint changes ij = giijgj-1 and Nj = gjNjgj-1.

Proof. The loop Ni = ijji = ijNj-ij1 is similar to Nj, so it also has no eigenvalue in
(-, 0]. For a primary matrix function f defined on the common spectrum of AB and BA,
Bf (AB) = f (BA)B [76, Chapter 1]. With A = ij, B = ji and f (z) = z-1/2,

                     jiij = jiNi-1/2ij Nj-1/2 = Nj-1/2jiij Nj-1/2 = I.               (2.19)

For the transformation law, Nj = gjNjgj-1 by eq. (2.12), and the principal square root commutes
with similarity, so (Nj)-1/2 = gjNj-1/2gj-1.

The reciprocal parts  form a representation in which reversal is inversion, as for the transport of
appendix D, while Nj records nonreciprocity. When ji = Tij, eq. (2.18) is the polar decomposition.

In eq. (2.17), N2 =  11        is positive definite and 12 = 5-1/2   2  1  is a rotation. The

the reciprocal parts on cycles of length at least three can carry reciprocal holonomy.

2.6 Dependence, direction, and inherited responses

Covariance constrains which law-only generators are possible. If a reference transformation fixes
all input laws and all supplied data, eq. (2.13) requires its matrix to commute with the resulting
generator. Identical centered laws invariant under every orthogonal transformation therefore cannot
select a distinguished off-diagonal direction through a fully orthogonally equivariant law-only rule.
Directional interfaces can carry additional information, but that information must be declared.

                                                                16
2. Law-Dependent Interactions                                   MAgent Theory 2.0

When links depend on the current laws, differentiation must include that dependence. At fixed
frames a variation of an objective has the form

                               dE = d E + dLiaj E, DLaij[d¯a].  (2.21)

                                                     a,i,j

This statement uses a differentiable statistical family and differentiable constitutive maps. It includes
both the sender and receiver occurrences, and every other law on which the generator depends.
Freezing the link during an update defines another declared dynamics; it is not generally the
derivative of the substituted objective. Nor does substituting live recognition laws into a likelihood
make that likelihood part of a fixed generative model during recognition variation.

An inherited parent's state must determine its future boundary response, including the law depen-
dence of its generators. If two child configurations with identical retained data give different future
responses, those data do not support autonomous closure.

Chapter 3

Geometry of Statistical Sections

A section's statistical change induces contextual geometry relative to a connection. We construct
that tensor, a collective rule for choosing the connection, and conditions for their inheritance.

The role of these objects in the rest of the manuscript is limited and should be stated at the outset.
No vector field, source row, channel, or record kernel in chapter 4 through chapter 13 depends
on a connection, on the collective connection selected below, or on their curvature; each context
evolves by a context-local flow. The formation chapters compute connections, pullback tensors,
and curvature as diagnostics of those evolved sections. The separate construction in chapter 16
adds the minimized contextual energy to the reciprocal potential and proves local well-posedness
for finite graphs and a regular periodic continuum chart. The remaining extensions are recorded in
open problem 3.11.

3.1 Regular law families

Definition 3.1 (Fisher geometry on an admitted family). Let N be a finite-dimensional smooth

manifold of probability laws on a standard Borel space Y. In each parameter chart   P, assume
differentiability in quadratic mean with centered square-integrable score  : Y  Rd. At a fixed ,
this means that the Lebesgue decomposition P+ = pP + P satisfies

P(Y) = o(||2),                  -  1  -  1               = o(||).  (3.1)
                             p           2
                                                 L2 (P )

For a tangent vector v, its scalar score v is the corresponding directional derivative in this expansion.

Require the Fisher tensor

                           gPF (v, w) = EP [vw]                    (3.2)

to be smooth and positive definite on the admitted tangent space. Redundant parameter directions
must be removed or treated as null directions before imposing this last requirement.

Condition eq. (3.1) is Le Cam's differentiability in quadratic mean [95]. These family-specific
hypotheses allow parameter-dependent supports: the laws of the family need not share null sets,
and no common positive density is required [6]. A finite-dimensional family satisfying eq. (3.1)
is nevertheless dominated. Differentiability in quadratic mean makes   P continuous in total
variation, and for a countable dense set {n} the mixture n 2-nPn dominates every P. The
choice of the Fisher tensor is not arbitrary: up to a constant factor it is the only Riemannian metric
on finite statistical simplices invariant under Markov congruent embeddings [28], with extensions
to general sample spaces under the hypotheses of Ay et al. [5]. That characterization concerns
the metric on one law space; it does not fix the relative weights of separate factors, which remain
constitutive below.

Proposition 3.2 (Fisher metric of the joint agent law). Let (dk, dm) = q(dk | m)s(dm) be

3.3 Null directions and quotients

Proposition 3.6 (Rank and quotient geometry). For the positive fiber Fisher metric in defini-

tion 3.1,

           rad h = ker D, rank h = rank D.                           (3.15)

If the latter rank is constant, K = ker D is a smooth subbundle and T U/K carries the positive-
definite metric h¯([X], [Y ]) = h(X, Y ).

Proof. The diagonal value of h is the squared Fisher norm of DX, so it vanishes exactly on the
derivative's kernel. For a positive semidefinite form, its diagonal null set is its radical. Rank-nullity
gives the second identity, and the constant-rank theorem for bundle maps makes K a smooth
subbundle. The pairing is independent of representatives because it annihilates K, and it is positive
on every nonzero quotient class.

A quotient vector bundle is not automatically the tangent bundle of a quotient manifold. Suppose
a smooth Hausdorff manifold U¯ and a surjective submersion q : U  U¯ with connected fibers
satisfy ker T q = K. The tensor descends to U¯ exactly when it is basic: besides annihilating K, it
obeys LZh = 0 for every vertical field Z  (K). Necessity follows by differentiating a pulled-back
tensor along a fiber. For sufficiency, use submersion coordinates (y, z): the annihilation condition
leaves only dyadyb components, and the Lie derivatives in the z directions make their coefficients
independent of z. Connected fibers make these local definitions agree across each fiber. The
resulting tensor is positive definite by eq. (3.15). A basic semidefinite tensor of this kind is a
bundle-like transverse metric for the foliation by the fibers [108, 124].

Integrability of the radical and basicness are both measured by the curvature. In a local frame
write V = DAp, j(p, ) = Jp, dpj for its derivative in p in a chart of N , and F = dA + [A  A] with
[A  A](X, Y ) = [A(X), A(Y )].

and eq. (3.16) reduces to V ([X, Y ]) = -JpF (X, Y ), which proves the involutivity criterion.

For eq. (3.17), write (LZh)(X, Y ) = Z(gp(V X, V Y )) - h([Z, X], Y ) - h(X, [Z, Y ]), expand the first
term with dp(Z) = -JpA(Z), and insert eq. (3.16) with V Z = 0. The terms containing  = A(Z)
combine into -(LgF )(V X, V Y ), the Lie derivative of the Fisher metric along the fundamental
field of , which vanishes because the action is isometric. The curvature terms remain. If F = 0,
both right sides vanish.

The criteria are sharp. On the trivial translation bundle over R3, use the unit-variance normal

location family, the constant section of mean zero, and A = dz - xdy. Its location Fisher metric is

one, so

         DAp = dz - xdy, hAp = (dz - xdy)2.                             (3.18)

This has constant rank one, but its null fields x and y + xz have bracket z, which is not null.
Here F = -dx  dy and V ([x, y + xz]) = 1 = -F (x, y + xz), as eq. (3.16) requires. The
connection in this example is supplied, not selected: for a single location family under translations
the minimizing connection of proposition 3.9 makes the tensor vanish, and proposition 3.10 shows
that the minimal tensor always has an involutive radical. Gaussian laws are not required for the
preceding results.

A contextual tangent quotient differs from a group-orbit quotient or measurable parent retention,
which may discard information having no Fisher tangent.

3.4 A collective choice of connection

Several law sections can determine a common comparison rule by minimizing their shared frame

Proposition 3.9 (Collective minimizing connection class). Suppose Jp(c) has constant rank on

Proof. Project -dp(X) orthogonally onto im J. Its preimages under J give all minimizing a, and

to residuals.

If infinitesimal isotropy is nonzero, the construction leaves stabilizer-valued components undeter-
mined. An arbitrarily chosen pseudoinverse representative need not obey the affine law. Global
minimizing representatives nevertheless exist on any paracompact domain of constant rank. Being
minimizing at c is a frame-independent property of a connection, and at each c the minimizing
values form an affine subspace. Given local minimizing connections  and a subordinate partition
of unity , the connection   is an affine combination of minimizers at every point and is

therefore minimizing. What requires ker J = 0 is uniqueness: then the local forms are unique, obey
the affine law, and agree on overlaps; discrete stabilizers do not obstruct this. Curvature statements
about a class should be made for JpF on the radical, which by eq. (3.16) is the same for every
representative, or after a representative has been fixed, since the full curvature depends on that
choice.

The collective construction is therefore classical. The minimizing connection is the mechanical
connection of Smale [134], the orthogonal separation of rotations from shape change studied for
molecules by Guichardet [70] and as a gauge field of the n-body problem by Littlejohn and Reinsch

pullback of the quotient metric of the Riemannian submersion onto shape space [114]. What is new
here is the use of the Fisher metric of the declared collective family as the kinetic metric. Rank is
bounded by the shape dimension, rank hmin  dim H = dim N n - dim(orbit). A single transitive
family has H = 0 and zero minimizing residual; a collective family need not.

The constant-rank hypothesis fails where infinitesimal isotropy increases. Agreement need not

cause such an increase: any number of unit-covariance planar normal laws with common nonzero

mean e1 has a free diagonal SO(2) action and positive locked inertia. If the infinitesimal stabilizer

does increase, the rank of J drops; a smooth extension of the minimizing Lie-algebra-valued

representative is then not guaranteed [99]. For example, let SO(2) act on the unit-covariance

normal family on R2 and take the section µ(c) = (, c) for one agent. Then J = (-c, ), k = c2 + 2,

The constant weights wi in definition 3.8 have a probabilistic reading. With i wi = 1, the weighted

on samples and not on labels, so the weight scores have zero Fisher pairing with every orbit
direction; the normal equation is unchanged and hmin gains that connection-independent term.
A correlated population law, whose Fisher metric sees dependence directions invisible to every
marginal (proposition 3.2), is not of this weighted product form and is not treated here.

Open problem 3.11 (Extensions of the contextual Fisher flow). Chapter 16 supplies a finite-
graph construction and a continuum local theorem on a flat torus. Auxiliary elimination diffuses the
law shape and leaves frame and source-row equations without independent diffusion. Global regu-
larity, changes of orbit type, physical boundaries, independently evolving rows and communication
links, and a graph-refinement theorem remain open. The quotient target can be open and positively
curved, so the local theorem alone gives no global continuation. Deriving a kinetic term for the
connection from a declared ensemble of contextual sections is a separate problem; that ensemble
is not supplied.

Set the fraction to zero where its numerator and denominator both vanish. It tends to zero in

probability. Moreover v/||2 is uniformly integrable as   0: the square-root expansion expresses
(V -1)/|| as a bounded finite-dimensional combination of the fixed L2 scores plus an L2 remainder

This score-projection mechanism is the one in Pollard [121, Theorem 7]; the Markov formulation
is also treated in Ay et al. [6]. It identifies local score sufficiency. It does not identify a kernel
recovering every law in the experiment; that an insufficient statistic can preserve Fisher information
is the phenomenon of Kagan and Shepp [81]. For example, take independent Bernoulli variables
with probabilities 1/2 + /4 and 1/2 + 2/4, and discard the second. At  = 0 its score vanishes, so
no Fisher information is lost. A fixed recovery kernel applied to the first Bernoulli law makes every
reconstructed event probability affine in , whereas the required second-coordinate probability is
quadratic. Such a kernel cannot recover the family on a neighborhood.

Proposition 3.14 (Moving-channel correction). Let the channel instead have density k(y¯ | y)

Consequently input-to-output Fisher change has no fixed sign for a moving channel. A constant input
followed by a Bernoulli output with success probability (1 + e-)-1 has zero input Fisher information

channel log density at all. Its actual weak derivative, schematically d(P K) = (dP )K + P (dK) when
these derivatives exist, must replace that expression. These distinctions apply to the law-dependent
channels used in the interaction potential.

Chapter 4

Free Energies and Coupled Dynamics of
Agent Laws

Interacting agents can be given three different objectives, and this chapter keeps them apart. In
the global picture all agents are parts of one normalized joint over their contents and records, and
each agent's local free energy is that global free energy viewed as a function of its own recognition
factor. In the per-agent picture each agent has its own normalized generative model in the sense of
definition 1.10, in which its own evaluator and the communicated laws of its peers are competing
sources of prior information. The third object is a direct interaction potential between laws, specified
without an observation likelihood. Its gradient flow moves each source toward the receivers that
attend to it. We first develop this reciprocal potential, its source rows, and its Fisher dynamics,
because the constructions of chapter 7 to chapter 13 use it. We then give the two free energies
and prove that the reciprocal potential is not the free energy of any fixed normalized model in which
the agent laws are recognition laws.

4.1 A potential for the two interacting sectors

Fix a context and a finite set of agents. Agent i has state and model spaces Ki, Mi, both standard
Borel. In this chapter its joint law is restricted explicitly to i = qi  si. Choose a proper model
reference ri and a normalized evaluator Gi : Mi  Ki. The reference joint is

Ri(dk, dm) = ri(dm)Gi(m, dk),  E0 = DKL(qi  siRi).  (4.1)

                                          i

The evaluator couples the sectors even though their recognition law is a product. Where the terms
are finite, disintegration gives

DKL(qi  siRi) = DKL(siri) + DKL(qiGi(m, ·))si(dm).  (4.2)

This is a conditional relative-entropy identity: the model marginal contributes the first term and the
state conditional contributes the second. In particular, the expectation of a log evaluator in this
objective is different from the log of the predictive mixture siGi.

Remark 4.1 (What the product restriction removes). Over unrestricted joint laws the unique
minimizer of DKL(iRi) is i = Ri, whose belief conditional is the evaluator. Under the
product restriction and an evaluator density gi, the belief minimizer at fixed si is instead
qi  exp log gi(m, ·)si(dm), which differs from the model prediction siGi. The restriction
therefore carries part of the distinction between belief and model. It is also not invariant under the

30
4. Free Energies and Coupled Dynamics of Agent Laws                     MAgent Theory 2.0

joint-law dynamics. For binary k, m  {-1, 1}, let the joint Fisher flow be t log i = -(h - Eih)
with h(k, m) = log(i/Ri)(k, m) + hq(k) + hs(m), where the peer terms hq, hs depend only on the

marginals. The additive terms cancel in the log odds ratio LOR() = k,m km log (k, m), so
t LOR(i) = -(LOR(i) - LOR(Ri)). Dependence between the sectors is generated at unit rate

whenever Ri is not a product. The product flow used below is the restriction of the dynamics to the

product family, not a consequence of it.

Let q = (qi)i and s = (si)i. For each allowed directed edge j  i, choose normalized channels
Kiqj[q] : Kj  Ki and Kisj[s] : Mj  Mi. Their dependence on the laws is part of the specified
interaction. A law-dependent channel is required to be a kernel Kiqj : S × Kj  Ki, jointly in the
configuration and the source value, and likewise in the model sector. Then x  iqj(x) is Borel by a

monotone-class argument, relative entropy is Borel on pairs of laws through its supremum over

finite partitions from a countable generating algebra [68], and the costs, Gibbs rows, and reduced

potential below are Borel functions of the configuration, as proposition 1.8 and the record appendix

require. Define

                 iqj = qj Kiqj [q], Diqj = DKL(qiiqj ),                 (4.3)
                 isj = sj Kisj [s], Disj = DKL(siisj ).

The source sets Niq, Nis are finite and nonempty, with positive normalized reference rows iq, is.
Belief routing uses i and model routing uses i on their respective sets.

Definition 4.2 (Reciprocal law potential). For fixed Tq, Ts > 0, set

The reference laws, evaluators, source priors, and temperatures are held fixed in the variations
below. The admissible domain consists of laws for which all displayed divergences are finite.

This potential is a constitutive choice at the level of agent laws. No distribution over these law
configurations is required to define it. It contains no record; records enter its dynamics only
through the assimilation events of definition 4.24. Its gradient is reciprocal: a law that serves as
a source appears in the cost of every receiver that attends to it, so the flow moves sources as
well as receivers (section 4.3). Section 4.6 gives the per-agent alternative in which peers' laws
are data, and proposition 4.21 shows that this potential is not a global variational free energy.
General probability laws enter eq. (4.4); differentiability will require stronger hypotheses. An identity
self-channel has Diqi = 0 throughout its domain, with the same convention in the model sector.
Independent opposite attending edges remain independent data.

The receiver side of eq. (4.4) is a pooling rule. With the other agents, rows, and channels
frozen, and with the appearances of qi as a source ignored, stationarity of qi gives log qi =
(1+ j ij)-1 log gi(m, ·)si(dm)+ j ij log iqj +const, a logarithmic opinion pool of the evaluator
and the compared laws [1, 63]. Iterated relative-entropy averaging over a network is the consensus

scheme of Battistelli and Chisci [12], with DeGroot [44] as its linear antecedent. The source side,

The correlated local inference of section 5.2 and proposition B.2 makes a different use of the same
generative-model definition: it conditions a declared joint exactly before any output projection. Its
component evidence weights and finite conditioning step do not identify it with the product-family
population flow considered here.

4.3 The derivative includes every interaction role

To display the variation, choose densities against fixed references on a regular dominated family.
Write a for the density of a receiver law and b for that of its compared law. For mass-preserving
variations and justified differentiation under the integrals,

                                dDKL(ab) = log(a/b)da - (a/b)db.                       (4.10)

Here the notation f da denotes integration against the signed variation of the law, rather than
differentiation of the sample coordinate. The formula follows by differentiating a log(a/b); the
additional integral of da is zero.

For a belief interaction the compared-law variation is

                                diqj = (dqj)Kiqj[q] + qjDKiqj[q](dq).                  (4.11)

The second term differentiates the prescribed channel itself. Thus an agent contributes when it is a
receiver, when it is a source, and whenever its law changes a channel elsewhere. For fixed discrete
kernels, the incoming contribution from j  i to a variation at source value v is

                                -ij     qi(u)        Kiqj  (v,                    u).  (4.12)
                                        iqj (u)

The model sector has the same expression with q,  replaced by s, . If the channels are constructed
from law-dependent moments or generators, eq. (4.11) also differentiates those moments and
generators. Keeping their numerical values fixed computes a different vector field.

An identity self-channel illustrates why the variable identification matters. Here a = b and da = db, so
eq. (4.10) is zero throughout the state space. Freezing the source as an old snapshot while moving
the receiver replaces this zero functional by a divergence from that snapshot. Its first derivative

                                        33
4. Free Energies and Coupled Dynamics of Agent Laws                     MAgent Theory 2.0

still vanishes at equality, but its curvature and its force after displacement differ. More generally,
directed source selection does not make the gradient of eq. (4.4) one-way: a source appears in the
energy of every row that attends to it. Each directed edge j  i therefore carries influence in both
directions. The force on the source is the receiver likelihood ratio qi/iqj pulled back through the
adjoint of the channel, so it is supported on what the channel reads; for a deterministic readout T it
is a function of T (v), and only the message marginal of the source moves. The communication
model of chapter 5 sends messages from source to receiver only. A population of communicating
agents realizes the reciprocal flow only if this reverse message is also modeled; otherwise each
source must be able to read the laws of every receiver that attends to it. Every agent descends
the same total E, so the population plays an identical-interest game in the sense of Monderer and
Shapley [109]. Section 4.6 shows what is lost when each agent descends only its own objective.

In a Gaussian covariance sector with identity channel, the source force on the variance vj from

source more confident than its receivers' spread is widened.

4.4 Fisher dynamics with equal mobilities

The kinetic metric in this chapter uses its declared product recognition family. It is the product
specialization of proposition 3.2, with separate Fisher blocks for the source rows. The contextual
tensor in definition 3.3 instead evaluates changes along the base through a connection; it does not
replace the vertical metric used for inference at a fixed context.

All blocks have unit mobility, and proposition 4.8 shows its price: under unit mobility, log-odds
contrasts within a row relax at rate exactly T , so rows that select sharply are slow. Exact Gibbs
rows are the singular limit of infinite row mobility, not a property of the unit-mobility flow. One may
optimize the source rows at each state and apply the same construction to Ered and the matter
tables alone; eq. (4.8) gives its complete derivative. The two flows are different vector fields with
different transients, but they share their critical points and their stability (proposition 4.9). Equal
mobility has a justification beyond convention. Unit mobilities are the Fisher metric of the single
product law of all tables, regarded as one law of all represented variables and source labels,
because the Fisher metric of a product law restricted to the product family is the sum of the factor
metrics. If the kinetic metric is required to be the restriction of a metric on the law space of all
these variables jointly that is invariant under Markov congruent embeddings, C encov's theorem [28]
forces it to be a constant multiple of the Fisher metric, so equal mobility is fixed up to one global
time scale. Imposing invariance on each table separately allows an independent constant for each
table, equivalent to replicating that table. A persistent slow model sector would have to follow from
the interactions and their state, rather than from an inserted small multiplier in its equation.

re-expression, the gradient therefore transforms as a tangent vector; this is passive covariance.
Active equivariance would further need equivariant constitutive maps for the law-dependent chan-
nels, as in eq. (2.13), and transported references and evaluators. These statements concern fixed
coordinate changes; coordinates that themselves evolve require their coordinate-velocity term.

4.5 A global free energy and its local free energies

Choose a proper prior P0(dy, dJ) on represented contents and source labels, and a normalized

record kernel R(do | y, J). Then P = P0R is normalized by integrating the record first. At a declared

factor incident on it.

In the global picture the represented contents of all agents are variables of one such model. Write

comparison record eq. (1.13) between agents i and j contributes a factor that depends on (yi, yj).
