eq. (4.25) is the sum of - log isl, - log il(m), - log iqj, - log ij(m, k), and - log i(o | k, m). Since
Fi = EQ[log Q - log Pi(·, o)], group each term with the entropy of the recognition factor it shares.
The label terms give DKL(iis) + DKL(iiq). Conditioning on L = l and integrating log si - log il
against si gives l ilDKL(siil). Conditioning on J = j and m and integrating log qi - log ij(m, ·)
against qi gives the third term. The record term remains. The row statement is proposition 4.3 with
Tq = Ts = 1.

At unit temperatures the peer terms of eq. (4.26) are exactly the peer terms of the reciprocal potential,
and the self terms reproduce the split eq. (4.2) of E0, now weighted by the self probabilities ii, ii.
The agent's own model competes with its peers for the role of prior, and the rows infer which source
to trust. Records add a likelihood term that persists in the objective. A temperature T = 1 multiplies
the label divergences; dividing by T shows that it corresponds to tempered peer and self factors, a
generalized-Bayes objective in the sense of Bissiri et al. [16] rather than a normalized model.

Definition 4.19 (Per-agent dynamics). On finite positive tables satisfying the hypotheses of
theorem 4.6, let each table ua belong to one agent i(a). The per-agent dynamics is eq. (4.15) with
hza = Fi(a)/uza, where the peer laws inside Fi(a) take their current values.

The proof of theorem 4.6 applies without change and gives a unique maximal interior solution.
The dissipation identity does not: each agent lowers its own free energy at the rate of its own
variances, while the free energies of the receivers that attend to it change through terms it does
not control. Let Ftot = i Fi, regarded as a function of all tables. The per-agent force on ua omits
from Ftot/ua exactly the derivatives of the other agents' free energies, namely the source-role
terms eq. (4.12) and the channel derivatives eq. (4.11) of edges that i(a) does not receive. The
Fisher gradient flow of Ftot keeps those terms and is the reciprocal flow of a potential of the form
eq. (4.4), with the agent's own model entering as the self source instead of as the additive term E0.
Results proved for the reciprocal flow therefore do not transfer to the per-agent dynamics without a
separate argument.

Proposition 4.20 (Per-agent dynamics need not be a gradient flow). Take three agents with
Bernoulli belief laws of log odds l1, l2, l3, a trivial model sector, evaluators equal to Bernoulli
references of log odds i, identity channels, and rows held fixed at ii = 1/(1 + w) and i,i+1 =
w/(1 + w) with w > 0 and indices modulo three. The per-agent dynamics is

   (1 + w)li = -(li - i) - w(li - li+1),                (4.27)

                                  41
4. Free Energies and Coupled Dynamics of Agent Laws  MAgent Theory 2.0

                                                                                      
whose linear part has eigenvalues -1/(1 + w) and (-1 - 3w/2 ± i 3w/2)/(1 + w). No Riemannian
metric makes eq. (4.27) the gradient flow of a function. By contrast, the linearization of the Fisher
gradient flow of eq. (4.4) at any interior critical point is self-adjoint for the Fisher metric and has real
spectrum.

Proof. For a Bernoulli law the Fisher flow in log odds is l = -F/p, and pDKL(Ber(p) Ber(p)) =
l - l, which gives eq. (4.27). Its linear part is circulant, with eigenvalues (-1 - w + w)/(1 + w)
for the cube roots of unity . At an equilibrium of a gradient flow x = -g-1F the linearization is
-g-1 Hess F , which is self-adjoint for g and hence has real eigenvalues; the same argument applies
to eq. (4.4).

The cross-derivative criterion of Monderer and Shapley [109] says the same in game-theoretic
terms: agent-wise objectives DKL(q1q2) and DKL(q2q1) have unequal mixed partial derivatives
unless q1 = q2, so they admit no exact potential. Damped oscillation on directed cycles is the
characteristic behavior of non-reciprocal interactions [62]. The reciprocal potential excludes it by
construction, and an exact inheritance of a Fisher gradient flow cannot create it, since differentiating
an exact intertwining by a submersion at an equilibrium shows that the parent spectrum is contained
in the real spectrum of the fine linearization.

4.7 The reciprocal potential is not a global free energy

Proposition 4.21 (No global free-energy identification). Hold the rows of eq. (4.4) fixed and
positive, and suppose agent i attends to a source j = i through an identity channel.

  (a) Let Ki = Kj be finite with at least two points. There is no normalized joint P over finitely
       many finite-valued variables, record value o, rule x  Q(x) assigning recognition laws, and
       constants a > 0, b with E(x) = aF (Q(x); o) + b on the interior of the configuration space.

  (b) Suppose in addition that the channels are fixed. There is no normalized joint P and record
       value o such that, with the product recognition Q = k k whose factors are the agent laws
       themselves, E = aF(Q; o) + b with a > 0 on an open set of interior configurations.

Proof. For (a), every finite value of F (Q; o) = DKL(Qo) - log Zo satisfies DKL(Qo) =
   Q log Q - Q log o  maxsupp o(- log o), a finite bound independent of Q. Every term

of eq. (4.4) is nonnegative, so E  ijDKL(qiqj). Let qi tend to the point mass at u and qj to the
point mass at v = u through interior laws. Then E is finite along the path and tends to infinity, which
no bounded function can match.

For (b), F(Q; o) is a sum of single-factor terms k log k and the integral of a fixed function against
   k k, which is affine in each factor. Hence the third derivative in a mass-preserving direction

w of qi and twice in a mass-preserving direction v of qj vanishes identically for i = j. For E the
same derivative is that of ijDKL(qiqj), namely ij w(v/qj)2 in densities against a common
reference. For two-point alphabets with w = v = (v1, -v1), this equals ijv13[qj(1)-2 - qj(2)-2],
which is nonzero whenever v1 = 0 and qj is not uniform. An affine identity on an open set would
equate the two derivatives there.

The obstruction concerns models in which the agent laws are recognition laws. The per-agent
picture evades it because each Fi is a fixed model only with its peers' laws held as data. Two
further identifications place the agent laws elsewhere. In the first, agent i receives n independent
messages from a source J  iq with law iqJ and registers whether their empirical type equals qi, a
type with denominator n. The method of types gives the registration probability |Tqi| exp{-n[H(qi) +
DKL(qiiqj)]} given J = j [35, Theorem 11.1.2], so the posterior of J given registration is the Gibbs
row eq. (4.5) with Tq = 1/n. There the laws are parameters of message laws. In the second, a prior
proportional to e-E/ against the Fisher volume on finite positive tables is normalizable because
E  0 and that volume is finite; records then add a likelihood, and the mode follows the Fisher flow
of E -  log . There the laws are latent variables of a hierarchical model. Neither construction
makes qi or si a recognition law.

The first identification is exact on a type lattice. Fix n  1, set Tq = Ts = T = 1/n, and let Xn be
a finite set of configurations x = (qi, si)i on finite alphabets in which every qi, si, and qi  si is a
type with denominator n and every compared law iqj(x), isj(x) and reference joint Ri is positive;
law-dependent channels are allowed. In the registered-agreement model, X is uniform on Xn, the
labels Jiq  iq and Jis  is are independent, agent i receives conditionally independent batches
Yi0  Rin, Yiq  iqJiq (X)n, and Yis  isJis(X)n, and it registers the binary records that the
empirical types of these batches equal qi  si, qi, and si. Write o for the event that every record is
registered, |Tp| for the size of the type class of p, and cn(p) = H(p) - n-1 log |Tp|.

Theorem 4.22 (Registered agreement). In the registered-agreement model the following hold.

   (i) P(oqi | x, Jiq = j) = |Tqi| exp{-n[H(qi) + Diqj(x)]}, and likewise in the model sector and for the
       reference batch with DKL(qi  siRi).

  (ii) The posterior of Jiq given x and o is the Gibbs row i(x) of eq. (4.5), and likewise for Jis.

  (iii) For recognition x  i i  i i of (X, J), with the batches integrated out, the free energy
       satisfies T F = E(x, , )+Cn(x)+T log |Xn|, where Cn(x) is the sum of cn over the registered
       targets and 0  cn(p)  | supp p| log(n + 1)/n.

 (iv) Ered(x) = -T log P(o | x) - Cn(x), and Ered(x) + Cn(x) + T log |Xn|  -T log P(o).

Proof. A sequence of type p has probability exp{-n[H(p) + DKL(p)]} under n [35, Theorem
11.1.2]; summing over the type class gives (i). In the posterior of a label the factor |Tqi|e-nH(qi) is
common to all sources and cancels, which gives (ii). For (iii), DKL(xUnif) = log |Xn|, the label
terms are DKL(iiq) and DKL(iis), and by (i) each expected negative log likelihood is n times a
divergence of eq. (4.4) plus ncn of its target; multiplying by T = 1/n gives the identity. The bounds
on cn are those on the size of a type class [35, Theorem 11.1.3]. For (iv), -T log P(o | x) equals
E0(x) + Cn(x) - T i log Ziq - T i log Zis by (i), and the free energy at the optimal rows bounds
the negative log evidence.

In this model the row temperature is the reciprocal number of exchanged messages, the Gibbs rows
are exact posteriors of which source was heard, and the reduced potential is, up to the receiver-only
term Cn, a negative log evidence at a point recognition of the configuration. The identification
needs equal temperatures and one batch size; unequal temperatures give a weighted composite
likelihood in the sense of Bissiri et al. [16]. A nonuniform configuration prior  adds -T log (x).

On general standard Borel spaces, registration of an empirical law in a neighborhood of the target
gives the divergence as a large-deviation rate through Sanov's theorem [38]; the double limit that
would make (iii) exact there is not established here. Resampling n messages from a table p has
covariance (diag p - ppT )/n, which is T times the inverse of the Fisher metric eq. (4.14), so the
same message count would set the temperature of a stochastic version of the flow; that version
and its metastability are open.

At frozen sources the same device needs no type lattice.

Corollary 4.23 (Frozen-source episodes). Hold the compared laws ij of agent i fixed, let

Proof. The chain rule gives DKL(ii) + j ijDKL(qiN ijN ), and relative entropy is additive
over independent copies. The posterior statement is (ii) of theorem 4.22 for one row.

Freezing the sources removes their source-role forces, so a sequence of such episodes is a
per-agent dynamics in the sense of section 4.6, not the reciprocal flow.

Definition 4.24 (Record-interrupted reciprocal dynamics). Let 0 < t1 < t2 < · · · be declared
record times and let Ao : S  S be declared measurable assimilation maps, for example the
conditioning updates of chapter 5. The record-interrupted dynamics follows the reciprocal Fisher
flow on each interval [tk, tk+1) and applies Aok at tk, with right-continuous paths.

This is a piecewise-deterministic process in the sense of Davis [41]. The reciprocal potential
decreases along each flow interval but need not decrease at an assimilation, since conditioning on
a record can move an agent away from the minimizer of eq. (4.4). In the free-energy pictures the
same record is a likelihood term, and the objective it enters is fixed between records.

Relative to a fixed normalized model, the reciprocal potential therefore gives up four things: an
evidence for model comparison, a posterior that the dynamics targets (its stationary points are
compromises among references and peers), one objective that spans both interaction and data
and is monotone across records, and a learning criterion for references, evaluators, priors, and
temperatures. Its stationary set does not depend on records, so after an assimilation event the flow
relaxes back toward record-independent states. A persistent record dependence must be declared.

Definition 4.25 (Evidence-augmented reciprocal potential). For registered records o = (oi)i
with declared densities of the record kernels i of definition 1.10, set

Eo = E +              - log i(oi | k, m)qi(dk)si(dm).          (4.29)

                   i

                      44
4. Free Energies and Coupled Dynamics of Agent Laws  MAgent Theory 2.0

The added term is the record term of eq. (4.26), so Eo is the reciprocal potential with the per-
agent record likelihoods kept in the objective. Its stationary points depend on the records. The
constructions of chapter 7 to chapter 13 are proved for E with records entering only as assimilation
events, and they are not claimed for Eo.

Open problem 4.26 (Relating the three objectives). Characterize the configurations and chan-
nels for which the per-agent models eq. (4.25) of a population are conditionals of one normalized
joint, so that the per-agent dynamics is coordinate descent of a global free energy as in proposi-
tion 4.14. Determine the families, such as linear Gaussian comparisons with fixed covariances,
on which the reciprocal, per-agent and global objectives have the same stationary points. Decide
whether a species in the sense of definition 1.11, with matched evaluators and information, admits
such a common joint. For each construction of chapter 7 to chapter 13, determine whether its
conclusions hold under the per-agent dynamics or under a global free energy.

Chapter 5

Prediction and Selective
Communication

A model law is useful through the records it predicts. Communication can preserve those predictions
while discarding other distinctions, and a receiver can combine a message with information already
present in its model. This chapter gives exact identities for both operations. The retained prediction
is always named; agreement about one output is not automatically agreement about every future
interaction.

5.1 Model presentations and their evaluators

Let Gi : Mi  Ki be a normalized local model and let Hi : Ki  Oi be a normalized record kernel.
Their composition

Kirec(m, A) = Hi(k, A)Gi(m, dk),  pirec = siKirec,  (5.1)

gives the model's predictive record law. An evaluator may also take a preparation, accessible
history, or chosen interaction as input; these are held fixed when two predictions are compared.
More general normalized evaluators need not factor through Gi and Hi.

Suppose a model link isj : Mj  Mi is a bimeasurable bijection. Exact compatibility of the two
evaluators, after identifying their record alphabets, means

Kirec(isjm, A) = Kjrec(m, A).                       (5.2)

Consequently, si = (isj)#sj implies equal predictive record laws. The compatibility is additional
information: two equal laws on a one-point model space can predict opposite deterministic bits

through different evaluators.

Theorem 5.1 (Exact predictive information identity). Let s, t be probability laws on a standard

Borel model space and let K be a common normalized record kernel. Assume DKL(st) < . Set
Ps(dm, do) = s(dm)K(m, do) and Pt(dm, do) = t(dm)K(m, do), and denote their conditional model
laws given o by so, to. Then

DKL(st) = DKL(sKtK) + DKL(soto)(sK)(do).            (5.3)

Proof. The common kernel cancels in the joint Radon­Nikodym derivative, giving DKL(PsPt) =
DKL(st). Disintegrating the same joint laws by their record marginal factors their density ratio into

46
5. Prediction and Selective Communication          MAgent Theory 2.0

the record ratio and the conditional model ratio. The logarithm is their sum. Integrating the first term
gives DKL(sKtK), and integrating the second first over m gives the displayed conditional term.
Finiteness makes the decomposition unambiguous.

Theorem 5.1 is the chain rule for relative entropy [35, 89], written for a joint law built from a common
kernel. Without the finiteness assumption the identity still holds in [0, ], both sides being infinite
together [68]. With a deterministic kernel K(m, ·) = T (m) it decomposes a divergence into the
divergence of the pushforwards and the expected divergence of the conditional laws given T , the
form used in corollary 5.3.

The second term is the model distinction that the record leaves unresolved. Its vanishing is an exact
sufficiency condition: DKL(sKtK) = DKL(st) exactly when the Bayesian inverse of K computed
at t returns s from sK, the classical case of Petz's recovery theorem [120]. A constant evaluator can
make all predictions agree while retaining no model distinction at all. Useful agreement therefore
requires a specified predictive task as well as a comparison of laws. For a common history kernel,
the same identity holds with the full finite record history in place of o.

If the model link depends on the current laws, theorem 5.1 applies to the resulting fixed comparison
at that configuration, provided eq. (5.2) holds there. Preservation of compatibility during an update
is a separate condition on the dynamics and the evaluator.

5.2 Conditional prediction within an agent

An evaluator can relate a cue to a different result, so that a record of one changes predictions for
the other. On standard Borel presentation, cue, result, and record spaces, choose normalized
kernels µm(du), Km(u, dv), and L(u, do), with a proper presentation reference r(dm). The joint

P (dm, du, dv, do) = r(dm)µm(du)Km(u, dv)L(u, do)  (5.4)

is an instance of definition 1.10, with represented contents (u, v) and evaluator G(m, d(u, v)) =
µm(du)Km(u, dv). For a record likelihood l(o | u) with finite positive evidence, the posterior has
the correlated form wo(dm)mo (du, dv) of eq. (B.3). The result prediction averages the component-
conditional results using the posterior model belief. The presentation selects a mechanism; its
posterior probability is distinct from the parameters defining that mechanism.

The local free energy retains this dependence. Under the finiteness conditions of proposition B.2, a
candidate s(dm)qm(dk) satisfies

F = DKL(swo) + DKL(qmom)s(dm) - log Z(o).          (5.5)

Exact conditioning minimizes this functional. Requiring one content law independent of the pre-
sentation changes the optimization, as in remark 4.1. Thus the general joint agent law supports a
concrete local inference operation beyond the product-family flows.

For an additive Gaussian cue record O = X + ,   N (0, C), the fixed-model response is

DE[Y | O = ] = Cov(Y, X | O = )C-1.                (5.6)

                                           47
5. Prediction and Selective Communication         MAgent Theory 2.0

Proposition B.4 states the moment and differentiation hypotheses and proves the identity. The
cross-covariance permits a negative or rotating response. This is conditional prediction through a
statistical relation, while the Fisher tensor measures distinguishability of the posterior law. Gaussian
mixture regression gives an explicit realization [24].

Returning only a Gaussian with the result moments is a further operation: it minimizes DKL(pYo qG),
not in general the reverse divergence of variational free energy. The exact loss of a product carrier
consisting of model weights and that Gaussian is

DKL(M o ,Y wo  qG) = Io (M ; Y ) + DKL(poY qG),   (5.7)

whenever these terms are finite. The chain rule proves the split; proposition B.5 supplies the
Gaussian projection proof. This local moment-matching operation is familiar from assumed-density
filtering [107]. A later Gaussian observation can distinguish the exact mixture from its carrier
(proposition B.6), so the retained interface must name which predictions it preserves. Appendix B
gives the self-contained construction, its frame laws, and an exact sequential filtering case.

5.3 Communication between conditional predictors

A message sampled from a peer's current prediction depends on that peer's private evidence.
Appendix C supplies a two-agent realization with a common preparation law for represented states
Zi = (Ai, Xi, Yi), private records Di, known encoders, and a reliably shared transcript H1:t. The
local marginals are the cue/result models above, and recognition retains model/content dependence.
A fixed alternating schedule chooses the speaker, which samples a fresh result from its conditional
prediction. The receiver integrates the resulting message likelihood over the unknown peer record
conditional on its own represented state and available information. The speaker's own random
output leaves its private posterior unchanged; an incoming message can change its next outgoing
distribution.

The common posterior has an exact reduced representation. If W (d, dz) = P (Z  dz | D = d) is
the fixed preparation conditional, with D = (D0, D1), then

t(dz, dd) = W (d, dz)t(dd), t = P (D  · | H1:t).  (5.8)

Every communication likelihood at a fixed history depends on the prepared variables only through
D, so it reweights t and leaves W unchanged. Each agent conditions t on its own private value
and reconstructs its local joint law with W . The retained state also includes the known policy, next
speaker, and persistent transcript whenever past-record queries are admitted. This is statistical
sufficiency within the declared family, without moment projection or a minimality claim. The appendix
gives its normalized finite-history law, correlated local and reduced free-energy identities, and a
binary two-way exchange whose expanded posterior is reconstructed from four private-record
weights.

The same construction has exact finite-dimensional Gaussian closure for one presentation per
agent with affine Gaussian kernels. Multiple presentations can produce a posterior outside every
finite Gaussian-mixture family after one message. A separate pair of reachable histories has
identical local joint beliefs but different next receiver updates, showing why local dependence alone

                                           48
5. Prediction and Selective Communication                           MAgent Theory 2.0

need not preserve cross-agent evidence. These conclusions concern a supplied common-model
protocol. Its fixed-history free energy does not identify the three population objectives, and its
fixed preparation supplies no new measurements during communication. The common/private
information organization is classical [112]; the appendix derives the specified transmission and
retention directly.

5.4 What the receiver reconstructs

A sending map Tj : Ej  H induces the message law µj = (Tj)#qj. Different laws can have the
same message law. Messages travel from source to receiver. The reciprocal flow of chapter 4 also
moves each source by the likelihood ratio of its receivers, so a communication model that realizes
that flow must include this reverse message; the per-agent dynamics of definition 4.19 needs only
the forward one. For linear maps Tj : Ej  H and Oi : H  Ei,

                             rank(OiTj)  rank(Tj).                  (5.9)

Writing a message into a larger space cannot by itself recover distinctions discarded by Tj. A richer
reconstruction uses the receiver's conditional model.

For a received value h and a declared likelihood i(h | k), Bayesian assimilation is

                             qi+(dk) =     i(h  |  k)qi-(dk)  )  ,  (5.10)
                                           i(h  |  k)qi-(dk

when the denominator is finite and positive. An unmeasured coordinate can change because it
is conditionally related to the measured one in qi-. The observation selects among possibilities
already related by the receiver's model. Under the reciprocal flow such an update is an assimilation

event in the sense of definition 4.24; its effect persists in the objective only in the free-energy

pictures or in the evidence-augmented potential eq. (4.29).

Proposition 5.2 (Exact conditional reconstruction). Let T : E  H be measurable on standard
Borel spaces. Let q, p be laws with q  p, and set µ = T#q. Choose a regular conditional law
p(dk | h) for p given T = h. Define

                             q(dk) = p(dk | h)µ(dh).                (5.11)

Then T#q = µ and, in [0, ],

DKL(qq) = DKL q(· | h)p(· | h) µ(dh).                               (5.12)

In particular, q = q exactly when the two conditional laws agree for µ-almost every h.

Proof. Absolute continuity gives µ  T#p, so the conditional version of p is defined at every h
needed up to a µ-null set. That conditional is supported on T -1(h) almost surely. Hence its mixture
has pushforward µ. The laws q and q have the same h-marginal and respective conditional laws

                                           49
5. Prediction and Selective Communication      MAgent Theory 2.0

q(· | h) and p(· | h). Factoring their density ratio by h proves eq. (5.12). Nonnegativity and the
equality condition of relative entropy give the last claim.

The reconstruction eq. (5.11) is Jeffrey's rule of conditioning the prior p on the marginal µ [46]. It
preserves the communicated marginal and supplies the discarded conditional from p. It makes
precise the sense in which a receiver contributes structure that the message alone does not
specify. The proposition assumes a common content presentation; a link or a separately declared
correspondence is needed before applying it across different fibers.

Corollary 5.3 (Pythagorean identity and information projection). Under the hypotheses of
proposition 5.2, in [0, ],

DKL(qp) = DKL(qq) + DKL(qp), DKL(qp) = DKL(µT#p).  (5.13)

Among all laws r with T#r = µ and DKL(µT#p) < , the reconstruction q is the unique minimizer
of DKL(rp).

Proof. Apply the deterministic-kernel case of the chain rule to (q, p), to (q, p), and to (r, p). The
pushforwards are µ and T#p in each case. The conditional term vanishes for q, equals the right
side of eq. (5.12) for q, and is nonnegative for r, with equality only when r has the conditional laws
of p, that is, when r = q.

This is the Pythagorean identity for information projections [37], and the minimization property is
the characterization of Jeffrey's rule by minimum relative entropy [46]. What proposition 5.2 adds to
these sources is its use as a receiver mechanism: the loss term measures exactly what a receiver's
prior conditional fails to restore.

Proposition 5.4 (Common recovery by likelihood descent). Let C : X  Z be a measurable

map between standard Borel spaces. Let P0 be a probability law and let P = LP0 be a family of
probability laws dominated by it. Choose the reference conditional R0(z, dx) = P0(dx | C = z), and
write L¯(z) = EP0[L | C = z]. Then

(C#P)R0(dx) = L¯(C(x))P0(dx).                      (5.14)

Consequently this one kernel recovers every P exactly when each L has a (C)-measurable
version, that is, exactly when C is sufficient for the family {P0}  {P}. No finite-divergence
assumption is needed.

Proof. For each measurable A  Z, P(C-1A) = A L¯(z)(C#P0)(dz), by the defining property of
conditional expectation. For a measurable B  X, disintegration therefore gives

((C#P)R0)(B) = L¯(z)R0(z, B)(C#P0)(dz)             (5.15)

                     = L¯(C(x))P0(dx).

                                    B

                                           50
5. Prediction and Selective Communication                   MAgent Theory 2.0

Equality with P is equivalent to equality of their Radon­Nikodym densities, L = L¯  C almost
surely. Conditional expectation fixes exactly the integrable (C)-measurable functions, proving both
directions.

A posterior-specific conditional always reconstructs that posterior from its own marginal. It need
not reconstruct the reference or other posteriors. The common kernel in proposition 5.4 makes
the stronger requirement explicit. Regular conditional laws and their almost-sure uniqueness are
understood in the standard Borel sense [82]. The equivalence in proposition 5.4 is the Halmos­
Savage factorization criterion for a family dominated by one of its members [71]; the common
reference conditional is the kernel that defines sufficiency, compare the adequate subfields of
Skibinsky [133], and the statement is an instance of abstract sufficiency in the Markov category of
standard Borel spaces [61]. What is used below is the explicit density eq. (5.14) of the reconstruction
when descent fails.

Corollary 5.5 (Recovery without reading the exterior). Let P0 now be a joint reference law of
(X, E) on standard Borel spaces, and let Z = C(X). Retain (Z, E) but reconstruct X using only
R0(z, dx) = P0(dx | Z = z), leaving E unchanged. This reconstructs P0 exactly if and only if X and
E are conditionally independent given Z. Under that condition it also reconstructs a dominated
family P = LP0 exactly if and only if each likelihood ratio descends to (Z, E).

Proof. The lifted reference has conditional law R0(z, dx) given (z, e). Because R0 is supported on
C-1(z) almost surely, its joint law with (Z, E) agrees with the true law exactly when P0(dx | Z, E) =
P0(dx | Z) almost surely. This is the stated conditional independence. In that case the exterior-
preserving lift is the reference conditional for the map (x, e)  (C(x), e). Apply proposition 5.4 to
that map.

Descent of the likelihood ratios alone does not suffice. Let P0 be uniform on {(0, 0), (1, 1)} for (X, E)
and let C be constant. The family {P0} has a trivially descending likelihood ratio, but the lift draws
X uniformly and independently of E, so it does not reconstruct P0; here X and E are dependent
given Z.

5.5 A predictive coding criterion

Lossy source coding makes fidelity part of the problem definition [131]. Decoder side information is
a realized variable correlated with the source, as in Wyner­Ziv coding [145]; knowing a prior without
such a realization does not supply that variable. A few noiseless real numbers also do not specify a
finite-bit channel. A communication rate requires a declared coding, precision, or noise model.

For a predictive criterion, let P (X, Y, Z) be a declared preparation law. The source X may be

represented content or a complete fine configuration; the choice is fixed in each application. Let Z

be accessible receiver information and let Y be a response to be preserved. An encoder T (du | X)

gives the conditional independence

                                           U - X - (Y, Z).  (5.16)

The decoder predicts Y from (U, Z). This is the setting of an information bottleneck, with the
relevant variable explicitly named [136].

                                           51
5. Prediction and Selective Communication                                          MAgent Theory 2.0

Theorem 5.6 (Predictive distortion and the optimal decoder). On standard Borel spaces,
assume the displayed information quantities are finite and eq. (5.16) holds. For any predictive
decoder (dy | u, z) with finite expected relative entropy,

                            EDKL P (Y | X, Z)(Y | U, Z)                            (5.17)
                                = I(Y ; X | U, Z) + EDKL P (Y | U, Z)(Y | U, Z) .

The optimal decoder is P (dy | u, z). Its distortion is

D(T ) = I(Y ; X | U, Z) = I(Y ; X | Z) - I(Y ; U | Z).                             (5.18)

Proof. Conditional independence gives P (Y | X, U, Z) = P (Y | X, Z). In the logarithmic ratio
defining the left side of eq. (5.17), insert the intermediate conditional law P (Y | U, Z). The first
resulting expectation is the definition of I(Y ; X | U, Z). In the second, averaging over X gives the
conditional law P (Y | U, Z), yielding the remaining divergence. The second term vanishes at the
stated decoder and is nonnegative for every decoder. Finally, expand I(Y ; X, U | Z) in both orders
and use I(Y ; U | X, Z) = 0.

The decomposition eq. (5.17) is the logarithmic-loss identity of source coding with soft reconstruc-
tions, in which the optimal reconstruction is a conditional law and the distortion is a conditional
mutual information [34].

The functional I(X; U | Z)+D(T ), for   0, is one possible criterion for selecting a representation.
Its first term is an information cost, not automatically the length of an individual message. An
operational coding theorem requires its own source and block-coding assumptions. Transmitting a
sample from (Tj)#qj and transmitting that whole probability law are also different protocols.

For parent formation, choose X to include the fine configuration and choose Y to be a future
boundary response over a specified horizon and interaction. Zero distortion means that U and Z
are sufficient for this target under this preparation. A subsequent interaction may read information
that this target ignored. Exact inheritance therefore requires the dynamical condition developed in
chapter 6, not only predictive sufficiency for one chosen response.

                                           52
Chapter 6

Inherited Parents and Recursive
Formation

A collection becomes a parent when its retained state supports inherited interaction and evolution.
A probability law obtained by compression is a first part of this construction. It does not determine
how that law will change, what the parent can communicate, or which information its children must
retain. We give exact conditions for these further steps, classify the mechanisms that make them
hold, and give a finite drive­response example in which exact lumping works through two levels.
The example supplies its reductions; formation of the reductions remains a separate question.

Most exactness criteria below are instances of classical mathematics, and we attribute them
where they are stated: factor maps of dynamical systems, exact lumping of differential equations,
strong lumpability and Markov functions of Markov chains, Riemannian submersions, equivariant
reduction, and conditional independence. What this chapter adds is their assembly into one
notion of an inherited parent with declared protocol and preparation classes, the counterexamples
showing which natural retentions fail, and the restrictions that these criteria place on the formation
constructions of later chapters.

6.1 Two objects that a parent must retain

Definition 6.1 (Sample compression and configuration retention). Let x  S be a complete
agent configuration and let Qx be its declared law on a standard Borel space Y of represented
contents. A normalized sample channel C : Y  Z gives the retained law

Qxc (A) = C(y, A)Qx(dy).                   (6.1)

A configuration retention is a measurable map R : S  Sc. Its value includes the parent laws and
the additional data needed for its declared interactions and update. Proposition 6.12 identifies the
smallest such data for a declared interface.

The distinction applies to both sectors. A parent carrying qI and sI also needs the evaluator that
makes sI predictive. Boundary channels, source rows, source marks, and memory can be further
components of R(x). Equal marginal laws do not imply equality of these components. When a
sample channel reads random links or source variables, those variables belong to the joint input
law of the channel. Substitution of a mean link or a selected source is a different retention.

A law of represented contents and a probability law over complete configurations are different
objects. Coupled deterministic evolution of law-valued agents requires no probability distribution
over x. If such a distribution is used below, its preparation or transition mechanism is stated. All

53
6. Inherited Parents and Recursive Formation               MAgent Theory 2.0

constructions admit general probability laws. A Gaussian parent is one possible family, subject to
its own closure conditions.

Throughout the chapter,  composes maps and juxtaposition composes kernels in the order in
which they act: for kernels K : X  O and D : O  O, (KD)(x, A) = D(o, A)K(x, do). A
measurable map used in a kernel product stands for its deterministic kernel. With this convention
every square below is a commutative diagram of Markov kernels between standard Borel spaces,
and the composition results are the pasting of such diagrams in the Markov category of these
spaces [61].

6.2 Exact deterministic inheritance

Proposition 6.2 (An update descends precisely when it respects retained states). Let S, Sc

be standard Borel spaces, let R : S  Sc be a Borel surjection, and let F : S  S be Borel. There is

a Borel parent update F c satisfying

                                      R  F = F c  R,       (6.2)

if and only if

                       R(x) = R(x) = R(F (x)) = R(F (x)).  (6.3)

The parent update is unique. The same conclusion holds on arbitrary measurable spaces when R
has a measurable right inverse.

Proof. Equation (6.2) implies the implication in (6.3). Conversely, set F c(z) = R(F (x)) for any x

with R(x) = z. The implication makes this independent of the choice of x, and surjectivity defines it
on all of Sc. Its graph is the image of S under the Borel map x  (R(x), R(F (x))) into the standard
Borel space Sc × Sc, hence an analytic set. A function between standard Borel spaces with analytic
graph is Borel [84, Thm. 14.12]. With a measurable right inverse , the formula F c = R  F   gives
measurability directly. Every parent state has a preimage, so (6.2) fixes F c uniquely. 

This is the factor-map (semiconjugacy) criterion of dynamical systems. The analytic-graph argument
matters because a Borel surjection need not have a Borel right inverse; the uniformization theorem
supplies only universally measurable ones [84, Sec. 18.A]. Repeated substitution gives R  F n =
(F c)n  R for every nonnegative integer n. This is an exact statement about the chosen update,
including its order and retained parameters. Replacing that update by descent of a newly defined
parent objective requires another argument.

For a differentiable version, suppose R is continuously differentiable and the fine and parent vector

fields B, Bc have unique local solutions. Their flows satisfy R  t = ct  R on their common

existence interval if

                                      DRxB(x) = Bc(R(x)).  (6.4)

Indeed, the chain rule makes R(t(x)) a parent solution with initial value R(x), and uniqueness
identifies it. Conversely, differentiation of the flow identity at zero gives (6.4). For a moving map
Rt, the left side becomes tRt(x) + DRt(x)Bt(x). Membership changes therefore need an explicit
handoff map; a differential identity on one fixed partition does not specify them. Condition (6.4)
is the exact-lumping condition for differential equations, introduced for linear kinetics by Wei and
Kuo [143], for nonlinear kinetics by Li and Rabitz [100], and for flows on manifolds by Horstmeyer

                                              54
6. Inherited Parents and Recursive Formation                            MAgent Theory 2.0

and Atay [79]; flow intertwining has also been proposed as a criterion of macroscopic emergence
[9]. The differentiable statement needs R to be continuously differentiable between manifolds on
which both flows are defined. A retention into spaces of laws that is differentiable only weakly, with
a parent law of motion given by a weak continuity equation, is not covered, and its intertwining must
be proved directly.

Proposition 6.3 (Projectable vector fields). Let R : S  Sc be a Ck+1 surjective submersion

between finite-dimensional manifolds, k  1, whose fibers are connected, and let B be a Ck vector

field on S. A Ck parent field Bc satisfying (6.4) exists if and only if, in every submersion chart

R(a, b) = a with B = (BA, BV ),

                                 bBA(a, b) = 0.                         (6.5)

For a linear surjection R = M on Rn this is the condition M (DB(x)v) = 0 for all x and all v  ker M .

Proof. In a submersion chart, DRxB(x) = BA(a, b). Condition (6.5) says that this map is locally
constant along each fiber; a locally constant function on a connected fiber is constant, so x 
DRxB(x) is constant on fibers, and conversely constancy on fibers gives (6.5). A submersion has
smooth local sections  through every point, and Bc = (DR · B)   is then well defined and Ck.
Since k  1, both fields have unique local solutions. In the linear case the fibers are affine, hence
connected, and the derivative of M B along v  ker M is M (DB(x)v). 

Remark 6.4 (Why inheritance is tested on a set of configurations). Dynamical inheritance
checked only along one realized trajectory carries no information. If x(t) is a smooth solution
on [0, T ] and R is smooth with z = R  x an embedded arc, the tangent field of the arc extends
to a smooth field Bc on a neighborhood of the arc, and R(tx0) = tc(Rx0) holds with unique
parent solutions. The same holds on a prepared family on which R is injective. The fiber test (6.3)
constrains a retention only over a set containing distinct configurations with the same retained
value. For this reason the inheritance identities are imposed below on a declared invariant set I of
post-handoff states (definition 6.16), and the formation standard requires an admitted class that is
open or a declared invariant family.

Proposition 6.6 (Equivariant descent). Let a Lie group G act smoothly, freely, and properly on a
finite-dimensional manifold S, and let  : S  S/G be the quotient map.

   (i) If a smooth vector field B is G-equivariant, there is a unique smooth field Bc on S/G with
       D · B = Bc  , and the flows intertwine. Every G-invariant measurable response kernel or
       channel on S factors through .

Equivariant descent holds on the whole configuration space, so the fiber test needs no restriction
to an admitted class. It forgets only orbit data. Without freeness the quotient is stratified by orbit
type and the statement holds on each stratum. On infinite-dimensional law charts, (ii) requires
in addition a closed complement to the orbit tangent in the Fisher metric and a quotient Banach
manifold, which must be verified for the chart in use.

Proposition 6.7 (Coordinate projections are exact only for isolated blocks). Let S = SA × SB
be a product of connected manifolds with metric g = gA(a)  gB(b), and let E  C2. The projection
R(a, b) = a intertwines - gradg E with an autonomous field if and only if abE  0, that is,
E(a, b) = EA(a) + EB(b). The discarded block is then autonomous as well.

Proof. The retained velocity is a = -gA(a)-1aE(a, b). Since the fibers {a} × SB are connected
and gA(a) is invertible, it is independent of b exactly when baE = 0, that is, when aE(a, b) =
(a). Integrating along paths in the connected factors gives E = EA(a) + EB(b), and then
b = -gB(b)-1bEB(b).

The Fisher flow of chapter 4 with product recognition has agent-local metric blocks and one potential,
and a source appears in the cost of every receiver that attends to it. Discarding whole agents or
whole sectors is therefore exact in that dynamics only for energetically isolated blocks, with no
peer cost in either direction between the retained and the discarded agents. Exact compression of
reciprocally coupled agents must come from symmetry (proposition 6.6) or from horizontal energy
structure (proposition 6.5), as in the center-of-mass example.

Proposition 6.8 (Exact inheritance of a gradient flow creates no oscillatory mode). Let B =
- gradg E with E  C2, and let x be a critical point of E. Then L = DB(x) = -g(x)-1 Hess E(x)
is self-adjoint for g(x) and has real spectrum. If a C2 submersion R intertwines B with a C1 field Bc
near x in the sense of (6.4), then R(x) is an equilibrium of Bc and spec DBc(R(x))  spec L  R.

Proof. At a critical point the Hessian is a symmetric bilinear form, so L is g(x)-self-adjoint. Eval-
uating (6.4) at x gives Bc(R(x)) = 0. Differentiating it at x, the term containing the second
derivative of R is multiplied by B(x) = 0, leaving DR  L = Lc  DR with Lc = DBc(R(x)). Hence
ker DR is L-invariant, and since DR is surjective, Lc is conjugate through DR to the map that L
induces on TxS/ ker DR. The characteristic polynomial of L is the product of those of its restriction
and of the induced quotient map, so every eigenvalue of Lc is an eigenvalue of L.

An exactly inherited parent of a Fisher gradient flow therefore has no underdamped linear mode at
an inherited equilibrium. Oscillatory collective modes require nonreciprocal fields, explicit driving,
or declared second-order kinetics.

Proposition 6.9 (Loss of dynamical roles under product recognition). Take Qx = Ber(p1)

This obstruction occurs while recognition remains a product. The missing datum is which probability

6.3 Exact stochastic inheritance

Proposition 6.10 (Finite strong lumpability). Let T be a transition matrix on a finite configuration
space S and let R : S  Sc be surjective. A single parent transition matrix reproduces the retained
process for every initial law if and only if, for every z  Sc,

          T (x, y) =                          T (x, y) whenever R(x) = R(x).  (6.14)

y:R(y)=z                      y:R(y)=z

In that case the common sum defines T c(R(x), z) uniquely.

Proof. The common sums are nonnegative and sum to one, so they define a transition matrix.
Conditional on any retained history ending at z, the hidden configuration lies in R-1(z). Every state
in that fiber gives the same next retained distribution T c(z, ·); averaging over its conditional law
leaves this distribution unchanged. Induction gives the parent path law from the pushed initial law.
Conversely, start the fine process at each point mass x. A common parent kernel must give the
same one-step distribution whenever these initial states have the same image. This is (6.14). 

This is the finite strong-lumpability criterion [85]; its general state-space form is Dynkin's criterion
for a function of a Markov process [51]. On standard Borel spaces the same argument applies
whenever x  T (x, R-1(·)) is constant on fibers: the analytic-graph argument of proposition 6.2,

                                              58
6. Inherited Parents and Recursive Formation                                                                       MAgent Theory 2.0

applied to this map into the standard Borel space of probability laws on Sc, makes the parent
kernel measurable. Closure for every initial law is stronger than closure for one chosen preparation.
The latter is weak lumpability [85], and the question whether a function of a Markov chain is itself
Markov goes back to Burke and Rosenblatt [23]; Buchholz [21] compares these notions with exact
lumpability.

An equilibrium conditional average of fine transitions defines a normalized candidate parent kernel.
It does not prove (6.14): the hidden conditional law during a transient can differ from the equilibrium
conditional. Likewise, agreement of invariant distributions does not establish agreement of histories.

Proposition 6.12 (The coarsest exact parent containing an interface). Let F : S  S and an
interface Q : S  Y be measurable. The interface collects what the parent must reproduce: its laws,
the responses of a declared protocol class, and the channels and evaluators it reads. Define

                                                (x) = (Q(F nx))n0  YN.                                                        (6.17)

Then  satisfies (6.3), with parent update the left shift on (S), and Q is its zeroth coordinate. If a
retention R satisfies (6.3) and Q = Qc  R for some Qc, then R(x) = R(x) implies (x) = (x).

                                                                   59
6. Inherited Parents and Recursive Formation      MAgent Theory 2.0

Thus  is, up to relabeling of its values, the unique coarsest exact retention through which the
interface factors. For a forward-complete flow, replace F n by t, t  0. If B and Q are real analytic,
(x) = (x) exactly when LBk Q(x) = LBk Q(x) for every k  0.
Proof. The identity (F (x)) = (Q(F n+1x))n0 is the shift of (x), so equal values have equal

The analytic case is the observability construction of Hermann and Krener [75]. For finite Markov

Proposition 6.13 (The coarsest strongly lumpable refinement). Let T be a transition matrix
on a finite space S and let B0 be the partition of S into level sets of an interface Q. Define Bk+1
by splitting each block of Bk according to the vector (T (x, B))BBk . The sequence stabilizes at a
partition B, which is the unique coarsest partition refining B0 that satisfies (6.14).

Proof. Each step refines the previous partition, so the sequence stabilizes after finitely many steps.
At the fixed point, states in one block have equal masses into every block, which is (6.14). Let B be
any strongly lumpable partition refining B0, and suppose it refines Bk. Each block of Bk is a union
of blocks of B, so two states in one block of B have equal masses into every block of Bk and lie in
one block of Bk+1. By induction B refines B. 

This is probabilistic bisimulation [91]; an efficient algorithm is given by Derisavi et al. [45]. The
two propositions make the phrase "the additional data needed" in definition 6.1 a theorem: given
the update and the interface, the canonical parent is determined. A larger interface gives a finer
canonical parent, so the protocol class decides how much a parent can forget. Unrestricted identity-
channel probes make it injective on exposed child laws (section 10.3, proposition 11.13). The
compression clause of the formation standard asks whether this canonical parent, for the interface
fixed before the retention, is noninjective on the post-handoff invariant set.

6.4 Boundary responses and composition

A parent must inherit what it does to the rest of the population. Fix a declared boundary protocol a,

including the preparation and receiving conditions. Let Ka : S  Oa be its normalized response
kernel and let Da : Oa  Oac retain the response of interest. An inherited kernel Kac satisfies

(KaDa)(x, A) = Kac(R(x), A).                      (6.18)

On standard Borel spaces, such a kernel exists exactly when x  (KaDa)(x, ·) is constant on
each fiber of R; the analytic-graph argument of proposition 6.2 gives measurability, and substitution
proves necessity. When several outputs are used jointly, this condition applies to their joint kernel.
Preserving each output marginal alone need not preserve their dependence.

The same applies to a response and the next retained state. For a stochastic update, response
inheritance concerns the joint kernel x  law(Da(Oa), R(X)) on Oac ×Sc, which must factor through
R. Separate descent of the response kernel and of the retained transition does not imply it. Let

                                              60
6. Inherited Parents and Recursive Formation                    MAgent Theory 2.0

x = (u, v)  {0, 1}2, R(x) = u, draw a fresh fair bit , set u = u, draw v freshly, and respond with
O =   v. Both the response and the next retained state are uniform from every configuration, but
at (0, 0) the joint law of (O, u) is uniform on {(0, 0), (1, 1)} and at (0, 1) it is uniform on {(1, 0), (0, 1)}.
If the randomness of the response is conditionally independent of the transition randomness given
x, separate descent suffices. For adaptive protocols, in which a receiver chooses its next action
from past outputs, the joint condition is required for each admitted action.

Proposition 6.14 (Exact elimination through a conditional separator). Let Z, U, V have a de-
clared joint reference law (dz, du, dv) = Z(dz)UV (du, dv | z) on standard Borel spaces. Denote
its conditional marginals by U , V . For bounded nonnegative likelihood factors LU (u, z), LV (v, z),
jointly measurable, define

              FU (z) = LU (u, z)U (du | z), FV (z) = LV (v, z)V (dv | z).  (6.19)

The identity

              LU (u, z)LV (v, z)UV (du, dv | z) = FU (z)FV (z)             (6.20)

holds Z-almost everywhere for every such pair precisely when U and V are conditionally indepen-
dent given Z. Under that condition, a nonnegative factor LZ(z) with finite positive total evidence
gives the unnormalized retained measure

              mZ (dz) = LZ (z)FU (z)FV (z)Z (dz).                          (6.21)

Proof. Conditional independence factors UV as U  V almost surely. Tonelli's theorem then
gives eqs. (6.20) and (6.21). Conversely, take indicator factors from countable generating families
closed under finite intersections for the two standard Borel spaces. Outside one Z-null set, the
conditional joint and product laws agree on every generating rectangle. Uniqueness of probability
measures extends this equality to the product sigma algebra, proving conditional independence.

The shared factor LZ appears once. If the hidden blocks are not conditionally independent, their
joint conditional factor must be retained. This elimination statement concerns the declared reference
and likelihood; it does not replace the law-dependent interaction potential by a fixed joint model. It
is the separator factorization of Dawid [42] that underlies junction-tree propagation [93].

The proposition presupposes the joint law. A gluing statement holds for two blocks: laws of (Z, U )
and (Z, V ) with a common Z marginal have exactly one joint law with U and V conditionally
independent given Z, namely the conditional product. Elimination of k  3 blocks needs mutual
conditional independence, not pairwise independence: with U, V independent fair bits, W = U  V ,
and Z constant, every pair is independent, but E[1U=11V =11W =1] = 0 = 1/8 = FU FV FW . Gluing
over a family of overlapping separators requires a junction tree. Edge laws on a four-cycle forcing
A = B, B = C, C = D, and D = A with uniform single-site marginals are pairwise consistent but
have no joint law; existence of a joint law for every consistent family characterizes the decomposable
(running-intersection) hypergraphs [141].

Proposition 6.15 (Inheritance composes). Suppose R10 : S0  S1 and R21 : S1  S2 intertwine

deterministic updates at successive levels. Then R20 = R21  R10 intertwines the first and third
updates. The analogous assertion holds for finite lumped Markov transitions. Let Ka : S  O be
boundary kernels, with response retentions D10 : O0  O1 and D21 : O1  O2. If

                          Ka0D10 = R10Ka1,         Ka1D21 = R21Ka2,  (6.23)

then Ka0D10D21 = R10R21Ka2.
Proof. For deterministic updates, R21  R10  F 0 = R21  F 1  R10 = F 2  R21  R10. For Markov
transitions and their deterministic retention kernels, in kernel order, T 0R10R21 = R10T 1R21 =
R10R21T 2, and the kernel R10R21 is the deterministic kernel of R21  R10. For boundary kernels,
associate the successive integrals and substitute (6.23). All integrands for events are nonnegative,
so interchanging the integration order is valid. 

When changes of gauge presentation act on the retained spaces, the retentions and boundary
kernels must transform compatibly with those actions. Re-expressing a commuting square then
gives the same square in the new coordinates. Neither a parent frame chosen for this purpose nor
the square itself determines a base connection. If the parent is also required to retain the collective
Fisher connection, the additional condition in proposition 3.17 must be checked.

Definition 6.16 (Inherited parent). An inherited parent of a block I consists of the following data,
declared in this order: a protocol class AI of boundary protocols, a preparation class PI of initial
laws (for stochastic dynamics), an invariant set I containing every post-handoff configuration that
arises from the admitted class with the block I, and a measurable retention RI : I  SIc . It must
satisfy four conditions.

 (D) Dynamics. In deterministic dynamics, (6.3) holds for all x, x  I ; in stochastic dynamics,
       a single parent kernel reproduces the retained process for every initial law in PI (strong
       lumpability when PI contains all laws, the intertwining of proposition 6.11 when PI = {}).

  (B) Responses. For every a  AI , the joint kernel of the retained response and the next retained
       state factors through RI on I , for each admitted receiver action of an adaptive protocol.

                                               62
6. Inherited Parents and Recursive Formation                                  MAgent Theory 2.0

 (C) Channels. Every channel and evaluator read by a protocol in AI or by the parent update
       factors through RI , including its dependence on the configuration.

 (G) Geometry, when declared. The condition of proposition 3.17 holds.

This is the sense of inheritance in clause (F3) of definition 6.31. Fixing AI before RI is essential.
An empty protocol class makes (B) vacuous, and an unrestricted one forces the retention to be
injective on exposed child laws. Dynamical, response, and connection inheritance are separate
conditions.

This notion differs from a Markov-blanket hierarchy [60, 86, 116]. A Markov blanket is a conditional-
independence property of a declared joint law over the states of a system. A parent here is
a retention that intertwines the given dynamics and the declared responses; no joint law over
configurations is assumed or derived, and conditional independence enters only where a separator
is eliminated as in proposition 6.14.

Definition 6.17 (Type closure). Fix a constitutive class C of agent dynamics, for example Fisher
gradient flows of reciprocal law potentials with normalized, possibly law-dependent channels
and evaluators. An inherited parent is type-closed for C if its descended update, channels, and
responses again belong to C, with the parent laws as agent laws and their Fisher metric as the
metric.

Type closure is what allows a result proved for primitive agents to be applied to parents without
change, and hence by induction at every level. For the gradient class, proposition 6.5 gives the
test under horizontal conformality: the retention must be horizontally conformal from the fine Fisher
metric to the Fisher metric of the parent laws, and the fine potential must satisfy (6.8) with a
reciprocal potential of the parent laws.

Open problem 6.18 (Type-closed parents). Determine which of the exact parents of the later
chapters are type-closed for the class of Fisher gradient flows of reciprocal law potentials. A first
case is the additive common-precision Wishart parent of chapter 12, where the first step is to test
horizontal conformality of matrix addition with respect to the two Fisher metrics.

Both parents reproduce the entire finite record history as well as the retained configuration history.
Indeed, write the fine path probability as its initial mass times its transition factors. Summing over
hidden coordinates gives the parent path law by proposition 6.10; the record at each step is already
a coordinate of that path. The next record has probability 1/2 + a/8 of being one, so the inherited
response is nonconstant. No independence of the initial coordinates is needed.

This construction has nontrivial reductions and coupled dynamics, but its retentions were specified
in advance. It proves exact two-level inheritance, without proving that the dynamics choose either
reduction. It is exact lumping of a drive­response chain: the fine configuration carries one law
pair and internal marks, so neither level groups two or more agents, and each retained block is
autonomous because the update of a reads only a and the update of (a, b) reads only (a, b). For
any coordinate projection, (6.14) is precisely such autonomy of the retained block in law. In the
reciprocal gradient dynamics of chapter 4, proposition 6.7 shows that this one-way mechanism is
unavailable between energetically coupled agents.

unique local solutions in both time directions. If an interior solution meets , uniqueness from that
meeting point identifies it locally, backward as well as forward, with the solution in . Along the
original existence interval, the set of times at which it lies in  is therefore open; it is also closed
by continuity. Connectedness of that interval makes it the entire interval, contradicting the initial
condition. 

The argument is the invariance of fixed-point subspaces of equivariant vector fields [67] combined
with backward uniqueness.

This result permits asymptotic synchronization, state-dependent threshold selection, and exact
quotients that do not require synchronization. It does not prove convergence. An alternative
retained state or a restricted invariant family must be tested against both inheritance conditions; the
calculations above do not exclude such constructions.

6.7 Memory and formation

When a proposed retention fails, one exact option is to retain more of the configuration. For a
declared stochastic process, another is to retain the conditional law of the hidden configuration
given the accessible retained history. That conditional law determines future predictions. In a
finite model it is a probability vector with an exact recursive update, derived in the supplement. Its
attainable values need not form a finite set. Introducing such a filter presupposes a process and a
preparation law; it is not compulsory for deterministic coupled agents.

The conditional law is not a configuration retention in the sense of definition 6.1. It is a function of
the retained history, and it evolves as a Markov process on the simplex of laws on S, an information
state, moving from p to pT Pz/(pT Pz1) with probability pT Pz1 in the notation of the supplement. It
compresses only when noise or nonobservability prevents the history from determining the fine
state. For deterministic dynamics observed through R, the filter is supported on the image under
F n of the initial configurations consistent with the history, a set that decreases to the observability
class of proposition 6.12 with interface R; when that class is a point, the filter becomes the fine
state. The intertwined handoffs of proposition 6.11 are the case in which the filter is a function of
the current retained value.

Theorem 6.23 (Information lost by a retained history). Let P be a probability law on Z0 × · · · ×
Zn-1, where each record space is standard Borel and the horizon n is finite. Set Ht = (Z0, . . . , Zt-1),
with H0 a point. For measurable maps into standard Borel statistic spaces, let Mt = ft(Ht). Write

                                              67
6. Inherited Parents and Recursive Formation      MAgent Theory 2.0

PtM (· | m) for a regular conditional law of Zt given Mt = m. Let Tt be any normalized kernel from
the statistic space to Zt, and let P be the causal path law whose next-record kernel is Tt(ft(h), ·) at
history h. Then, in [0, ],

                        n-1                       (6.40)

DKL(PP) = IP(Zt; Ht | Mt)

                        t=0
                           n-1

                 + EPDKL PtM (· | Mt)Tt(Mt, ·) .

                            t=0

The first sum is the minimum path divergence among these predictors, attained by choosing
Tt = PtM . Its t-th term vanishes exactly when the true next-record law has a version depending on
Ht only through Mt.

Proof. Let Pt(· | h) be the true conditional law given Ht = h. The relative-entropy chain rule
expresses the path divergence as

n-1                                               (6.41)

    EPDKL Pt(· | Ht)Tt(Mt, ·) .

t=0

To decompose its t-th summand, compare the true joint law of (Ht, Zt) with the law obtained by
keeping its Ht marginal and drawing Zt from Tt(Mt, ·). Disintegrate these two laws by (Mt, Zt).
The divergence of their marginals is EPDKL(PtM (· | Mt)Tt(Mt, ·)). In the second joint law the
conditional history given (Mt, Zt) is the true conditional history given Mt alone. The conditional
divergence term is consequently IP(Zt; Ht | Mt).

The chain rule on standard Borel spaces is an equality of nonnegative extended quantities. A
singular marginal or conditional contributes infinite divergence; no subtraction of infinite terms is
used. Applying it to each summand of eq. (6.41) gives eq. (6.40). Choosing the true statistic-
conditional rows makes every term in the second sum zero. Conditional mutual information vanishes
exactly when the corresponding conditional joint law is the product of its conditional marginals.
Since Mt is a function of Ht, this is equivalent to Pt(· | Ht) = PtM (· | Mt) almost surely.

The finite-window case is the Markov approximation of a record process [68, Thm. 7.3.1]; the
theorem permits any measurable history statistic. Its two terms separate forgetting information from
predicting incorrectly with the information kept. Vanishing of the first sum is predictive sufficiency of
the statistic [130], and for a statistic of a coarse process it is the stochastic autonomy criterion of
Barnett and Seth [9, Sec. 2.3]. A statistic alone need not have a compact recursive realization. To
update from the retained state and new record only, one additionally needs Mt+1 = Ut(Mt, Zt), or a
sufficient enlargement of Mt; this is the determinism of causal states in Shalizi and Crutchfield [130].
The theorem concerns one preparation and protocol. Sufficiency for every admitted intervention
requires the corresponding conditional-law identity for each such protocol.

A handoff initializes the parent from the actual fine state or its declared conditional law, including the
source marks and memory read by future interactions. Proposition 6.11 gives the class of declared
conditional laws for which the parent is memoryless. When evidence is shared across levels, its
likelihood belongs to the joint model once. Reusing a child's record through a complete same-

                                              68
6. Inherited Parents and Recursive Formation                MAgent Theory 2.0

episode parent posterior requires the appropriate conditional or cavity accounting. A subsequent
predictive prior is a different operation.

No parent in the later constructions acts as a source for its children. A parent law can enter a
child's cost as a law-dependent source, but the exact reverse channel exerts no force: if I is the
pushforward of iI i under a retained statistic and KiI is the regular conditional law of child i
given that statistic, then I KiI = i, the marginal of a disintegration. Downward action therefore
needs a declared reverse channel that differs from the exact conditional, and its inheritance must
be tested with the moving-map form of (6.4); no such construction is given here.

6.8 Statistical partitions and their limits

An independence partition is a property of a declared joint law. A tuple of individual agent laws
does not itself specify a cross-agent joint law; taking their product would impose independence in
the input. The following constructions apply when such a joint law has been supplied.

Proposition 6.24 (The finest independent partition). Let V be a finite nonempty index set and

let P be a probability law on iV Yi, with standard Borel coordinate spaces. Call a partition 
independent when

                                              P = PB,       (6.42)

                                              B

where PB is its marginal on block B. There is a unique finest independent partition (P). Relabeling
the coordinates relabels this partition, and separate bimeasurable changes of their presentations
preserve it.

Proof. The one-block partition is independent. Suppose  and  are independent. Marginalizing
the  factorization to a block B   gives

PB =                                                PB D .  (6.43)

                                                D
                                              BD= 

Substituting these marginals into the  factorization proves independence of the common refinement
consisting of the nonempty intersections B  D. There are finitely many partitions of V . Refining
all independent ones therefore gives an independent partition finer than every one of them, which
is necessarily unique. Relabelings and coordinatewise bimeasurable maps commute with taking
marginals and product laws. Applying the inverse transformation gives the reverse implication, so
the set of independent partitions and its unique finest member transform as stated.

This statistical target is the finest-independent clustering problem [128]. Its existence does not
require Gaussian laws or densities, but does not identify statistical independence with agency. In
particular, it makes no statement about autonomous dynamics or future boundary responses.

across the proposed partition would make these endpoints conditionally independent after the other
coordinates were fixed, forcing ratio one. No nontrivial independent partition exists. Continuity of
each of the finitely many probabilities gives the convergence in total variation. 

Exact independence is therefore not a continuous soft-membership criterion.

Proposition 6.27 (Symmetry constrains a deterministic hard selector). Let all coordinate
spaces equal Y, and suppose a deterministic partition selector  reads only a law on YV . Assume
relabeling naturality: (#P) = (P) for every permutation  of V . Let HP = { : #P = P} be
the stabilizer of the law. Then (P) is invariant under HP. If HP is transitive, the blocks of (P) form
a block system of HP; if it is primitive, (P) is either the singleton or the one-block partition. In
particular this holds when P is invariant under all permutations.

Proof. For   HP, naturality gives (P) = (#P) = (P). An invariant partition of a transitive
group is by definition a block system, and a transitive group is primitive when its only block systems
are the two trivial partitions [48]. The full symmetric group is primitive. For |V |  2 only the trivial
partitions exist. For |V |  3, if an invariant partition had a block B with 2  |B| < |V |, choose

                                              70
6. Inherited Parents and Recursive Formation                                                  MAgent Theory 2.0

distinct i, j  B and k / B. The transposition exchanging j and k sends B to a distinct block that
still contains i, which is impossible for a partition.

For a law on a four-cycle invariant under its dihedral group, the only nontrivial block system
is the diagonal pairing {{1, 3}, {2, 4}}, so a relabeling-natural law-only selector cannot output
adjacent pairs; adjacent pairing needs asymmetric preparation data. A distribution over partitions,
soft memberships, asymmetric realized histories, or additional geometric inputs are outside this
proposition. An information-based hierarchy can also be retained before choosing a cut [29]. None
of these possibilities supplies the required dynamics without a further construction. The symmetry
result does not exclude symmetry breaking from asymmetric initial conditions.

The four results of this section need a cross-agent joint law, and the dynamics of chapter 4 evolves a

tuple of agent laws with product recognition. The product of the agent laws has the singleton partition

as its finest independent partition. The one joint law that the dynamics produces is the pushforward

(t)#µ0 of a preparation ensemble µ0, and coupling makes it dependent across interacting agents:

for x = Ax with A =      -1-            and  x(0)    N (0,  I ),  Cov(x1(t), x2(t))  =  1  (e-2t  -  e-2(1+2)t)  >  0

for , t > 0. These results are therefore constraints on admissible selectors rather than formation

mechanisms; the selectors of the later chapters are declared thresholds for this reason.

6.9 Architectures whose selection cannot see the interaction

Two exact statements show that some architectures cannot satisfy the interaction-necessity clause
of the formation standard, whatever selector they use within a natural class.

Proposition 6.28 (Scalar additive closure fixes the membership order). Let scalar parameters
