12. Two-Stage Selection with Exact Inheritance on a Wishart Family      MAgent Theory 2.0

the counterfactual part of (F6) is not met either. The construction is a two-stage selection with exact
inheritance along a prepared contraction ordering.

12.6 Exact joint response histories

The response interface is noninvasive. At each query, draw fresh samples independently across
children and sectors from i(qi  si). For the current disjoint partition , form the entire vector

Z = ((XI , YI ))I,  XI = Xi, YI = Yi.                                   (12.21)

                                     iI                             iI

An action may choose any normalized readout kernel on this vector. It can report overlapping unions
of whole current blocks using the shared batch, so no independence between such overlapping
reports is assumed. Query times and readouts may depend measurably on carried record history
and retained state. Recording an output does not reset a belief or model law.

Corollary 12.9 (Adaptive extensive-response inheritance). For every admitted preparation and
every finite sequence of finite query times selected by the preceding protocol, the fine and parent
descriptions have the same joint law of records, actions, query times, and retained states. This
includes the membership events of theorem 12.8.

Proof. Independence across disjoint blocks and lemma 12.1 give the conditional batch kernel

K = [W2(AI , P)  W2(BI , Q)].                                           (12.22)

           I 

Initialize the retained process from the same fine configuration. Condition on the retained state
and carried history at a query. The same policy chooses the next waiting time and readout in both
descriptions. Theorem 12.5 gives equal retained states after waiting, and definition 12.6 gives the
same intervening events and addition handoffs. Freshness makes the next conditional batch law
exactly eq. (12.22); composition with the same normalized readout gives the same next-record
kernel. Induction proves equality of every finite joint history. Independent external randomization
can be conditioned on in the same proof.

The result is a corollary of two facts: the interface exposes only block sums, whose law depends on
the fine allocation only through AI and BI , and the retained state is a deterministic function of the
preparation and time. Records never feed back into laws, so adaptivity selects only query times
and readouts, and the induction carries no further content. Every decision functional of the joint
record law, such as the expected cost of an adaptive policy or the entropy of the record history,
takes the same value in both descriptions; information gain about the discarded allocation does not
transfer, because the parent has no such coordinate. The informative extension, in which records
drive updates of the laws, is outside the declared interface.

The corollary compares two descriptions of each given preparation. A final aggregate is not claimed
to reconstruct previously discarded records or the distribution of earlier records from a different
preparation. Queries cutting through a current block need additional intersection data. For example,

                    139
12. Two-Stage Selection with Exact Inheritance on a Wishart Family  MAgent Theory 2.0

same-batch sums over primitive subsets C, D have

Cov(tr(U XC ), tr(V XD)) = ACD tr(P-1U P-1V ),                                                (12.23)

which can expose a discarded shape sum. Repeated hidden-child sampling, child-specific Bayesian
updates, and interventions changing the reference potential are outside the declared interface.

Use the trivial principal bundle C×SO(2) and the common left sample action X  gXgT , Y  gY gT .

rotations of the two sectors, and nothing in the potential ties them. Use the collective product-law

Remark 12.12 (Persistent contextual geometry from anisotropic references). Replace the
belief evaluator by W2(0, (c)) with (a, ) = R diag(ea, e-a)RT , the belief channel target by
W2(0, q) with q =  + Mq/N , and the model reference by W2(0, diag(ea~, e-a~)), with the
analogous model channel. The calculation of proposition 12.2 gives Cq = q +(/N )(Mq -N 0q-1)
and P = -2P +  + Cq, with the same shape law. Precisions remain common, evaluators and
targets still add under sums, and theorem 12.5, corollary 12.9, proposition 12.7, and the selection
schedule are unchanged. With the section P(0; a, ) = (a, ), the eigenvalues converge to the
zeros of -2p + 2 + 20/p - 0p/(p + 0) with  = e±a, which differ and depend on a; the
limit tensor and curvature are computed from these fixed points. For the example constants at
a = a~ = 3/10 the block tensor tends to diag(1.168, 0.199) and the curvature to approximately -1.689,
so rank two and nonzero curvature persist at infinite time. Both sectors need anisotropic local data;
with an isotropic model reference the model sector isotropizes and the curvature tends to zero. The
local data are then contextual sections that transform under the common action, so the statement
above that the references are invariant no longer holds; the curvature remains a property of the
declared contextual data, not of the interaction.

The context-constant allocation assumption is substantive. If d1 = 1, d2 = -1 while precisions
and all other shapes are fixed, the parent model sum has zero derivative, whereas the fine score is
the centered difference of two log determinants with positive variance. It is orthogonal to rotation
scores because determinant is conjugation invariant. Its fine minimized length is positive and its
retained length is zero. Such a contextual direction violates exact tensor inheritance.

Open problem 12.13 (Approximate inheritance off the common-precision family). The
common-precision family has positive codimension, and exact sum laws fail off it. By eq. (12.10)
and the shape law, the ratio of precision spread to shape spread is constant in time, so at a join
the precision mismatch is  times a preparation constant. Under moment matching, the first-order
term of the log-Laplace transform of a sum of Wishart laws with nearby precisions cancels, so the
sum law deviates from the Wishart family at second order in the precision spread. Prove that on an
open set of Wishart preparations with unequal precisions the moment-matched parent inherits the
law, the dynamics, and the extensive responses up to a stated relative-entropy defect at each join
that decays afterward, and determine its order.

Chapter 13

Preferential Two-Stage Selection from
Open Law Classes

This chapter concerns the reciprocal law potential of definition 4.2 with exact Gibbs rows (proposi-
tion 4.3); no statement below is transferred to the per-agent or global free energies of chapter 4.
The common-precision construction selects an exact additive description within a prepared family.
The construction given here instead admits initial laws ranging over a full open neighborhood.
Native source rows, read by a fixed threshold selector, select three pairs and then a pair of their
parents. The selection reads only a transmitted bit. The compression is an orientation symmetry of
a fixed selective channel; it exists before the selected events and descends for every partition at
every time. What the events change is the resolution of a declared external response interface, and
the information discarded at a handoff is exactly the information that this interface stops resolving
there. Measured against the formation standard definition 6.31, the main theorem establishes
selection, exact inheritance, and compression on an open class over a finite window. It does not
establish interaction necessity (F5): in the regime of its proof, integrations indicate that the null
flow of definition 6.30 produces the same membership history (remark 13.6). Every block relation
is transient, and the selector later merges the exterior pair (corollary 13.10). The construction is
therefore a two-stage selection with exact inheritance, not a recursive formation.

13.4 Orientation compression and inherited dynamics

For an angle a, let (af )(z, ) = f (z,  - a). An active rotation of agent i applies ai to its belief
and model laws in fixed sample coordinates. It changes the laws, unlike the passive changes of
presentation of chapter 2. The energy, metric, rows, and eq. (13.7) are invariant or equivariant under
independent active rotations of every belief and every model angle, a group (S1)2N . Below we use
the diagonal subgroup (S1)N that rotates both laws of one agent by the same angle. Whether an
active rotation is detectable is a statement about a declared observable algebra (definition 13.14):
no agent, channel, row, or evaluator of the population resolves it, and only the external response
protocol of the next section can.

13.5 Responses and retained histories

Declare one recursive response rule before any selection. A query to current block I draws
independent constituent samples (Zi, i)  qi and returns

(Zi)iI , i (mod 2) .                                        (13.43)

               iI

The model sector has its corresponding independent joint response. Native source draws, transmit-
ted bit samples, and joint measurable functions of whole-block outputs are also admitted. A policy
may depend on past records, but cannot split a compressed block to reveal an individual absolute
angle. Queries are observational and do not reset the law state. The querier is not an agent of the
population and does not act on its dynamics; it reads angles in a fixed angular frame that no agent
holds, since every channel twirls the angle.

Definition 13.14 (Declared observable algebra). For a current partition P, let Apop be the algebra
of bounded measurable functions of the configuration generated by the quantities the population
reads: rows, channel output laws, evaluators, and costs. The vector field is equivariant, so the
population's evolution of these quantities does not depend on the orbit representative. Let AP be
generated by Apop and by the probabilities of finite adaptive response histories under eq. (13.43)
for P. A distinction between two configurations is resolved by an algebra if some element takes
different values on them.

Every element of Apop is invariant under (S1)2N , by proposition 13.8 and the invariance of the
potential. Thus no active rotation is resolved within the population, and the words gauge and
physical have no content here without the response protocol. The kernel in eq. (13.43) is a
normalized pushforward of a product law. Since i ai = 0, it is exactly the same pushforward of
the parent law in eq. (13.36). Its first angular moment is i ui, generally nonzero, so an aggregate
angle is resolved by AP . Joining concatenates bit vectors and adds angle sums. Thus the same
experiment composes at each level.

Equal retained states have equal waiting-time evolution and equal next-record joint kernels. Con-
ditioning successively on the realized history proves equality of every finite adaptive joint-history
law. Prior records are carried forward. A finite collection of sampled angular records does not
deterministically identify the erased offsets: all the densities are positive, leaving continuously
many compatible configurations for the same finite history. An exact record of constituent laws
would instead invalidate the loss assertion. An individual absolute-angle query also fails descent

156
13. Preferential Two-Stage Selection from Open Law Classes  MAgent Theory 2.0

immediately because its first moment changes under eq. (13.34). These experiments are outside
the declared interface after the handoff.

Remark 13.15 (How much is lost). The loss is non-identifiability, not absence of information.
Before a merge every agent is its own block, so eq. (13.43) returns samples of its angular marginal.
For an angular marginal f , the Fisher information about its phase carried by one sample is the
rotation inertia Ef [( log f )2], which is I() below for a von Mises factor. On the product reference
family the phases are constant, so ni pre-merge records of agent i carry information ni times its
inertia about the offsets that the merge discards, and their circular mean estimates those offsets
with error of order (niEf [( log f )2])-1/2. This information is finite for every finite record set and
grows linearly with the number of records. A uniform loss statement needs a protocol that bounds
the number of pre-merge angle queries or discards records at merges; the present protocol does
neither.

13.6 Collective geometry on actual parent laws

Take the common collective group to be S1, acting on every belief and model angle simultaneously.
This tie is a declared representation. The constitutive data are also invariant under independent
belief and model rotations; for the untied group Sq1 × Ss1 the minimizing connection below is
Aq = -d, As = 0, which is flat, and the minimized tensor has rank one. The curvature computed
below belongs to the tied representation. No row, channel, record, or vector field of this construction
reads the connection; AF is a diagnostic of the evolved sections.

The common rotation commutes with the independent active rotations. Use the original sum Fisher
metric and convention DAp = dp + JpA. At fixed time the constants ai in eq. (13.35) do not vary with
evaluation context. Hence dqi = aidqi and similarly for si. A product score is a sum of centered
independent factor scores, so all cross terms vanish. Rotation preserves the remaining integrals.
For every contextual direction X and scalar gauge velocity  this proves

g(dRpX + J, dRpX + J) = g(dpX + J, dpX + J).                (13.44)

Equality holds before minimization. The orbit inertia, contextual momentum, minimizing connection
class, and minimized tensor are therefore identical. On a regular chart their curvature agrees. This
is a calculation from normalized laws, rather than assigning the fine tensor to retained metadata. It
is consistent with fixed-statistic Fisher sufficiency results [5], but the present retention is section
valued.

Under a passive common rotation 0(c), each anchor phase shifts by 0(c), leaving every ai
unchanged. Parent sections transform by the same 0(c), and A = A - d0 gives the usual
covariant derivative. The local Lie-algebra stabilizer is preserved. Globally the total phase has |I|
roots; a common rotation 2/|I| lies in the discarded group (remark 13.11). The construction stays
on compatible local charts.

13.7 The combined existence statement

The inheritance statements above never use the selection. This is the content of the following
proposition, which makes the division of labor in the main theorem explicit.

Proposition 13.16 (Symmetry reduction for every partition). Let P be any partition of the
agents, let t0  0, and suppose every anchor moment is nonzero at t0. Put HP = IP HI . Then
every row, block row, selector input, and event time is invariant under (S1)2N , hence under HP ; the
anchored retention of P at t0 has the original-time flow of proposition 13.12; every finite adaptive
history of eq. (13.43) for the current partition P descends; and the collective minimizing costs satisfy
eq. (13.44).

Proof. The first statement is proposition 13.8. The proofs of proposition 13.12, of response descent,
and of eq. (13.44) use only equivariance under HI , the anchor, and the product form of the parent
laws, and none uses an event time or a selected block.

The selected partition is therefore not distinguished by inheritance. Native routing contributes a law-
determined and relabeling-natural choice of partition and of times. The response rule contributes
the coarsening that makes the discarded directions unresolvable. Before an event the current
partition is finer: a singleton query returns i, whose first moment changes under a rotation in
H{i,j}, and a block query returns a sum whose first moment changes under a rotation in HIJ that
is not in HI × HJ . After the event these responses are no longer admitted. The distinction discarded
at a handoff is exactly the one the declared interface stops resolving at that handoff; the handoff
loss is created by the response interface, not by the selection.

Theorem 13.17 (Open-law two-stage selection with exact inheritance). Consider the reciprocal
law potential definition 4.2 with the constitutive data of this chapter: six agents, bit-circle sample
spaces, the selective channel eq. (13.2) on every edge including self, uniform references and
evaluators, uniform all-source priors, unit Fisher mobilities, and one fixed temperature. There exist
T > 0, a finite horizon, and a nonempty relabeling-invariant set of independently variable positive
belief and model laws, open in the Cr chart, on which the following hold over that horizon and on
compatible local phase charts.

  (a) Selection. Definition 13.2 selects three pairs, which coexist over a positive window, and then
       joins two of their parents while the third pair is a nonempty exterior with strictly smaller routing
       masses. Rows and events depend only on the bit marginals.

  (b) Interface coarsening. At each event the response interface eq. (13.43) passes to the coarser
       partition. A continuous distinction between laws, along the newly discarded subgroup, is
       resolved before the event by admitted queries and after it by no admitted query; no element
       of Apop resolves it at any time. Records acquired before the event carry finite information
       about it (remark 13.15).

  (c) Exact inheritance. For the selected partitions, the anchored section-valued parent laws, inher-
       ited port channels, original-time parent flow, and every finite adaptive history of eq. (13.43)
       descend exactly.

                                                              159
13. Preferential Two-Stage Selection from Open Law Classes  MAgent Theory 2.0

  (d) Geometry. On the declared contextual family eq. (13.49), the handoffs preserve the tied
       collective minimizing connection and a rank-two tensor with nonzero curvature.

The temperature is not quantified (remark 13.7). The theorem does not establish interaction
necessity, and the block relations it selects are transient (remark 13.6 and corollary 13.10).

Proof. Use proposition 13.5 to fix finite A, R, h and its horizon, then proposition 13.9 to obtain
a full positive-law neighborhood. Choose the angular profiles with nonzero first moments and
the equivariant sections of eq. (13.49). Shrink this neighborhood in the Cr chart to preserve the
geometric bounds, phase chart, and all routing windows. Intersection remains nonempty because
the same product trajectory satisfies them with strict compact margins.

The primitive laws are distinct and stay distinct at finite regular times by uniqueness on the invariant
equality diagonals. The selector and inherited rows are exactly definition 13.2 and eq. (13.9), and
(a) follows. The first joins discard their HI directions; the later join discards an additional relative
parent direction. Small active rotations stay within the open neighborhood, and equivariance of
the assigned sections preserves these fibers after all retained profile data are included. Rows
and event times are invariant along them. Statement (b) is the paragraph after proposition 13.16,
together with the invariance of Apop and positivity of the anchor moments. Parent normalization,
port channels, recursive composition, original-time flow, and history descent in (c) follow from
eqs. (13.36) and (13.38) and proposition 13.12 and proposition 13.16. Equation (13.44) preserves
the actual minimizing costs, and eqs. (13.46) and (13.47) establish their nontrivial geometry
throughout the same finite interval, proving (d).

Against definition 6.31 the theorem gives (F1) with the Cr topology, (F2) with finite-window per-
sistence, (F3) with the response class declared before selection, and (F4), since each retention
is non-injective and a pre-handoff query distinguishes its fibers. It does not establish (F5) (re-
mark 13.6). The first part of (F6) holds: the parent pair consists of first-stage parents under
inherited rows, without reset or retuning. Its counterfactual part is not verified, since the second
stage depends on the first only through the partner exclusion of definition 13.2 and occurs when
the supplied core separation has contracted to order one. The construction is therefore a two-stage
selection with exact inheritance in the sense of the standard, with that qualification, and not a
recursive formation. The symmetry enabling compression is fixed in the selective architecture, and
the parent is not a fixed-size ordinary KL agent. The result gives neither a preferred threshold nor
generic selection for arbitrary channels or all initial laws.

Remark 13.18 (Finite depth by collapsed clusters). In eq. (13.17), two clusters of m coincident
agents at ±a have inherited cross mass B = v/(1 + v) with v = e-2a2, and a = -a(1 + 4B),
independently of m: each member's row has m unit entries and m entries v. The late comparison
in the proof of proposition 13.5 therefore applies to collapsed clusters of every size. An induction
over geometric scales would plausibly give any finite number of selected stages on a finite horizon,
at a temperature that decreases with the depth. The uniformity of the tube estimates in the depth
and the effect of the self mass on the contrast at large depth have not been checked, and we do
not claim the result.

Open problem 13.19 (Interaction-necessary selection in the bit-circle architecture). Prove a
version of theorem 13.17 on an open set where the null flow does not reproduce the membership

                                                              160
13. Preferential Two-Stage Selection from Open Law Classes                                         MAgent Theory 2.0

history, so that (F5) holds; integrations of the limit field at moderate separations suggest that such
sets exist. Separately, find an architecture with a forward-invariant set on which a block relation
holds and a later join of first-stage parents occurs; a compression symmetry produced by the
dynamics rather than fixed by the channel, for example through an angle-transmitting channel
of small concentration that makes the compression approximate on the selected blocks with a
computable defect; a loss statement in which the information about discarded coordinates given all
admitted records stays bounded; and explicit or validated witness constants.

Chapter 14

Per-Agent Grouping with Persistent
Records

This chapter concerns the normalized per-agent model of definition 4.17, rather than the reciprocal
potential used in chapters 7 and 13. Each agent changes its own recognition laws while treating
the communicated laws of its peers as current model data. Records remain in its free energy. The
first construction transfers a conditional channel to these dynamics and exhibits a grouping that its
prescribed null never selects. A second construction gives persistent grouping and a physically
noninjective parent with exact original-time dynamics, admitted response histories, and nonflat
collective geometry on a declared family. Its sufficient interface is supplied before selection, and no
second compressive handoff is established.

14.1 What changes under an own-objective derivative

All source priors below are positive and normalized. Source rows are minimized exactly at unit

temperature; this is the Gibbs-reduced convention, not finite-mobility row evolution. At a fixed
configuration let Diqi = DKL(qiGi(m, ·))si(dm) and Disi = DKL(siri), with the nonself costs
defined by the communicated laws. Then

             ij =  iqj e-Diqj   ,       ij =         isj e-Disj   .  (14.1)

The envelope derivative is the row-weighted derivative of the costs. It does not differentiate the
optimized row again. Each law follows its own agent's Fisher field, so derivatives of another agent's
free energy are absent. The probability-coordinate form is the replicator equation associated with
the Shahshahani metric [129]; the construction here concerns its particular normalized sources,
records, and exact inheritance.

The null of definition 6.30 deletes the nonself costs, not their labels or priors. If a = iqi, its content

14.4 A physical quotient with inherited records

Fix the operational protocol before selection. It admits fresh public and marked-coordinate queries
on the primitive ports, normalized generative or recognition-predictive record transactions with the
likelihood family eq. (14.23), and adaptive choices of ports, strengths and waiting times from the
retained history. These two kinds of predictive law are declared separately and need not agree. A
prediction is not automatically assimilated. An evidence transaction appends its actual outcome and
adds its likelihood to the persistent objective. Every finite continuation has finite record coefficients.
Hidden absolute-angle queries are excluded at all stages. An external source-label readout does
not change the agent's conditioning convention; revealing such a label to the inferring agent would
specify another source-row update.

Proposition 14.6 (Canonical phase parent). On the invariant family eq. (14.19), replace each
hidden phase by zero and retain li, Ai, Ci, bi, the presentation laws, primitive port labels, all
constitutive data, event information, and the full record history. For a selected block take the product
of these normalized canonical laws. This retention is physically noninjective at every finite time,
intertwines the original-time full and null flows, and preserves every admitted finite adaptive joint
response-record history, including its dependence with retained next states.

Proof. All full and null costs and retained velocities are independent of i, and i = 0. The canonical

distinguishes a phase fiber because I1(b)/I0(b) > 0 for b > 0. Thus the retention loses a continuous
physical distinction after event data and records are included.

The current retained state determines every admitted next response law. Conditional on its actual
outcome, the same likelihood adds the same binary and marked-vector coefficients to the retained
objective and the same entry to history. The joint response and retained next-state kernel therefore
factors through retention. Deterministic waiting also factors by the exact equations. Induction
over the causal product of these kernels proves every finite adaptive joint history. This is the
predictive-equivalence requirement familiar from causal-state constructions [130], proved here
directly for the declared controlled protocol.

The parent carries primitive ports and their directed own-objective field. No claim is made that it is
a fixed-size agent with one new source row, or the Fisher gradient of the sum of its children's free
energies. Such a sum would add source-role derivatives. Normalized inherited channels act by
projecting to the selected primitive source port, applying the existing public channel, and appending
normalized canonical factors on other output coordinates. No new parent force is fitted.

14.6 The remaining formation obligations

The construction meets the admitted-family, persistent-selection, conditional-inheritance, physical-
compression, and interaction-necessity requirements at one stage. Its selector and phase-
insensitive interface are constitutive choices. In particular the phase quotient is available before any
group is selected and also under the null. Coupling the marked sector to public communication
does not make the separate erased phase endogenously invisible.

Joining two already canonical parent products is associative and preserves their inherited port fields
and histories. It erases no new phase. It therefore supplies neither a second noninjective handoff
nor the counterfactual dependence required by (F6b). The next obligation is a genuinely collective
or interaction-selected sufficient interface, followed by a further compressive inherited selection that
depends on the first handoff. The present conditional theorem does not close open problem 6.32.

a second realization. A causal local phase memory removes the reference evaluation when the
initial collective direction is coherent across context. That preparation condition is explicit; it is not
generated by the recurrence. The unrestricted local-parent question remains inconclusive, with
obstructions for specified memory classes rather than every possible mechanism.

Theorem 15.6 (Finite differential-order obstruction). Consider a rich smooth open class of

Proposition 15.7 (One regular finite encoding cannot hold arbitrary profiles). On a C2-open
class of sections, no single smooth state of dimension m can reproduce every direct public response
law at every c, if retention and response evaluation are C1 on finite-dimensional smooth section
variations and all finite smooth memory is counted in m.

Proof. On one retained-history stratum choose m + 1 disjoint contextual neighborhoods and points

flow. Strict census and window margins persist for small coefficients. The Jacobian of the m + 1
direct sign probabilities is diagonal with positive entries, since Pr(Z = 1) = sigmoid(L1) and
L1/l1 = 1. Its rank is m + 1. Factoring through an m-dimensional state would bound the rank by
m, a contradiction.

This is a statement about one encoding of an indexed contextual experiment, not the addition of
context-relocation actions to the protocol. It excludes neither one initialized local germ, compatible
local fields, a finite generator family, nonfinite memory nor irregular encodings.

Corollary 15.9 (Smooth bounded-jet causal memories). Suppose a finite-dimensional deter-
ministic memory is initialized smoothly from c, jckx(t) and the original initial records. Between
transactions let m = G(m, jckx, c, h); let record updates and the actual-law readout also be smooth

smooth open section class, such a parent cannot erase the common physical phase and inherit
both the original minimizing marked affine classes and minimized tensors.

Proof. At a fixed finite word h, the native k-jet and memory form a closed smooth ordinary differential
system. Its memory value is a smooth function of the initial k-jet. The native fixed-record flow
is locally invertible on its reached regular image; record appends do not reset the law. Its jet
prolongation is locally invertible as well. Hence the actual parent law has the finite-order form
Ft,h(c, jckx(t)). Apply theorem 15.6, including its joint-L2 history argument. The chronological law

past law from a current snapshot or add a reverse-time protocol.

The coherent preparation family of eq. (15.27) does not permit the independent phase-gradient
variations used in these obstructions. Its causal construction therefore coexists with them. The
unrestricted question remains inconclusive: an admissible causal source of the initial contextual
phase relation outside these classes, or an obstruction covering it, is still needed. Genuinely un-
bounded contextual-order memory, differently specified infinite-dimensional memory and stochastic
mechanisms outside theorem 15.8 are not classified by corollary 15.9. Temporal records do not
supply an undeclared contextual calibration channel. The physical symmetry remains predeclared;
interaction-created invisibility and a new second compressive handoff remain open.

Chapter 16

Contextual Coupling of Statistical Laws

The collective connection of proposition 3.9 acquires a dynamical role when its minimized contextual
cost is added to the reciprocal law potential. This chapter gives two constructions on supplied
contextual bases. On a finite graph, regular auxiliary alignment produces neighboring-context forces
and a locally unique Fisher flow. On a flat torus, algebraic elimination of the spatial connection
gives a shape Dirichlet energy and a coupled parabolic and ordinary differential system. The finite
and continuum theorems use explicit regular-family hypotheses. Neither is a refinement theorem,
and neither changes the formation results of the preceding chapters.

The evolving laws remain general normalized probability measures within declared finite-
dimensional product families. Gaussian laws appear only in explicit examples. The selected
potential is the reciprocal objective of chapter 4; its full derivative includes every receiver, source,
and channel role. The normalized product experiments below define the Fisher metrics and do not
turn this objective into a global ELBO. The finite contextual vertices and the continuum coordinates
are separate supplied descriptions of the base.

16.1 Finite contextual graphs

16.1.1 Statistical and contextual data

orientation e : u  v for each edge, positive vertex masses mv, and positive edge weights we.
The graph, masses, weights, agent census, and comparisons below are fixed. They are supplied
contextual data. A change in the agent census is outside the evolution defined here.

At each context there are n agents with normalized laws on standard Borel spaces. For the
reciprocal potential studied here impose the product restriction

finite sample alphabet is imposed.

with the stated smoothness and positive Hessian there. Choose a small neighborhood on which
the Hessian remains positive and the critical point is unique. Compactness and uniqueness give a
positive cost gap on its complement at the initial pair. Uniform continuity preserves a smaller gap
for nearby endpoints. Every global minimizer then lies in that neighborhood and equals the implicit
branch. Under these added hypotheses C is the actual minimized energy locally. For noncompact
groups, attainment and exclusion of escaping minimizing sequences require separate hypotheses.

These hypotheses hold on a nonempty neighborhood of agreement when G is compact and its
action at a common law point p0 is free. At (p0, p0), only the identity gives zero distance. Its
group Hessian is Gp0(Jp0·, Jp0·), which is positive definite because freeness makes Jp0 injective.
Squared distance is smooth near the diagonal. The local implicit branch and compactness argument
therefore give a unique smooth global minimizer for endpoint pairs sufficiently near (p0, p0). This is
a local sufficient condition, not a statement about distant endpoint pairs.

Positive-definite group Hessians exclude infinitesimal stabilizers of the endpoints. With isotropy, the

cost is invariant under

                         Ue - hvUehu-1,      hv  Gpv , hu  Gpu ,         (16.18)

so transport representatives can be nonunique. A quotient version requires a specified smooth
law stratum and a smooth bundle of minimizing classes, with positive normal Hessian in a smooth
transverse slice. It also requires a smooth local representative and constancy of the cost along each
minimizing fiber. On that stratum the same chain-rule proof gives a representative-independent
differential. The gradient uses the induced Fisher metric, equivalently the Fisher-orthogonal
projection of (16.15) onto the stratum tangent. These are additional hypotheses, not consequences
of constant orbit rank. The main theorem below uses hypothesis 16.2 on an open chart and does
not assert unrestricted passage through singular or competing-minimum configurations.

Under a fixed gauge change, transport the branch neighborhood and the chosen initial minimizer
by (16.13). Isometry identifies the two minimization problems. Local uniqueness then gives

                         Ue(pu, pv ) = hvUe(pu, pv)hu-1.                 (16.19)

A numerical branch rule defined by a preferred coordinate angle must satisfy this condition;
coordinate-dependent branch switching need not.

Proof. Use ordinary coordinates for the law families and the first r - 1 entries of each interior

this integral equation gives the variational equation and the corresponding differentiable dependence.

Compatible local solutions concatenate by uniqueness, giving the maximal solution. Interior

normalization is built into the coordinates; the displayed row equations also have zero sum.

The envelope identity shows that the full vector field is - gradG F. Pairing it with dF gives
minus its squared metric norm. Substitution of the law and row components gives (16.29). Metric
isometry, invariance of the transformed local potential, and (16.19) imply covariance of the gradient.
Uniqueness then gives covariance of trajectories. Setting  = 0 deletes precisely Bv and leaves
(16.28) unchanged.

The law and row solution can be continued whenever it remains in a compact subset of the regular
domain. A finite endpoint therefore requires leaving every such compact subset: possibilities
include a statistical-family boundary, a row approaching zero, unbounded coordinates, loss of KL
regularity, a geodesic cut locus, or loss of the selected minimizing branch. Energy decrease alone
excludes none of these in general. At  = 0 total-energy stationarity places no condition on U at all.
The law and row ODE is still unique; a separately chosen diagnostic transport does not become
dynamically determined. Time-dependent frame changes add their coordinate-velocity term and
are not covered by fixed-gauge covariance.

16.1.8 What the contextual energy controls

Auxiliary elimination penalizes variation of collective law shape after group alignment. Pure common
frame variation can have zero cost. A single family on which G acts transitively has zero minimized
contextual cost wherever alignment is possible; collective laws are needed if the common action
otherwise removes every difference. The example retains shape mismatch despite optimizing the
common rotation.

With the local potential absent, the contextual flow decreases C by its own negative squared
gradient. With the local potential present, only the total dissipation (16.29) is asserted: local
forces can increase contextual cost, and individual edge costs need not decrease even under
the contextual flow. In a finite graph, smoothing means this aligned law-variation penalty and its
gradient, not a continuum regularity theorem.

Independent rows have no contextual penalty in this model. Their local equations can react to
changing laws, but this supplies no separate spatial regularity estimate for rows. Independent
communication links and frames have no new evolution equation here. Law-dependent chan-
nels inherit whatever regularity follows from their declared constitutive maps, without becoming
independent smoothed fields. The contextual graph, comparisons, reference data, and transport
branch selection remain supplied; the laws and rows evolve, and the auxiliary transports follow their
algebraic minimizers.

The continuum construction in section 16.2 supplies these data and a local theorem on a flat torus.
It does not follow by taking a graph-refinement limit of this finite model. Chapter 17 separately
constructs contextual displacement transport from regular law, interface, and inter-agent link data.
Its comparison metric is a constitutive choice and need not be the law-Fisher metric minimized
here. No formation, recursive inheritance, global convergence, or graph-refinement result follows
from the local finite-system theorem.

16.2 A periodic continuum base

We now use x for the contextual coordinate and V for the context-local reciprocal potential. These
symbols replace the vertex labels and Ev of the finite construction. The statistical target is again
denoted N and carries the same unit-weight collective Fisher convention. The following hypotheses
and proofs specify the continuum problem directly.

16.2.1 Declared geometry and normalized statistical data

Fix an integer d  1 and the contextual base

C = Td = Rd/(2Z)d, µ = µ , dµC = (2)-ddx1 · · · dxd.      (16.51)

Every field and constitutive datum is periodic. There is no boundary contribution. The base metric,
measure, agent census, and contextual dimension are supplied and independent of evolution time.
Work in the trivial principal bundle C × G. This choice excludes the additional patching problem for
nontrivial base bundles and avoids implicit boundary conditions.

                                             196
16. Contextual Coupling of Statistical Laws                         MAgent Theory 2.0

At each x, agent i has normalized belief and model laws qi and si on standard Borel sample spaces.
Impose the admitted product restriction

                   i(dk, dm) = qi(dk)si(dm).                                           (16.52)

Each factor belongs to a finite-dimensional regular family: it is differentiable in quadratic mean, its
scores are centered and square integrable, and its Fisher tensor is smooth and positive definite
after redundant parameters are removed. This is a restriction of the evolving statistical model.
Unrestricted joint Fisher dynamics need not preserve the restriction. The sample spaces need not
be finite, and the general construction makes no Gaussian assumption.

Fixed bimeasurable comparisons identify the agents' product laws with compatible target spaces.
These comparisons are independent of x in the chosen trivialization and of the evolving state. Write
p = (pi)i  N for the collective target configuration. Its metric is the Fisher metric of the normalized
product experiment

            n  Gp(U, V ) = gpFi (Ui, Vi),                     gpF (U, V ) = Ep[U V ].  (16.53)

Pp = pi,                              i

          i=1

The identity follows by adding product scores: centered independent scores have zero cross
expectation. For (16.52), each summand is the transported sum of belief and model Fisher tensors.
Unit agent weights are part of the declared metric. Other weights give other mobilities. This product
experiment specifies a normalized statistical metric; it does not make the reciprocal energy below
an ELBO of a fixed population generative model. Fisher gradient descent follows the metric principle
of natural gradients [3].

Let a finite-dimensional Lie group G act on N by smooth diagonal pushforward. One group element
acts on both sectors, through their respective sample actions. Fixed sample bijections preserve
score integrals, so assume the admitted family is stable and the induced action is isometric. Define

               Jp  =  d                          exp(a) · p,    g.                     (16.54)

                      da                     a=0

No nontrivial continuous action on a finite alphabet is presumed.

Hypothesis 16.5 (Regular quotient and one adapted chart). There is a G-invariant open region
N0  N on which the action is free and proper. Its smooth quotient Q = N0/G has the submersion
metric induced by G. The initial field lies compactly inside one adapted product coordinate chart

p = (u, r), u  Rnu, r  Rnr , nr = dim G,                                               (16.55)

where u coordinates the quotient and r the group fiber. All metric coefficients are smooth on a
neighborhood of this chart.

Freeness makes the infinitesimal action injective. Properness and the isometric action supply a
smooth local quotient and a positive quotient metric. These are substantive hypotheses. An action
with stabilizers, a rank-changing orbit, or an initial image requiring several charts is outside the
theorem as stated. The theorem is local in this regular region; it does not infer orbit regularity

                                             197
16. Contextual Coupling of Statistical Laws                                    MAgent Theory 2.0

from normalization alone. Riemannian submersion geometry provides the horizontal/vertical
decomposition [114]; rotational shape geometry gives a classical mechanical-connection example
[101].

Intrinsic variation and gauge covariance
At fixed A, set Xµ(p) = JpAµ(x). The derivative of vµ in a law variation U is

                             U vµ = µU + U Xµ.                                              (16.80)

Periodic integration by parts therefore gives the negative gradient of the contextual term as

                   A(p) =                           µvµ + vµ Xµ .                           (16.81)

The second summand accounts for the state dependence of the fundamental vector field. The

envelope derivative from varying A(p, dp) vanishes by (16.65). Since the reduced contextual

energy depends only on u, its metric gradient is horizontal. Comparing its first variation with (16.71)

gives

            A (p) = Hah(u)a,                        pt = - gradG V + A(p).                  (16.82)

The full flow need not be horizontal, since grad V may have a vertical component.

For a smooth frame re-expression g : C  G fixed in evolution time,

       p = g · p,         A = Adg A - (dg)g-1,                  DA p = gDAp.                (16.83)

Push references and evaluators forward as well, and transform each sector channel by Kij(gjy, S) =
Kij(y, gi-1S) in its corresponding agent coordinates. Relative entropy and the Fisher norm are
unchanged. The auxiliary minimizer transforms by (16.83), by uniqueness, and the gradient
equations are covariant. This statement applies wherever both field descriptions admit the regular
charts in the theorem. A time-dependent g(t, x) adds Jp((tg)g-1) to the velocity. An associated
temporal connection or modified evolution would be required; it is not part of the present system.

The principal second-order operator in law coordinates is a horizontal projection of the Laplacian. It
is degenerate in frame directions. Harmonic-map heat flow supplies the shape operator [52], but a

                                                    201
16. Contextual Coupling of Statistical Laws                                   MAgent Theory 2.0

uniformly parabolic theorem for all law coordinates cannot be invoked. The next proof retains the
frame equation coupled to ut.

Dissipation controls the total energy, not each summand separately. It gives no general bound on

obstruction to this local proof. Global harmonic-map results with additional curvature hypotheses
[52] cannot be imported as global conclusions for this coupled nonbasic system. Related sigma-flow
work studies statistical-manifold energies but leaves its general existence question open [27]; the
present result uses the declared Levi-Civita quotient metric, fixed flat base, and explicit regularity
class.

Zero coupling is a separate local ODE theorem

Setting  = 0 in the metric-gradient equations removes exactly the contextual term and recovers
the chosen pointwise reciprocal Fisher flow. Smooth composition makes this an ordinary differential
equation in the Banach space (Hm)nu+nr+nb, locally Lipschitz on bounded compact-image subsets.
The integral contraction therefore gives a unique local Ct1Hxm solution. The energy identity holds
with the contextual term absent. The energy at zero coupling does not select A.

The constants in Lemma 16.8 are not uniform as   0. Nor is the extra Hs regularity of u automatic
for the zero-coupling equation. For example, Euclidean Fisher coordinates of Gaussian location

16.2.7 Scope and remaining obligations

The theorem establishes local well-posedness on a supplied flat torus and a regular finite-
dimensional family of general normalized laws. It retains nonbasic fixed-reference forces. Global
continuation requires the stated Sobolev and compact-image bounds. Unrestricted infinite-
dimensional law dynamics, changes of orbit type, nontrivial base bundles, multiple-chart solutions,
physical boundaries, an evolving base metric, and alternative statistical connections require
additional analysis.

The construction does not derive its base, agent census, references, or channel data. It proves no
graph-refinement limit, formation, or recursive inheritance. Deriving displacement transport from
peer links is the separate construction of chapter 17; substituting its selector into this energy would
require its full constitutive variation and a new evolution theorem. Independent frames and source
rows acquire no separate diffusion. The exact Gaussian sector illustrates the continuum coupling
within these boundaries.

                                             209
Chapter 17

Base Transport from Contextual Agent
Data

A smooth family of agent interactions can determine a connection once its cross-context comparison
rule is specified. This chapter constructs such rules from law moments, receiving interfaces,
and directed links. A full-rank message matrix gives displacement maps with identity at zero
displacement; their first derivative gives the connection, and products along refining paths give its
parallel transport. A second construction aligns the contextual link data directly and admits nonzero
curvature even when every agent backtrack is the identity.

The comparison data are constitutive choices. The message metric and an augmented link metric
need not be the Fisher metric of the joint law in proposition 3.9. The new selectors therefore
need not equal that chapter's collective Fisher connection. They supply a conditional construction
for open problem D.4; they add no evolution equation or formation result to the contextual-flow
extension in chapter 16.

17.1 Contextual data and their transformation laws

Let C be a smooth finite-dimensional contextual base, P  C a principal matrix-group bundle, and
E = P ×G V an associated vector bundle. Fix one sector temporarily. The explicit construction
first uses G = GL(K, R) and V = RK. Section 17.7 treats a smaller declared matrix group. A
context is denoted c; agent labels i, j are not base coordinates. All derivatives below are contextual
derivatives at fixed evolution time.

On a patch choose a reference presentation of E. Agent i displays vectors in a coordinate copy Ei
through an invertible map Ui : V  Ei. Its normalized law i may be a belief or model marginal. A
passive change of displayed coordinates and a change of common reference act differently:

Ui = giUi,  i = (gi)#i,                               ¯i = (Ui-1)#i.   (17.1)
Ui = Uih,   ¯i = (h-1)#¯i,                                             (17.2)

The presentation maps and coordinate changes are C2 and may vary with context. Reference-
independent statements must satisfy both rules.

A directed, invertible interaction at one context is

ij = UiKij Uj-1 : Ej - Ei,                            Kij = h-1Kij h.  (17.3)

For example, Kij = exp(Lij), where Lij = OiTj is a receiving­sending product on V that may
depend on the current laws. General normalized channels need not be invertible; the factorization

            210
17. Base Transport from Contextual Agent Data                   MAgent Theory 2.0

arguments here apply to invertible links only. Neither ij nor its exponential generator is already a
displacement map between c and c + c.

Our convention for a reference connection is Da = d + a, with

             a = h-1ah + h-1dh.                                                   (17.4)

In agent i's displayed coordinates the same connection is

             Bi = UiaUi-1 - dUiUi-1,           Fi = UiF aUi-1,  F a = da + a  a.  (17.5)

Thus Bi = giBigi-1 - dgigi-1 under eq. (17.1), and Bi is unchanged by eq. (17.2) together with
eq. (17.4). Products of matrix-valued forms include matrix multiplication; (aa)(Y, Z) = [a(Y ), a(Z)].

The issue is to derive a from stated contextual agent data. Merely declaring aµ and inserting
exp(-aµcµ) supplies the answer as additional data. The construction below begins with finite

cross-context messages and differentiates their normalized alignment.

17.2 What an agent frame does determine

Proposition 17.1 (A square frame selects flat local transport). Let Q(c) be a C2 invertible

matrix whose columns are declared marked frame vectors, expressed in one reference coordinate

system. Put

             aQ = -dQQ-1, TQ(c, c) = Q(c)Q(c)-1.                                  (17.6)

Then TQ(c, c) = I, DaQQ = 0, F aQ = 0, and TQ(c, c)TQ(c, c) = TQ(c, c). If Q = h-1Q, then aQ
obeys eq. (17.4) and TQ = h(c)-1TQh(c).

Proof. Identity, composition and covariance follow by multiplication. Taylor expansion gives TQ(c +
c, c) = I - aQ(c) + O(|c|2). The identity dQ-1 = -Q-1(dQ)Q-1 gives daQ = -aQ  aQ, proving

flatness.

An agent frame can therefore select a connection if declaring that frame parallel is part of the model.

When the frame is only a coordinate choice, that declaration changes the model under an arbitrary
change of frame unless the connection is transformed with it. In particular Bi = -dUiUi-1, with Ui
as in eq. (17.2), holds the reference connection a = 0 fixed. Replacing Ui by Uih(c) while again
setting a = 0 changes Bi by -Uidhh-1Ui-1. This rule is not independent of the common reference.

Several individually flat connections can give a curved affine average. They must already be

connections on the same bundle. For two such connections a1, a2, put  = a1 - a2 and let  be a
smooth scalar. Then a = a2 +  has

             F a = d   - (1 - )  .                                                (17.7)

can produce Abelian curvature, and noncommuting disagreements can produce non-Abelian
curvature even at constant weight. The weights and identification of the individual connections

17. Base Transport from Contextual Agent Data                               MAgent Theory 2.0

remain constitutive inputs. Averaging square frames and applying eq. (17.6) still gives a flat

17.3 Retaining reciprocal and backtrack information

Suppose each backtrack Nij,j = jiij has spectrum disjoint from (-, 0]. The ordered-pair
subscripts distinguish loops from different neighbors. Define

Sij,j = Ni1j/,j2,  ij = ij Si-j,1j ,                ij = ij Sij,j .         (17.8)

The principal real matrix root is smooth on this spectral domain and commutes with similarity [76].
Since Nij,i = ijNij,j-ij1, multiplication gives

ji = -ij1,         ij = giij gj-1,                  Sij,j = gj Sij,j gj-1.  (17.9)

This factorization retains the original directed pair exactly. It does not impose inverse relations on
the original  fields. An interaction loop at one context is also distinct from a loop in the contextual
base.

The construction may use raw  fields directly, without any square-root branch. Where the branch
exists, including both -transformed and -transformed messages makes their different roles
explicit. Storing  and S retains all directed links, even though their eventual connection need not
encode them injectively.

17.4 A full-rank contextual message construction

Fix a finite census and persistent message labels. Their message space is H = Rr, with a stated,
context-independent Euclidean inner product. A fixed positive message metric can be absorbed
into the columns. Identifying these labels between contexts is an assumption; agent labels or
fixed receiving-interface columns give one realization. Section 17.10 treats changing message
coordinates.

For a normalized law with a finite first moment, let µi = Ei[v]  Ei and µ¯i = Ui-1µi. The law
need not be Gaussian. Smoothness of its moments is an assumption on the law family, not a
consequence of normalization. Define

Rij = Ui-1ij Uj ,                                   Kij = Ui-1ij Uj .       (17.10)

One permissible collective message matrix is a chosen concatenation

X(c) = {µ¯i}i, {Rijµ¯j}(i,j), {Kijµ¯j}(i,j) : H - V.                        (17.11)

Each column has a stated label. Receiving-interface columns Oi : Hi  V , or their link-transformed
columns, can replace or supplement the means. Gauge-invariant scalar column weights may
depend smoothly on laws and rows; their derivatives are included in dX. Column selection, weights
and message metric specify the rule. The identity self link does not imply that these columns span
V.

                                               212
17. Base Transport from Contextual Agent Data                                  MAgent Theory 2.0

Under passive agent re-expression every reference column is unchanged. Under reference rechoice

it obeys

                                 X = h-1X.                                     (17.12)

For example (h-1Rijh)(h-1µ¯j) = h-1Rijµ¯j. The same calculation applies to raw link and interface
columns. Thus the construction is reference consistent when its original link and interface rules are
reference consistent.

17.5 Reversal, finite paths, and zero displacement

The cross-map C generally fails both reversal and composition. These failures do not invalidate
its first jet as a connection, but matter before calling a finite map parallel transport. Discrete
connections and their infinitesimal limits are classical geometric constructions [97].

Proposition 17.4 (Reciprocal displacement maps with the same derivative). After shrinking
the neighborhood of the diagonal, define

                      N (c, c) = C(c, c)C(c, c), T (c, c) = C(c, c)N (c, c)-1/2.                                 (17.20)

                   N (c + c, c) = I + O(|c|2), T (c + c, c) = I - ac(c) + O(|c|2).                               (17.21)

Proof. At the diagonal N = I, so its principal root is smooth nearby. The calculation in eq. (17.9)

proves reversal and endpoint covariance. Differentiating XQX = I gives XdQX = -dXQX , so the
two factors of N have opposite linear terms. Its root is I + O(|c|2), proving the expansion.

The new N (c, c) is a cross-context reconstruction defect. It differs from the agent backtrack Nij,j(c),
retained in the input state through eq. (17.8). Reciprocalizing a displacement map does not delete
the backtrack data that determined X.

17.9 What pointwise links do not determine

Proposition 17.9 (An invisible gauge subgroup). Suppose the only input fields are reference
links and their contextual derivatives, with links transforming by simultaneous conjugation. If a

                                               218
17. Base Transport from Contextual Agent Data       MAgent Theory 2.0

nonzero Z  g commutes with every admitted link field, then no full connection selector from these
inputs alone can obey eq. (17.4) for every smooth reference change h(c) = exp(f (c)Z).

Proof. Every link field is unchanged as a function of c, so all its derivatives are also unchanged. A
selector of those data returns the same a. Choose a point c0 and f with f (c0) = 0 and df (c0) = 0.
At that point the affine law requires a = a + Zdf , a contradiction.

For group-valued links the Lie algebra of the center is always invisible to conjugation. For arbitrary
endomorphism-valued links, the relevant ambiguity is their actual common commutant within the
represented group; a central group element need not commute with arbitrary maps between
inequivalent representation blocks. In the defining GL(K) representation scalar matrices are
invisible to every conjugation link. An Abelian group acting on its own group-valued links is entirely
invisible. The SO(3) example avoids this obstruction because the two nonparallel axes have zero
common infinitesimal stabilizer.

Laws, labeled vectors, or interfaces can resolve an ambiguity if their combined infinitesimal action
is identifiable. Full row rank of X is sufficient in the fundamental representation. It is not implied by
many links: centered invariant laws and deficient interfaces can fail it.

Even after identifiability is supplied, several covariant comparison rules can select different connec-
tions. Column sets, weights, message metrics, and augmented target metrics affect the selector.
Gauge covariance does not choose these data. A finite link collection at one context supplies no
contextual derivative; the constructions require a smooth contextual field of such data.

17.10 Message coordinates, dynamics, and remaining scope

The fixed message space assumption has an intrinsic formulation. If X maps a message bundle
into E and the message bundle has connection , use

a = -(dX - X)QX .                                         (17.39)

For a change w = s(c)w of message coordinates, X = Xs-1,  = ss-1 - dss-1 and QX = sQX ,
provided the message metric is transformed as well. Hence dX - X = (dX - X)s-1, and
eq. (17.39) is unchanged. Fixed labeled coordinates with  = 0 give eq. (17.16). Resetting  to
zero after a context-dependent message re-expression changes the model. A supplied nonflat
message connection can contribute additional curvature beyond eq. (17.23).

The contextual laws, rows, interfaces and links remain supplied fields; no evolution theorem is
implied. If the selected connection is inserted into a contextual energy, its complete constitutive
dependence must be varied. An envelope simplification requires stationarity for that same energy.
Agreement with a law-Fisher selector requires matching its target, action, metric and inputs; the
shared affine law alone transfers no Fisher-flow theorem.

Dynamic selection of the comparison rule, preservation or recovery of rank, singular continuation,
and inheritance of the link sector remain open. The base, its dimension and topology are supplied;
no formation result follows.

Chapter 18

Communication Codes and Learned
Alignment

A communication channel can preserve a transmitted marginal while leaving the receiver to supply
its conditional interpretation. An invertible dictionary instead aligns complete content spaces.
Keeping these objects separate permits a precise account of lost information, learned alignment,
and the distinctions that a loop of communicating agents can resolve.

The constructions take place at one context of the principal bundle P of chapter 1. One group
G acts on belief and model contents through q and s. A frame change is one group element
acting in both sectors. General-law reconstruction uses standard Borel spaces and normalized
kernels. For the matrix calculations, write the belief representation as V = RK with G  GL(V )
and suppress the sector superscript. The model-sector calculation uses its own representation and
codes; using one dictionary for both sectors requires the tied-link hypothesis. Opposite attending
dictionaries remain independent.

For sender j and receiver i, selective transmission has the form

qj - (Tj)#qj - transmission noise - receiver conditional law - qi.  (18.1)

This is a law-reconstruction protocol when the message law is supplied. Conditioning on one
realized message is a different operation. The general-law information identities below apply to both
finite alphabets and continuous contents. Gaussian assumptions enter only the explicit decoder
and tangent posterior calculations.

18.1 Codes and dictionaries

Definition 18.1 (Code of a modality). For general laws, a modality is a normalized Markov kernel

from a standard Borel content space to a standard Borel message space. A noiseless modality

is a measurable map. The linear realization used for identifiability below is more restrictive. A
modality c, such as speech, drawing or gesture, has a public message space Hc = Rrc and a noise
covariance Rc, either positive definite or zero for a noiseless code. The message space carries no
frame of its own: its coordinates are public conventions. Sender j's code in modality c is a linear
map T¯jc : V  Hc of rank rc  K on reference coordinates. Its displayed form is Tjc = T¯jcUj-1. A
message produced from displayed content yj is

h = Tjcyj + ,   N (0, Rc).                                          (18.2)

                             220
18. Communication Codes and Learned Alignment                MAgent Theory 2.0

Under a passive change Uj  gjUj the displayed content becomes gjyj and the displayed code
becomes Tjcgj-1, so the message is unchanged. Under a common reference rechoice Uj  Ujh,
the reference code becomes T¯jch and the reference dictionary becomes h-1¯ijh. Re-expressing
these constitutive data is the reference-consistency requirement. Public messages therefore do
not depend on the sender's frame, and the reference code T¯jc is unchanged by passive display
changes at fixed reference coordinates. Codes are agent specific. A shared language is part of a
shared generative model in the sense of section 1.4: members of a species use codes related by
the frame map of their shared model.

Definition 18.2 (Dictionary). Receiver i's dictionary for sender j is

ij = Ui¯ij Uj-1  G,                                 ¯ij  G.  (18.3)

The general dictionary is unrestricted in G. The local parameterization ¯ij = exp(ij) with ij  g is
used for tangent learning. It can cover less than G: a single real matrix exponential need not cover
even GL+(K, R) [39]. The global coset and exact-identification results below concern the stated
group, and a restriction to the exponential image retains only the solutions lying in that image.

It is owned by the receiver: it is i's hypothesis about how j's internal reference coordinates sit
relative to its own. Content with reference coordinates y¯ for i corresponds, according to i, to ¯i-j1y¯
for j. The effective code that i attributes to j is therefore

A^icj = T¯jc¯i-j1.                                           (18.4)

The dictionary ji is j's hypothesis about i. It is an independent datum, learned by a different
agent, so ji need not equal i-j1. The product ¯ij¯ji is the holonomy of the two-cycle i  j  i:
the composite of what i thinks j means with what j thinks i means. It is the identity exactly when
the two agents' translations of each other are mutually inverse; otherwise it measures mutual
misunderstanding. Geometric reversal of one particular dictionary is its inverse; the separately
learned opposite attending edge is independent.

Remark 18.3 (Why the dictionary is group valued). A model that i holds of j need not in
general be a group element, and the group-valued form is a hypothesis with a stated scope. Four
considerations support it within a species. First, the two agents' internal spaces are copies of one
G-space, and the relative position of two frames of one principal bundle at a context is a group
element; partial access is carried by the code, not by the dictionary. Second, one dictionary serves
every modality, which is what lets several codes pool their evidence in corollary 18.11. Third,
invertibility is used: the consensus theorem theorem 18.16 needs inverses to show that transported
beliefs are well defined along different paths, and group-valued holonomy composes invertible links;
singular path products can still have trace invariants, but do not define transport by group elements.
Fourth, i's knowledge of j is a probability law over G, or over ij in a declared exponential chart;
uncertainty about the dictionary is carried by that law. For agents of different kinds, whose internal
spaces differ in dimension or representation, an invertible dictionary need not exist. The natural
replacement is a linear or Markov map between different spaces, with consistency measured by
global sections of a sheaf rather than by holonomy [72].

                                               221
18. Communication Codes and Learned Alignment       MAgent Theory 2.0

18.2 Reception through a code

Fix a receiver i, a sender j and one modality, and suppress the indices. In i's reference coordinates

let p be i's prior law of the content and let q = (¯)#q¯j be the sender's belief carried into i's
coordinates by the dictionary. Write A = A^ for the effective code.

A conditional law decodes a message under a receiver prior. Reconstructing an entire sender

law uses that decoder for every possible message. For a measurable code T and laws q, p on a

standard Borel space, choose a regular conditional law p(dy | h) of p given T = h, and define the

reconstruction

                q^(dy) = p(dy | h)(T#q)(dh).                                 (18.5)

It keeps exactly what the code transmits, the message law T#q, and fills every discarded direction
with the receiver's own conditional belief.

Corollary 18.4 (Meaning lost through a noiseless code). If DKL(qp) < , then

                DKL(qq^) = DKL(qp) - DKL(T#qT#p).                            (18.6)

This is the conditional-lift construction of proposition 5.2 after transporting the sender into the
receiver's reference coordinates. The decisive proof is the chain-rule argument in corollary 5.3: its
two nonnegative terms are finite under the hypothesis here, so subtraction gives eq. (18.6). The
code is sufficient for the pair precisely when the discarded conditional laws agree.

In words, the meaning lost when a belief is sent through a code and rebuilt by a receiver equals the
full disagreement between sender and receiver minus the disagreement that the code makes visible.
It vanishes exactly when the code is sufficient for the pair, that is, when the sender's conditional
belief given the message already equals the receiver's.

Corollary 18.5 (Noisy codes). Let a noisy code be a Markov kernel K from the content space
to a standard Borel message space, for example the Gaussian kernel K(y¯, ·) = N (Ay¯, R). Let
ph and qh be regular versions of the posteriors of p and q given h, and define the reconstruction
q^ = ph(qK)(dh). If DKL(qp) < , then

                DKL(qq^)  DKL(qp) - DKL(qKpK).                               (18.7)

Proof. The chain rule applied to the joint laws of (y¯, h) under q  K and p  K, which share the
kernel, gives DKL(qp) = DKL(qKpK) + DKL(qhph)(qK)(dh). Since q = qh(qK)(dh), joint
convexity of relative entropy bounds DKL(qq^) by the integral.

The proof uses only the chain rule and joint convexity, so the bound holds for every kernel and every
pair of laws with DKL(qp) < . For q = N (a, q), p = N (m, p), and the Gaussian kernel, q^ has
mean m + OA(a - m) and covariance p - OAp + O(AqAT + R)OT with O from eq. (18.8).

The receiving map is therefore derived. It is the gain O, fixed by the receiver's own uncertainty p

This is the Gaussian instance of conditional decoding. That the decoder is a linear map, that the

the precision in at most r directions are features of the Gaussian family, not of decoding in general.

Proposition 18.7 (Gaussian reconstruction). Let q = N (a, q), p = N (m, p) with positive-
definite covariances, and let A have full row rank. Put

                                    G = pAT (ApAT )-1, P = GA.                                                  (18.10)

Then AG = Ir, P 2 = P , ker P = ker A, the range of P is the range of pAT , and the reconstruction
through the noiseless code A is

                        q^ = N (I - P )m + P a, (I - P )p(I - P )T + P qP T .                                   (18.11)

Proof. The identities for G and P are immediate. Conditioning p on Ay¯ = h gives N (m + G(h -

Am), p - GAp). Mixing over h  N (Aa, AqAT ) gives mean m + GA(a - m) = (I - P )m +
P a and covariance p - P p + GAqAT GT . The last term is P qP T . The matrix P p =
pAT (ApAT )-1Ap is symmetric and satisfies P pP T = P p, so p - P p = (I - P )p(I -
P )T .

The reconstructed belief adopts the sender's belief along the communicated directions and keeps
the receiver's own belief along the discarded ones. Its update of the mean,

                                         µi = µi + GA^ij ¯ijµ¯j - µi ,                                          (18.12)

is a projected message of the kind computed by attention. The direction in which a communicated
coordinate is lifted, the range of pAT , is set by the receiver's own correlations: two receivers with
different priors read the same message as meaning different things. This is the formal content of
the statement that the receiver internalizes the message through its own conceptual structure. The
loss eq. (18.6) evaluates in closed form for eq. (18.11).

18. Communication Codes and Learned Alignment       MAgent Theory 2.0

Remark 18.8 (The link with a code-shaped generator). For matrices O of size K × r and T of
size r×K, eOT = I +O1(T O)T with 1(z) = (ez -1)/z [76, Section 1.8], and det eOT = etr(OT ) > 0.
With the gain of eq. (18.10), AG = Ir gives eP = I + (e - 1)P : the invertible link whose generator is
the reconstruction projector is a dilation along the communicated directions, not the reconstruction.
Reconstruction is the affine use (I - P )m + P a of the projector; as a map of the sender mean a
with fixed receiver mean m, it is noninvertible when r < K. For a square full-rank code, P = I and
this particular loss disappears. This is the precise sense in which no group element factors through
a lossy code and the two are related only through the Lie algebra.

18.3 What messages reveal about the dictionary

A dictionary can be tested only against something both agents refer to. Let a referent have law 
on V in i's reference coordinates, with finite positive-definite second moment M = E[y¯y¯T ]. The
sender encodes the referent in its own coordinates, and the receiver models the message as

h | y¯  N T¯¯-1y¯, R ,                              (18.13)

with R positive definite.

Theorem 18.9 (Identifiability up to the code stabilizer). Let StabG(T¯) = {g  G : T¯g = T¯}. For
parts (i) and (iii), allow any fixed additive-noise law on Rr, independent of the referent; part (ii)
assumes the Gaussian noise of eq. (18.13).

(i) Two dictionaries ¯, ¯ give the same conditional message law for every referent if and only if
¯-1¯  StabG(T¯).
(ii) For the perturbation ¯e,   g, the Fisher information of eq. (18.13), averaged over , is

F (, ) = tr R-1T¯CT T¯T , C = ¯-1M ¯-T ,            (18.14)

and its kernel is {  g : T¯ = 0}, the Lie algebra of StabG(T¯).
(iii) For G = GL(K, R) and T¯ of rank r, StabG(T¯) has dimension K(K - r), and the identifiable part
of the dictionary has dimension Kr.

Proof. (i) A probability law on Rr has no nonzero translation symmetry: its characteristic function is
nonzero near the origin, where translation by a would require eit,a = 1 and hence a = 0. Thus two
translates of the same noise law agree exactly when their locations agree, and T¯¯-1y¯ = T¯¯-1y¯
for every y¯ means T¯¯-1 = T¯¯-1, that is, T¯¯-1¯ = T¯. The set StabG(T¯) is a subgroup because
T¯g1g2 = T¯g2 = T¯. (ii) The mean T¯e-¯-1y¯ has derivative -T¯¯-1y¯ at  = 0, and the Fisher
information of a Gaussian mean with fixed covariance R is E[(T¯¯-1y¯)T R-1(T¯¯-1y¯)], which is
eq. (18.14). Since C and R-1 are positive definite, F (, ) = 0 exactly when R-1/2T¯C1/2 = 0, that
is, when T¯ = 0. For such  every power of  is annihilated by T¯, so T¯et = T¯ for all t. (iii) T¯g = T¯
means that g - I maps V into ker T¯, which has dimension K - r; such g form an open subset of an

affine space of dimension K(K - r) containing the identity.

Messages never test the part of the dictionary that the code discards. Relative to the observable
algebra of coded messages that part is gauge in the sense of the observable-algebra convention

                                               224
18. Communication Codes and Learned Alignment          MAgent Theory 2.0

of chapter 1: no message distinguishes two dictionaries that differ by an element of the stabilizer.
The stated full identification uses shared referents with a positive-definite second moment. If only
one referent vector were supplied, the conditional means would determine T¯¯-1 only on one vector.
Noise rescales the Fisher information but does not change its kernel.

Remark 18.10 (Noise laws beyond the Gaussian). Gaussian noise is a computational simplifica-

tion here. Let the grounded model be the location family h = T¯¯-1y¯ +  with  independent of y¯ and

of a fixed law  on Rr. Parts (i) and (iii) of theorem 18.9 hold for every , because a probability law

origin, and eit,a(t) = (t) there forces a = 0. If  has a continuously differentiable density f with

finite Fisher information Jf = E[ log f () log f ()T ], positive definite, then part (ii) holds with R-1

replaced by Jf ,

                         F (, ) = tr Jf T¯CT T¯T ,     (18.15)

with the same kernel, since the score of the perturbation is  log f ()T T¯¯-1y¯ and  is independent
of y¯. Corollaries 18.11 and 18.12 and the structural results of section 18.7 therefore hold for every
such noise law. The Gaussian value Jf = R-1 is the instance with the least Fisher information at a
given covariance, by the Cramér­Rao inequality for location families. Codes whose messages are
not a location family, such as codes into finite alphabets, are open problem 18.34.

18.4 Several modalities

Corollary 18.11 (Pooling modalities through one dictionary). Let modalities c = 1, . . . , C have
codes T¯c and noises Rc, all read through the same dictionary ¯. Assume the messages are

conditionally independent given their referents and dictionary. Then the dictionary is identified up
to c StabG(T¯c), and the Fisher information is c Fc with kernel {  g : T¯c = 0 for all c}. For
G = GL(K, R) the identifiable dimension is

                  K dim row T¯c  K min K, rc ,         (18.16)

                         c                          c

If c rc  K, equality in the bound holds exactly when the row spaces form a direct sum. If
   c rc  K, equality holds exactly when their sum is V ; independence of the row spaces is then

unnecessary. The dictionary is fully identified exactly when the row spaces span V .

Proof. Identity of the conditional laws of all messages requires identity for each modality, which

gives the intersection by theorem 18.9. Fisher information adds over conditionally independent

messages, and a sum of positive-semidefinite forms vanishes exactly where each does. For
GL(K, R), T¯c = 0 for all c means that the range of  lies in c ker T¯c, whose dimension is K minus
the dimension of the sum of the row spaces.

Modalities that overlap, in the sense that their row spaces share directions, add less than their
widths suggest; complementary modalities, such as speech and drawing when they convey different
aspects, add fully. The corollary depends on the dictionary being shared across modalities. Without
it each modality would have its own effective code to learn, and the modalities could not pool their
evidence about the other agent.
