18. Communication Codes and Learned Alignment       MAgent Theory 2.0

Corollary 18.11 assumes that receiver i hears sender j in every modality. A receiver with several
senders instead chooses, separately in each modality, whom to listen to. Let i(jc) be the probability
that modality c of receiver i carries a message from j, and let Fc(j) denote the form eq. (18.14) for
the code T¯jc, the noise Rc and the dictionary ¯ij.

Corollary 18.12 (Routed modalities). In each exchange let a referent y¯   be drawn, and for
each modality c independently let a source label Jc be drawn with P(Jc = k) = i(kc) and a message
with law N (T¯kc¯i-k1y¯, Rc) given Jc = k and y¯. Consider the dictionary ¯ije of one edge j  i.
(i) If the labels are observed, the Fisher information about  per exchange is c i(jc)Fc(j).

(ii) If the labels are latent, the Fisher information is at most c i(jc)Fc(j) in the Loewner order.

(iii) With observed labels the information vanishes exactly on {  g : T¯jc = 0 for every c with i(jc) >
0}.

Proof. (i) Given y¯ and the labels, the messages of different modalities are independent, so the
complete-data log likelihood is a sum over c. A term with Jc = k = j does not depend on
¯ij and contributes nothing. A term with Jc = j contributes the information of theorem 18.9.
Averaging the indicator of Jc = j gives the weight i(jc). (ii) By the missing-information principle [103],
the information of the observed data equals the complete-data information minus the expected
information about  carried by the conditional law of the labels given the messages, which is positive
semidefinite. (iii) A sum of positive-semidefinite forms with positive weights vanishes exactly where
every form vanishes, and theorem 18.9 identifies the kernel of each.

A modality that never listens to j teaches i nothing about its dictionary for j, and the directions that
the attending modalities' codes discard stay invisible. When the receiver must infer who was heard,
it learns less than the routing-weighted sum.

Proposition 18.13 (A receiver's reading of a code is a dictionary modulo the stabilizer). Let
T¯ and S be r × K matrices of full row rank r. Then {  GL(K, R) : T¯-1 = S} is a single left coset
0 StabGL(K,R)(T¯), and for r < K it meets GL+(K, R).

Proof. Complete the rows of T¯ to a basis of the dual space and let P be the invertible matrix whose
first r rows are those of T¯; define Q likewise from S. With E = (Ir 0), T¯ = EP and S = EQ, so
0-1 = P -1Q satisfies T¯0-1 = S. For r < K, changing the sign of a completing row of Q changes
the sign of det 0 without changing EQ. Finally T¯-1 = T¯0-1 exactly when T¯0-1 = T¯, that is,
when 0-1  Stab(T¯).

A receiver that reads a sender's code through an arbitrary full-rank map S therefore holds exactly
the identifiable part of a dictionary, a point of the rK-dimensional quotient of theorem 18.9. The
proposition also applies to the stacked code (T¯1; . . . ; T¯C) and the stacked readings (S1; . . . ; SC).
When both stacks have full row rank c rc  K, there is one dictionary ¯ with Sc = T¯c¯-1 for
every c, unique modulo c Stab(T¯c): readings learned independently for each modality are then
automatically readings of one shared dictionary. For arbitrary stacks, equal ranks alone do not
establish compatibility.

18. Communication Codes and Learned Alignment       MAgent Theory 2.0

Proposition 18.14 (Compatibility of stacked readings). Let T, S be m × K matrices, with no
full-rank assumption. There is a dictionary   GL(K, R) satisfying T-1 = S exactly when

ker(TT ) = ker(ST ).                                (18.17)

When this holds, the solution set is 0 StabGL(K,R)(T) for any one solution 0. If the common rank
is less than K, the solution set meets GL+(K, R).

Proof. Right multiplication by an invertible matrix preserves every linear relation among rows,
proving necessity. Conversely, equality of the kernels makes the map aT T  aT S a well-defined
linear isomorphism between the row spaces. Extend bases of these row spaces to bases of (RK).
Extending that isomorphism to the full dual space gives right multiplication by an invertible matrix
A, with TA = S. Put  = A-1. The coset statement follows as in proposition 18.13. When the
common rank is less than K, the extension can reverse one unused basis vector, changing the

determinant sign without changing the rows of S.

For example, T1 = T2 = (1, 0), S1 = (1, 0), and S2 = (2, 0) give two rank-one stacks but no common
dictionary: the relation T1 - T2 = 0 fails for the readings. Sharing also constrains the readings when
one dictionary must serve routing and content roles, as discussed in remark 18.15.

Remark 18.15 (Attention heads as modalities). The separation of a sending map, a receiver
reading, a decoder, and a routing row provides a structural comparison with multi-head attention
[140]. A head reads a finite-width code and routes sources, but the usual query, key, value, and
output maps are independently parameterized. Such an architecture is not automatically the
Bayesian message model above. Under the full-row-rank hypothesis of proposition 18.13, a reading
map can be expressed as a dictionary modulo its stabilizer; several readings share a dictionary
precisely under eq. (18.17). Requiring that same dictionary for source selection and content
interpretation, and deriving the decoder from the receiver prior as in eq. (18.8), imposes additional
restrictions. A learned output matrix alone does not establish those restrictions.

18.5 Curvature as dissonance

Let the communication graph  have a directed edge j  i when i receives from j, with dictionaries
¯ij. For a directed closed walk  = (i0  i1  · · ·  ik = i0) define its holonomy H =
¯ikik-1 · · · ¯i1i0, the composite of the receivers' dictionaries along the walk. Reference belief means

(µi)i are in consensus when

µi = ¯ijµj for every edge j  i,                     (18.18)

so that every receiver, translating each sender's belief through its dictionary, finds agreement.

Theorem 18.16 (Consensus and holonomy invariance). Let  be strongly connected and fix
i0. Suppose the dictionaries act as bimeasurable bijections on a standard Borel content space.
The map (qi)i  qi0 is a bijection from transported consensus laws, satisfying qi = (¯ij)#qj on
every edge, onto laws invariant under every directed closed-walk holonomy based at i0. In the

                                               227
18. Communication Codes and Learned Alignment                       MAgent Theory 2.0

linear realization, the map (µi)i  µi0 is a linear bijection from the solutions of eq. (18.18) onto
   Fix(H).

Proof. Composing the edge relations around a closed walk proves that a consensus base law is
invariant under its holonomy. Conversely, let q0 have that invariance. For each vertex i, choose
a directed path p from i0 to i and set qi = (p)#q0, where (p) is the ordered product of the
dictionaries. If p is another such path, strong connectivity supplies a directed return path s from
i to i0. Both (s)(p) and (s)(p) are loop holonomies and preserve q0. Pushforward by the
bimeasurable inverse (s)-1 gives (p)#q0 = (p)#q0. The definition is independent of the path.
Appending an edge to a path gives the required edge relation, and the base law determines the
entire family. For vectors, replace pushforward by matrix multiplication in the same argument. This
gives path-independent values µi = (p)v for every common fixed vector v, and both directions are
linear.

The theorem uses the invertibility of the dictionaries and the directed return paths. A two-cycle is
included among its loops and constrains consensus alongside longer loops. If the matrix holonomies
have no common nonzero fixed vector, the only consensus mean is zero. This does not exclude
a nontrivial invariant law: a centered isotropic Gaussian, for example, is invariant under rotation
holonomies. For Gaussian laws, consensus constrains both mean and covariance; for general laws,
it constrains every feature moved by the holonomies.

Corollary 18.17 (Frustration). For positive weights wij, the consensus energy E(µ) =
   ji wijµi - ¯ijµj2 is a positive-semidefinite quadratic form whose kernel is the solution

set of eq. (18.18). Its least eigenvalue on configurations of unit norm is positive exactly when the
holonomies have no common nonzero fixed vector.

Proof. E(µ) = Bµ2 for the weighted incidence operator B with blocks wij(I, -¯ij), so E =
µT BT Bµ and its kernel is ker B. The least eigenvalue of BT B is positive exactly when ker B = 0,
and theorem 18.16 identifies ker B.

For orthogonal links on undirected graphs with the inverse convention this is the connection
Laplacian, and its least eigenvalue as a measure of frustration was studied by Singer and Wu [132]
and Bandeira et al. [8]. The directed version above admits independent opposite dictionaries.

Definition 18.18 (Dissonance of a loop). The dissonance of a directed closed walk  is the
conjugacy class of H. A declared elementary cycle, or plaquette, is consonant when its holonomy
is the identity and dissonant otherwise. A quantitative label is any conjugation-invariant defect of H,
for example H - IF for orthogonal dictionaries; for general dictionaries the covariance-dressed
loop defect of proposition 2.13 supplies an invariant measure.

Remark 18.19 (A law comparison and a dressed link comparison). The covariance-dressed

defect

        Q(H; )  =  1  -1/2(I                   -  H)1/2F2 ,   > 0,  (18.19)
                   2

vanishes only at H = I and has a positive-definite tangent form on every matrix Lie algebra. Its
nonlinear use does not introduce law-stabilizer directions. In contrast, the law-comparison penalty
DKL(qH#q) vanishes whenever H#q = q and can have a larger null space. Its local information

                                               228
18. Communication Codes and Learned Alignment                                                       MAgent Theory 2.0

geometry requires a declared regular family of laws. For a quarter-turn H and q = N (0, I2), the

Observability depends on the record experiment. Comparing coded means tests the weaker
condition T¯jc(µj - ¯i-j1µi) = 0 on each edge and modality. Grounded messages with a positive-
definite referent second moment instead identify the whole effective code, modulo its stabilizer,
as in theorem 18.9. The tangent statement proposition 18.24 concerns this latter experiment. A
perturbation can fix one operating content while changing the code on other referents, so invisibility
at one content does not imply invisibility to grounded messages. Separately, the law-comparison
cost DKL(qH#q) is blind to any holonomy stabilizing q. The covariance-dressed link defect
eq. (18.19) is an observable of the link and covariance together and vanishes only at identity. These
are different comparisons.

18.7 Learning the dictionaries

Dictionary learning requires a likelihood and a prior in addition to the communication maps. Theo-
rem 18.9 says what messages can teach: a coset of the stabilizer of the code. This section asks
what a prior that rewards agreement around loops adds to that, and answers the question exactly
in the tangent model, the linearization at the identity dictionaries. Centering the prior at identity is a
declared alignment hypothesis: before observing messages, the receiver expects the sender to use
its own reference coordinates.

The tangent model is a computational simplification in two respects: it linearizes at the identity
dictionaries, and it takes Gaussian noise and a Gaussian anchor. Its conclusions split accordingly.
The invisible directions, the unreachable directions and their sheaf count, the split of the loop
space into filled and detectable directions as a dimension count, and the exact identification
results propositions 18.28 and 18.29 depend only on the identifiability kernel and on the loops;
by remark 18.10 they hold for every location family of noise and every prior. The limiting law as a
conditioned Gaussian, the shrinkage and bias formulas, and the variances of remark 18.30 are
features of the Gaussian family.

The proposition states the cost of the loop prior. Every loop direction in which agreement around
loops completes a dictionary is a direction in which the community assumes an agreement it cannot
check. If the truth is dissonant there, a strong loop prior can select a flat representative of the same
message laws, as quantified by the bias term of eq. (18.27). Dissonance is detectable only in the
loop directions that the invisible directions cannot reach.

Corollary 18.26 (Complete exchange). Let every pair of agents exchange in both directions, and

The sufficient condition is not necessary. In K = 3, suppose the pairwise intersections of the two
code kernels are three linearly independent lines. A section in H0 has its three successive vertex
differences on those lines, and their sum is zero. Linear independence forces every difference to
vanish, although no pairwise kernel intersection is zero. Thus triangles can remove invisible flat
directions that remain for each pair separately.

Proposition 18.27 (Reciprocal pair). Let two agents exchange in both directions with L the

A pair detects its mutual misunderstanding only in what both can say, repairs its dictionaries through
reciprocity in what at least one of them can say, and leaves what neither can say at the prior.
When the two row spaces are independent and together have dimension K, the invisible flat-truth
coordinates are recovered as the loop weight grows, while every tangent loop discrepancy can also
be absorbed by an invisible change. Recovery under the flat-truth hypothesis therefore differs from
detecting whether that hypothesis holds.

18.7.5 Without linearization

The next results use unrestricted group-valued dictionaries and are exact without linearization. They
identify the configurations consistent with grounded messages and exactly flat loops. Restricting
dictionaries to a single-exponential image requires intersecting the stated solution sets with that
image. The following two statements hold for the grounded model eq. (18.13) itself, in the constraint
form of the loop term.

18.7.6 Receiver-owned recognition laws

Remark 18.30 (Ownership and the loop term). Under a variational restriction with factors owned
by receivers, each receiver infers its own dictionaries, so its dictionary recognition law is one factor
qi(i·) of a law factorized over receivers. A two-cycle couples two receivers and a directed triangle
three, so the loop term couples the factors. In the tangent model the factorized law closest to the
posterior in DKL(qposterior) has the exact posterior means and, as covariances, the inverses of
the diagonal blocks of the posterior precision [15, Section 10.1.2]. These are smaller in the Loewner
order than the exact marginal covariances. For this one Gaussian target, the factorization therefore
leaves the estimates of the dictionaries unchanged and makes each receiver overconfident about
them. Exact means are a feature of Gaussian targets: for a non-Gaussian posterior a factorized law
generally has means different from the exact ones, so for general laws the factorization can change
the estimates as well. To update its factor, receiver i needs the current means of the dictionaries
that other agents hold along its loops: a loop prior can be used only if agents communicate about
how they read each other, in addition to communicating about the world.

18.8 Extensions beyond the declared experiments

Open problem 18.31 (Learning the dictionaries beyond the tangent model). Theorem 18.22
and proposition 18.24 settle the learning problem in the tangent model, and propositions 18.28

                                               236
18. Communication Codes and Learned Alignment       MAgent Theory 2.0

and 18.29 settle the constraint form of the loop term for a flat truth without linearization. The
remaining questions have separate scopes. For the full grounded model eq. (18.13) with a prior
on G or on a declared exponential chart, establish the limiting conditional law on the identified
fiber e ¯e Stab(T¯e), or on its preimage in the chart, and determine the selection within the fiber
for a dissonant truth and a finite loop weight. The nonlinear covariance-dressed defect and the
law-comparison penalty defined above lead to different learning problems; the latter requires its
own regularity and stabilizer analysis. Another extension treats latent routing labels, which lower
the information below the routed sum of corollary 18.12, and loop weights built from the routing
weights. For location-family noise and a non-Gaussian anchor, determine the limit of the recognition
law on the fiber, which is no longer a conditioned Gaussian, and whether the filled directions are
still recovered exactly as the loop weight grows.

Open problem 18.32 (Codes as part of the species model). Let codes be learned as well, so
that a shared language is a joint fixed point of code and dictionary learning. The expression-map
dynamics of Hansen and Ghrist [72] is the vector-valued analogue on a sheaf. Determine when the
learned codes of a species become related by its frame map, and when learning drives code-visible
dissonance to zero while leaving dissonance in unread directions.

Open problem 18.33 (Dictionaries in the free-energy pictures). The Gaussian tangent learning
calculation fixes a normalized likelihood and an anchored loop prior. Extending it to fully nonlinear
receiver-owned dictionaries and learned codes requires separate global, per-agent, and reciprocal
objectives, with every law dependence differentiated in the chosen objective. Whether those
dynamics reduce code-visible dissonance is a further dynamical question; posterior conditioning
within the tangent model alone does not establish it.

Open problem 18.34 (Beyond Gaussian codes). Corollaries 18.4 and 18.5 and proposition 18.20
already hold for general laws and measurable codes, including codes into finite alphabets such
as words, and the consensus theorem holds for laws as well as means. Remark 18.10 extends
identifiability to every location family of noise. Extend the identifiability, learning and dissonance
results to codes whose message laws are not a location family, such as codes into finite alphabets,
where the Fisher form is replaced by the information in the induced discrete channel and the
stabilizer by the subgroup that leaves the channel unchanged, and to agents of different kinds,
whose dictionaries are not invertible.

The relation to discourse sheaves is the use of private content spaces and restriction maps into
shared message spaces [72]. The reconstruction step additionally specifies a receiver conditional
law, while invertible dictionaries supply loop products. Unknown frame conventions have also been
studied as communication constraints [10]. These comparisons do not identify graph loops at one
context with transport between contexts.

                                               237
Chapter 19

Learning Directed Links under Three
Objectives

The receiver-owned dictionaries of definition 18.2 can be uncertain and learned together with the
contents they interpret. Their dynamics depends on which of the three objectives in chapter 4 is
chosen. A global model differentiates every comparison record at both endpoints. A per-agent
model updates only the receiver's variables while treating the source law as data. A reciprocal
potential differentiates both arguments of a divergence between communicated laws. These
distinctions concern the objective; the recognition family supplies the Fisher metric that turns its
derivatives into velocities.
The general dependency statements and the pointwise record invariance below do not require
Gaussian laws. Explicit mean flows, grounding rates, and confidence formulas use a linear-
Gaussian tangent family with fixed operating contents. The fixed-covariance reciprocal mean
theorem is followed by the coupled flow of all content and dictionary means and covariances, with
either relaxing or Gibbs-optimized source rows. Its global-existence theorem and exact stability
example concern the restricted family of definition 4.10; they do not assert that a full law-space flow
preserves Gaussianity.

19.1 The tangent communication model

Two agents who exchange messages about something they both represent can register whether
a message matches what the receiver expected. A comparison record is a noisy linear function

from its own content translated into the sender's coordinates. The following construction linearizes
that record and places it in the two free energies.

19.2 What conversation determines

Remark 19.4 (The interpretation gauge without linearization or Gaussian noise). Let the
records be oe = T¯e(¯e-1yi - yj) + e with noise of any law, independent of everything else, or more
generally let each record kernel read (y, ¯) only through the coded discrepancy T¯e(¯e-1yi - yj). Let
K  2 and let G contain GL+(K, R). For every configuration (y, ¯) and every belief displacement
y  y with yi = 0 and ve = ¯e-1yi + yj - yj = 0 on every edge e : j  i, there are dictionaries
¯e  GL+(K, R) with ¯e ve = yi, because GL+(K, R) acts transitively on RK \ {0} for K  2. Then
¯e-1yi - yj = ve - yj = ¯e-1yi - yj, so (y, ¯) gives every record the same law as (y, ¯). The
interdependence of belief and meaning is therefore not a feature of the Gaussian tangent model: it
holds pointwise, without linearization, for every record kernel of this form, and only terms other than
the records can separate the two readings.

An exchange that disagrees with the receiver's belief can be explained by changing the belief or by

grounding removes dictionary freedom modulo Ne, common content shifts remain invisible to every
pairwise discrepancy.

The Gaussian conditional update assigns a discrepancy to receiver adjustment, sender adjustment,
and reinterpretation through the three cross-covariances in eq. (19.7). Observation noise leaves
a residual gap, so these adjustments need not reproduce the record exactly. In the per-agent
model the sender's uncertainty widens the receiver's likelihood while the sender remains fixed. The
interpretation variance grows as |ci|2 under the isotropic anchor; at ci = 0 the first-order dictionary
term cannot absorb a discrepancy. These linear shares are features of the Gaussian family.

Corollary 19.7 (Grounding turns reinterpretation into persuasion). Let e be the orthogonal
projection of g onto Ne. Then T¯eCT¯eT = T¯eieVeeiT T¯eT , so only the uncertainty of the identified
part of the dictionary can absorb a disagreement. If the grounded information on edge e is gG¯e with
ker G¯e = Ne, then eVee = O(1/g) and the reinterpretation share of a record is O(1/g).

Proof. For   Ne, T¯ei = T¯eci = 0, so T¯ei = T¯eie. With a positive-definite prior precision 
on e and grounded precision gG¯e, block inversion in the orthonormal bases of Ne and Ne shows,

by taking the Schur complement of the fixed invisible block, that the covariance restricted to Ne is
O(1/g).

Grounding therefore suppresses the part of the response attributable to uncertainty about the

19.5 Confidence under ownership

Mean agreement does not imply agreement about uncertainty. The following example isolates one
coordinate that records and grounding do not read, so all information coupling it to other dictionaries
comes from one declared loop factor.

Proposition 19.12 (Echo around a loop). Let  > 0 and let   2 edges form one loop, with

distinct receivers and one coordinate ze per edge that no record or grounded term reads, with

anchor  N  (0,  2)  and  loop  factor  exp(-     (  e ze)2). Every recognition below has mean zero, and the
                                              2

variances of ze are as follows.

(i) Exact joint posterior: 2(1 + ( - 1)2)/(1 + 2), which tends to 2( - 1)/ as   .

(ii) Receiver-factorized global recognition: (-2 + )-1, which tends to zero.

(iii) Per-agent law-level recognition at its symmetric covariance fixed point: the unique positive

solution v of

                                       v-1 = -2 + -1 + ( - 1)v -1,            (19.11)

which tends to 2( - 2)/( - 1) for   3 and satisfies v = -1/2(1 + o(1)) for  = 2.

(iv) Cavity recognition, in which each receiver's loop source uses its partners' laws with its own
     contribution removed, so that those laws are the anchors: (-2 + (-1 + ( - 1)2)-1)-1,
     which equals (i) for every .

Proof. All terms are even in z, so the means vanish. (i) The precision is -2I + 11T , and the
Sherman­Morrison formula gives the diagonal entry 2 - 4/(1 + 2). (ii) The factorized

covariance is the inverse of the diagonal of the precision. (iii) By symmetry each receiver's loop

source is the convolution of the loop factor with  - 1 partner laws of variance v, which gives
eq. (19.11). With  = -1, clearing denominators gives ( - 1)-2v2 + (-2 + 2 - )v -  = 0, whose
roots have product -2/( - 1) < 0, so exactly one is positive. As   0 it tends to 2( - 2)/( - 1)
for   3, and for  = 2 it satisfies v2 + v - 2 = 0, so v = 1/2(1 + o(1)). (iv) With  = -1,
(-2 + ( + ( - 1)2)-1)-1 = 2( + ( - 1)2)/( + 2), which is (i) after multiplying numerator

and denominator by .

All four constructions have the same zero mean and different variances. Factorized reverse-KL
recognition suppresses the correlations by which the exact law satisfies the sum constraint. The
per-agent update instead treats a partner's current marginal as new independent information, even
though that marginal already contains information received from the same loop. For a two-cycle
its fixed-point variance tends to zero while the exact marginal tends to 2/2. Removing the loop
contribution from the peer messages gives the anchor laws and restores the exact marginal here.
This is belief propagation on the tree consisting of one factor connected to  variables [119]; it is
not a general exactness theorem for overlapping loop factors.

The recycled-information mechanism can occur for non-Gaussian laws as well. The displayed fixed
points, rates, and equality of factor means are conclusions only for this Gaussian single-loop model.

19.6 The reciprocal potential

The reciprocal potential is a function of agent laws. It moves each source through the costs of
receivers that attend to it. The following extension includes dictionary laws as configuration variables.
Registered comparison records are absent from this potential; adding persistent likelihood terms
would define another objective.

For a regular exponential-family source q with sufficient statistic t, differentiation gives

moment instance, including the squared discrepancy about the sender's mean. Its contribution
is multiplied by e in the full potential. The scalar result proves increasing stationary variance
with disagreement only while the other specified quantities are frozen. Competing self terms,
receiver roles, other source roles, moving means, and changing rows determine the full covariance
velocity, so no monotone loss of certainty is asserted for that flow. General non-Gaussian Bayesian
posteriors may also change their uncertainty when records change.

For product dictionary laws in definition 19.14, covariance stationarity gives Ve-1 = -2I +

W = I, the loop diagonal block is the number of simple loops containing e times the identity, so
Ne is invariant under this precision. In the single-loop setting of proposition 19.12, the variance on
an unread coordinate is (-2 + )-1, the same value as factorized global recognition. No general
marginal-variance formula for overlapping loops is implied.

Theorem 19.18 (Global flow in the Gaussian tangent family). Fix a finite graph, fixed codes and

point; along either flow the squared Fisher-gradient norm is integrable and tends to zero, and every
accumulation point is stationary.

operating contents and changes of the reference laws.

19.8 An exact stability threshold with changing uncertainty

The following example keeps every content and dictionary mean and variance dynamic. It shows
why the fixed-covariance mean theorem does not decide stability after source selection and
uncertainty are allowed to respond.

Theorem 19.20 (A three-agent coupled threshold). Take three scalar content laws qi = N (µi, vi),

uncertainty growth, hysteresis, grouping, nor formation of an inherited parent.

19.10 Scope and open problems

Open problem 19.22 (Coupled dynamics beyond the finite example). Proposition 19.17 and the-
orem 19.18 give the complete Gaussian tangent flow and global forward existence, and theo-
rem 19.21 resolves the local critical mode of the three-agent example as a subcritical pitchfork
with nearby asymmetric saddles. Determine its distant stationary branches and long-time desti-
nations, the corresponding behavior on graphs with cycles, and well-posedness beyond regular
finite-dimensional law families. Neither the scalar certainty result nor this local instability establishes
grouping or formation.

Open problem 19.23 (Convergence of per-agent flows). Find conditions on the self, record,
and loop precisions under which the per-agent fixed point is unique and its mean flow converges.
Determine whether the law-level covariance updates have a unique fixed point. The directed ring
supplies one stable non-gradient example, not a general convergence theorem.

Open problem 19.24 (Beyond the tangent model). Keep the product e(yi - ci) and let the
operating contents follow the beliefs. Factorized recognition then acquires second-moment terms,
and the interpretation gauge of theorem 19.5 becomes a nonlinear orbit. Determine whether
grounding still separates belief from meaning at the nonlinear level.

               257
19. Learning Directed Links under Three Objectives  MAgent Theory 2.0

Open problem 19.25 (General laws). The Gaussian tangent model is a computational simplifica-
tion. Extend its conclusions to general laws, with record kernels that read the coded discrepancy
and location-family noise. Four parts are open: the attribution of a coded disagreement among
receiver persuasion, sender persuasion and reinterpretation when contents and dictionary priors
are not Gaussian; the grounded limit, in which the reinterpretation share should vanish as grounding
identifies the dictionaries; whether disagreement changes certainty in the two free energies, and
how that Bayesian effect compares with the source-role moment matching of the reciprocal potential;
and the echo and cavity statements for non-Gaussian loop factors, where cavity messages are
belief propagation without Gaussian closure and the factorized means are no longer exact.

Open problem 19.26 (What agents must exchange). A receiver using a loop prior needs
information about dictionaries owned elsewhere. An echo-free protocol must specify which prior
contributions are removed from each transmitted law. Formulate that exchange through declared
codes and record kernels, and determine the loop information it makes observable.

258
Chapter 20

Curvature Costs and Supplied
Hierarchies

Integrating out contents can couple dictionaries even when the model contains no loop prior. The
resulting action is the negative log evidence of the observed records at fixed dictionaries. In
a Gaussian tangent model its quadratic part measures coded reinterpretations that changes of
contents cannot absorb. Its linear part depends on the records, so this calculation does not imply
that flat dictionaries are always preferred. A second construction restricts a supplied hierarchy to
rigid clusters. It gives a parent density under explicit normalization hypotheses and a Gaussian
minimizer limit, without selecting the clusters or establishing inherited responses and dynamics.

cycles containing each edge. Adding a sufficiently large multiple of that circulation to any signed
cycle makes it nonnegative. Both nonnegative circulations decompose into directed cycles, so their
difference lies in the directed-cycle span.

Remark 20.4 (Which experiment sees a dictionary). The matter term at one fixed operating

Corollary 20.6 (Equal gains cancel the linearized loop sum). Let the operating content be a

Nonzero stationary loop action therefore requires both disagreement and variation of the gains in
this fixed-topic tangent experiment; those conditions are not sufficient. The gains depend on code,

convex global energy has the common-content, zero-dictionary minimizer. Conflicting self means or
other registered records change this conclusion. For general laws the evidence depends on the
complete content distributions, and one operating vector need not determine a stationary dictionary.
Even within the Gaussian example, cancellation of B is a first-order statement: higher terms in
the ordered product of exponentials are not removed by this argument.

Proposition 20.9 (Flat wall walks and a common boundary dictionary). Consider two clusters
I, J whose internal dictionaries are identity. Assume that bridges exist in both directions. For every
bridge e : j  i from J to I and every bridge g : i  j from I to J, require directed internal paths
i  i in I and j  j in J. Internal strong connectivity is sufficient. Cross-scale edges may be
included only when they supply the required directed paths. Let the bridge dictionaries be arbitrary
elements of a group G.

Every directed walk that uses e, such internal paths, and g has holonomy ¯g¯e. All these walks are
flat exactly when there is one ¯D  G such that all bridges J  I carry ¯D and all bridges I  J
carry ¯D-1. At first order the corresponding condition is e = D, g = -D.

For rigid clusters with common operating content c and zero bridge records, if the free bridge
dictionaries satisfy proposition 20.5, the linearized wall loop acts on c by (Fe - Fg)(yI - yJ ). More
generally, with identity internal dictionaries but nonzero internal disagreements, that action is

                                  (e + g)c = (Fe - Fg)e + Fg(e + g).                                                   (20.23)

Proof. The internal factors are identity, so the ordered product is ¯g¯e. The path hypothesis realizes
every opposite bridge pair as a walk of this kind. Fix one bridge in each direction, which is possible
by nonemptiness. The equations ¯g¯e = I for all pairs imply that every forward bridge is the inverse
of the fixed backward bridge, and every backward bridge is the inverse of that common forward
value. The converse follows by multiplication. Replacing products by their first-order sums gives
the generator condition. The stationary bridge equations give ec + gc = Fee + Fgg, which is
eq. (20.23); rigidity makes g = -e.

Without the path hypothesis, separate reciprocal bridge pairs can each be flat while carrying
different dictionaries. For I = {a1, a2} and J = {b1, b2} with no internal directed paths, let b1  a1

                                                               265
20. Curvature Costs and Supplied Hierarchies                                    MAgent Theory 2.0

carry scalar dictionaries 1, 1 and b2  a2 carry 2, 1/2. Every available directed loop is flat, but the
bridges from J to I disagree. Parent-to-child edges alone supply no return paths between these
pairs.

When the proposition applies, all records in one bridge direction read a common dictionary through
their own codes. Grounded referents with positive-definite second moment identify it up to the
intersection of those code stabilizers; an injective stacked code identifies it completely for the
location-family experiments. The group-level flatness statement is independent of Gaussianity.
Its stationary gain formula is a Gaussian tangent statement. Neither licenses replacing distinct
dictionaries by one merely because a single-topic experiment fails to distinguish them.

Remark 20.10 (Repeating a supplied rigid restriction). The density factorization can be repeated
along a supplied hierarchy whenever the required measures and normalizers exist. In the Gaussian
family the parent self term pools child information through eq. (20.21), while the bridge factors retain
the boundary records. At finite coupling, integrating out children instead gives a Schur complement;
representing it within the prescribed comparison-record family is an additional closure requirement.

These statements do not select a partition, prove its persistence, or construct an inherited response
and update kernel for a predeclared probe class. They also do not establish compression on a
post-handoff invariant set, interaction necessity against a null flow, or a second selection depending
on the first. Those are separate requirements of the formation standard. A supplied rigid parent
density therefore does not by itself establish recursive formation or complete dynamical inheritance.

20.5 Remaining extensions

Open problem 20.11 (Formation with top-down feedback). Determine whether a specified
dynamics can select persistent blocks and create parents whose feedback supports further selection.
The construction must retain the laws, records, evaluators, and complete response and update data
required by its admitted protocols, and must meet the compression, null-flow, and counterfactual-
recursion conditions. The supplied partitions and minimizer limits above do not settle these
questions.

Open problem 20.12 (Fluctuations beyond the fixed tangent experiment). In the present

tangent model CP is dictionary independent, so its determinant contributes no dictionary force. For

a nonlinear link model with Gaussian conditional content precision J(), information vector b(),

and  scalar  energy  term  k(),  Gaussian  integration  gives  k()  -  1  b()T  J ()-1b()  +  1  log  det  J ()
                                                                       2                      2

up to a constant, provided J() is positive definite. Determine the complete action in a declared

nonlinear communication model, including its off-topic directions and the signs of the resulting loop

terms. The quadratic penalty of theorem 20.3 alone does not supply that calculation.

Open problem 20.13 (General content laws). Identify hypotheses under which the evidence
action for general laws admits a useful decomposition into absorbable reinterpretations and residual
incompatibility. Such a result must preserve record dependence and distinguish an invariance of the
likelihood from an invariance of the content measure. Establishing a normalized soft-to-rigid limit
also requires more than the finite product normalizers used for the static restriction. The stationary
rank-one and gain formulas are not claimed outside the Gaussian tangent family.

                                              266
20. Curvature Costs and Supplied Hierarchies       MAgent Theory 2.0

Open problem 20.14 (Learning gains from loop records). For a declared grounded or relay
experiment, determine which combinations of code, noise, and dictionary-anchor strength can be
inferred from observed loop effects. The gain-weighted formula is an identity at a stationary tangent
state; an identifiability theorem requires the full admitted record experiment and cannot be inferred
from that identity alone.

                                              267
Chapter 21

Beyond the Existence Constructions

The communication and link constructions of chapters 18 to 20 add a declared observation model to
the dictionary sector. General-law reconstruction and identifiability statements distinguish a code, its
stabilizer, and the receiver's conditional reconstruction. The normalized tangent prior and Gaussian
recognition formulas give a bounded model of learning those dictionaries. The global, plug-in per-
agent, law-level per-agent, and reciprocal calculations retain different forces and metrics; equality
of one derivative does not identify their flows. The induced curvature cost includes its record-
dependent affine term. Rigid-cluster calculations assume a supplied partition and do not establish
its dynamical formation. The Gaussian tangent extension in proposition 19.17 and theorem 19.18
includes joint covariance and source-row evolution with global forward existence under fixed proper
references. Its three-agent example has the local subcritical pitchfork of theorem 19.21, with nearby
asymmetric saddles. Nonlinear dictionary learning, distant branches and destinations on general
graphs, unrestricted law-space dynamics, and inheritance of a learned link sector remain open.

The theory distinguishes three objectives for interacting agents. In the global picture one normalized
joint covers the contents and records of every agent, and local updates are coordinate descent
of one free energy (proposition 4.14). In the per-agent picture each agent has its own generative
model in which its own evaluator and its peers' communicated laws compete as sources of prior
information (proposition 4.18). The reciprocal law potential is a third object, and proposition 4.21
shows that it is not the free energy of any fixed normalized model in which the agent laws are
recognition laws. Every construction of chapter 7 to chapter 13 concerns the reciprocal potential or,
in chapter 7, a nonsmooth modification of it. Chapter 14 separately derives the own-block forces
and null control of normalized per-agent examples. It establishes persistent interaction-dependent
grouping and a conditional compressive parent; it does not transfer the earlier reciprocal theorems
wholesale.

Appendix C supplies a different composition: exact correlated inference under a common prepa-
ration, private records, and a known posterior-sampling communication protocol. Its joint private-
record posterior and fixed conditional reconstruction preserve the declared future messages;
complete local beliefs alone need not do so. The affine singleton-presentation Gaussian case
closes, whereas multiple presentations need not remain a finite Gaussian mixture. Smaller suffi-
cient representations, new private measurements over time, adaptation of the common model, and
interactions between agents using different models remain open. None of those extensions follows
merely from composing normalized local evaluators.

Measured against the formation standard definition 6.31, no construction in this manuscript is yet a
recursive formation under the smooth potential. The Wishart construction of chapter 12 selects
two parents and then their union with exact original-time inheritance, but its membership schedule
is the centroid dendrogram of the initial belief shapes and does not depend on the coupling; it

                                                              268
21. Beyond the Existence Constructions       MAgent Theory 2.0

is a two-stage selection with exact inheritance. The six-agent construction of chapter 13 admits
a full open neighborhood of positive laws and inherits a moving-representative flow, but in the
regime of its proof the null flow reproduces its membership history, and its handoff loss is created
by the response interface rather than by the selection. Both smooth constructions supply their
compression architectures. Their quotients exist before membership occurs, so the dynamics
selects when a description is used without creating a new operational equivalence. The nonsmooth
fusion construction of chapter 7 meets interaction necessity at the cost of changing the interaction,
and its fused parents compress nothing. Every construction is therefore a single-stage or two-stage
selection with exact inheritance, and each chapter states which clauses of the standard fail.

The supplied-architecture results retain their scopes. The profile hierarchy of chapter 11 is an
equivariant symmetry reduction with a supplied tree; the data it discards are invisible to the fine
energy, metric, and admitted records. The collective phase of chapter 10 is an asymptotic-phase
projection that loses ordinary child sampling. The erasure construction of chapter 9 keeps public
child states and its heterogeneity is transient. The per-agent parent of proposition 14.6 preserves
complete admitted histories and persistent records, while proposition 14.7 and theorem 14.8
preserve the actual collective geometry on sections with context-constant discarded phases. Its
phase quotient is also supplied before grouping. Adding a future hidden-angle probe destroys that
quotient, and joining already canonical parents erases no new coordinate. Response sufficiency
depends on the interface: an unrestricted identity-channel Gibbs interface identifies distinct exposed
laws, and child-specific probes, exact constituent-law records, or feedback can require discarded
distinctions.

The collective alternative of chapter 15 exposes every proper block through fixed relative-angle
probes and permits one common physical orientation to be lost only collectively. Its reference-
memory realization closes a local two-jet in the original time and preserves the actual normalized-law
Fisher cost. A finite preparation generator yields a complete conditional whole-patch realization,
with the full chronological record retained. The causal accumulator of proposition 15.4 instead
integrates the local angular velocity from the actual preparation time. It preserves the original
native dynamics and every admitted joint history, while theorem 15.5 requires initial collective-
phase coherence for actual geometric inheritance. That condition is not generated by the memory.
Equation (15.29) identifies the missing initial contextual phase relation for arbitrary preparations.
Theorem 15.8 and corollary 15.9 exclude specified value-path and smooth bounded-jet causal-
memory classes, in addition to the finite-order and finite global-encoding obstructions. They
leave the unrestricted causal-local-parent question inconclusive. More general admissible mem-
ory mechanisms, interaction-created invisibility and a new second compressive handoff remain
unresolved.

The remaining problems are more specific than an existence question. Open problem 6.32 asks for
a construction that meets every clause of the standard with a derived selector and interface. The
per-agent example meets interaction necessity at one stage, but still needs an interaction-selected
sufficient interface and a second compressive handoff with counterfactual dependence. Under
the reciprocal potential, interaction-sensitive selection requires receiver-dependent targets, since
shared references with additive moment channels make every pairwise law comparison relax
on a common clock. Open problem 4.26 asks how the three objectives are related and which
conclusions survive a change of objective. The connection remains diagnostic in the formation

                                        269
21. Beyond the Existence Constructions       MAgent Theory 2.0

constructions. Chapter 16 separately gives it a dynamical role through auxiliary alignment: the
finite graph has a regular-branch Fisher ODE, and a flat periodic base has a locally well-posed
shape PDE coupled to frame and source-row ODEs. Independent smoothing of those rows, frames,
and communication links, global continuation, and graph refinement remain open. Chapter 17
supplies displacement maps and their connection from regular contextual agent data, including a
curved reciprocal-link example. The message or target metric remains a declared comparison rule.
Selecting that rule, continuing across rank or orbit degeneracy, and proving dynamical or parent
inheritance of the resulting link sector remain open. Full permutation symmetry still constrains
deterministic law-only selection as in proposition 6.27. Persistent membership under the fixed
per-agent record episode does not extend its geometric theorem beyond the declared finite window.
None of the results establishes an indefinite spacetime metric, a thermodynamic limit, typicality
under random initialization, or unbounded recursive formation.

A Normalized Internal Record Process

This appendix constructs a finite-history law from an internal interaction rule. The rule is supplied;
normalization does not select it. Let S and O be standard Borel spaces. A state x includes an
accessible record register. Write  : S  O for its readout.

Proposition A.2 (Consistent finite histories). For an initial law µ0 on S, the iterated kernel

finite history, the intersection of these probability-one events still has probability one.

By the Ionescu-Tulcea theorem [82], the consistent family (Pn)n extends to a unique law on
infinite histories, on which persistence statements about later readouts can be posed. When each
record is binary, the records of a finite history carry at most n log 2 nats about any variable, since
I(X; O1:n)  H(O1:n)  n log 2.

Nothing in this construction requires a variable external to the agents. It does require a declared
accessible register and an update. A stochastic A is handled by replacing its Dirac kernel with a

normalized kernel supported on the registration condition. A deterministic transition is recovered
when R is a Dirac kernel as well.

A.1 Prediction followed by assimilation

Proposition A.3 (The Bayesian history identity). For a fixed normalized observation density k

p(o1, . . . , on) =                              n                              (A.5)

Proof. After t - 1 records, the posterior is proportional to s0(dm) r<t k(or | m). The next predictive

Let the presentations m be the laws on a finite record alphabet, let k(o | m) = m(o), and let s0 be

This identity applies to the stated fixed observation model. If the likelihood itself is changed
using the current state, the product of the actual predictive kernels still defines a normalized
process, but it need not equal the fixed-latent expression. Likewise, replacing Bayes' rule by a finite
natural-gradient step defines a different assimilation mechanism unless the updates coincide. The
normalization of a process and its interpretation as Bayesian conditioning are separate statements.
Their difference has an exact measure.

Appendix B

Conditional Prediction and Generative
Memory

A generative model can relate a cue to a different result. Evidence about the cue then changes
the predicted result through that relation. This appendix realizes the general agent model of
definition 1.10 with correlated recognition, derives its exact local inference, and separates that
inference from a subsequent compression of the posterior. The construction begins with general
probability laws. Gaussian mixture regression supplies an explicit finite-dimensional example [24];
its use here makes the model-presentation sector and the retained information explicit.

B.1 A normalized cue and result model

Definition B.1 (Conditional prediction model). Fix a context. Let M, X, Y, O be standard Borel
spaces. Choose a proper presentation reference r(dm), a normalized cue kernel µm(du), a
normalized result kernel Km(u, dv), and a normalized record kernel L(u, do). All kernels are jointly
measurable in their conditioning variables. Define

P (dm, du, dv, do) = r(dm)µm(du)Km(u, dv)L(u, do).                             (B.1)

Successive integration gives total mass one. In the agent notation, take K = X × Y, evaluator
G(m, d(u, v)) = µm(du)Km(u, dv), and record kernel ((u, v), m; do) = L(u, do). Thus eq. (B.1) is
precisely rG. It declares conditional independence of the result and record given the cue and
presentation.

presentation evidence depends on the cue and record mechanism, while the conditional result

B.4 Frames, sharing, and sequential records

One group GL(d) acts on the doubled content by h · (u, v) = (hu, hv) and trivially on the finite labels.
Re-expressing the evaluator and record data requires

a = ha, a = ha, La = hLahT , Qa = hQahT ,                                    (B.20)
         Fa = hFah-1, C = hChT ,  = h.

The evidence densities acquire the same factor | det h|-1, so the weights are invariant; the condi-
tional means and covariances transform by h and congruence. This follows directly by substitution
into eq. (B.10). In local token frames Ui, the reference cue (Ui-1µi, Ui-1iUi-T ) is invariant under a
simultaneous passive change of frame and local moments. A singular Fa still defines a normalized
response kernel; it is not a group-valued dictionary.

Sharing a bank supplies common reference and evaluator data. Sharing a generative model
in the sense of definition 1.11 also requires matched record kernels under the declared frame
maps. Different covariances Ci instead give a shared family of conditional mechanisms indexed by
supplied side information. The distinction must be stated if uncertainty varies between agents. A
diagonal reference parametrization is not closed under arbitrary rebasing: if hDhT is diagonal for
every positive diagonal D, its off-diagonal entries force hikhjk = 0 for i = j, so invertibility makes h
a permutation times an invertible diagonal matrix. This restriction on the reference parametrization
does not remove local passive covariance with that reference fixed.

Definition B.7 (An exact carried-presentation filter). Let the finite label evolve by a fixed row-

Appendix A distinguishes normalization of a history from exact Bayesian assimilation under its
record mechanism. That distinction applies here. If O2 = f (O1) and O1 is already registered,
conditioning on (O1, O2) is the same as conditioning on O1; an independent-replicate likelihood
would count the evidence again. Communication may bring information that is new to one receiver
even in a deterministic population computation. A repeated conditional-prediction agent must
therefore specify its accessible history, communication-generated record, retained joint law, and
any projection. The local identities above establish neither a common free energy for an arbitrary
composition nor a new formation result.

                                                 280
Appendix C

Interacting Conditional-Prediction
Agents

The conditional model of appendix B becomes an interacting system once a transmitted result
has an actual record law. This appendix supplies one such law. Two agents share a normalized
preparation and a communication protocol, receive separate private records, and exchange fresh
samples from their current result predictions. The receiver conditions on the sender's sampling
mechanism, including its inaccessible private evidence. For every finite history outside the usual
conditioning null sets, the resulting posterior can be reconstructed from the joint posterior of the
private records and one fixed conditional kernel. This is an exact representation before any moment
projection.

The common preparation, its cross-agent coupling, the private sensors, and reliable registration
of the transcript are constitutive assumptions. Sharing a local bank does not supply them. The
distinction between common information and privately evaluated prescriptions is familiar from
decentralized control [112]. Here the prescription is fixed to posterior-predictive transmission; the
results below concern its normalized law and Bayesian conditioning, without an optimal-control
assertion. All variables are defined at one context. No connection, continuous-time flow, or
identification with the reciprocal law potential is assumed.

C.1 Preparation, information, and transmission

For i  {0, 1}, let Ai, Xi, Yi, and Di be standard Borel spaces of model presentations, cues, results,
and private records. Write Zi = (Ai, Xi, Yi) and Z = (Z0, Z1). A proper presentation law ri, a
normalized cue kernel µi,a, and a normalized result kernel Ki,a define the local bank

                i(da, du, dv) = ri(da)µi,a(du)Ki,a(u, dv).                          (C.1)

Choose a probability coupling P0 of 0 and 1. For example, any coupling  of the two presenta-
tion/cue laws gives

                P0(dz0, dz1) = (da0, du0, da1, du1)K0,a0 (u0, dv0)K1,a1 (u1, dv1).  (C.2)

Each result factor integrates to one, so this is normalized and has the required local marginals.
More general couplings with those marginals are allowed in the general construction.

Let Li : Xi  Di be normalized private-record kernels, and put D = (D0, D1) and E = (Z, D). The

preparation is

                0(dz, dd) = P0(dz0, dz1)L0(u0, dd0)L1(u1, dd1).                     (C.3)

         i,0(dai, dui, dvi) = P (Zi  · | Di = di) = si,0(dai)qi,0(dui, dvi | ai).  (C.4)

The preparation may be realized by concealed internal values Z followed by their records. Alterna-

Proof. Condition eq. (C.12) further on Dj = dj. Its message factor is constant in every remaining
variable, so it cancels from the conditional numerator and denominator. This proves invariance of
the entire private posterior; eq. (C.8) gives the same conclusion without densities. For the receiver,
first condition the actual message kernel on (Zi, Di, Ht). The remaining private coordinate has law
eq. (C.14); integrating it gives the first equation of eq. (C.15). Marginalizing the private joint update
then gives the second.

The conditional law Rij,t carries the relationship between the receiver's represented state and the
sender's evidence. A local marginal i,t does not in general specify it. If a message policy reads only
common information, its factor is independent of both private values and cancels from the common
posterior as well. A deterministic echo of an already registered message has this property in the
kernel formulation. A fresh posterior sample can instead convey the speaker's private evidence to
its peer, while leaving the speaker's own posterior unchanged.

There is an exact information restriction for the fixed preparation. Every factor in eq. (C.10) depends
on E only through D at a fixed transcript. Thus Z and H1:n are conditionally independent given D,
and, when the mutual informations are finite,

I(Z; H1:n | Di) = I(Z; D1-i | Di) - I(Z; D1-i | Di, H1:n).                                 (C.16)

Indeed, expand I(Z; (D1-i, H1:n) | Di) in the two possible orders; the term conditioned on both
private records vanishes. The protocol redistributes evidence from the preparation. New measure-
ments require an additional observation mechanism.

The sufficient state for an agent includes the fixed preparation, reconstruction and encoders, its
private value, the joint t, and the next speaker. When queries of actual past records are admitted,

Ri,t = P0, L0, L1, W, C0, C1, di, t, jt+1, H1:t .                                      (C.23)

                                              285
C. Interacting Conditional-Prediction Agents             MAgent Theory 2.0

Equality of these states gives the same current private posterior and, by theorem C.5, the same
joint conditional laws for all future protocol messages and represented-variable readouts. The
last coordinate preserves the literal transcript; its values need not be recoverable from t. This
separates inferential sufficiency from persistence of the full admitted record interface.

On the family {W }, the map W    is invertible by the fixed reconstruction. It removes
redundant changing coordinates, rather than asserting a lossy parent compression in the sense
of definition 6.1. The fixed W can be large, and a law on continuous private-record spaces need
not have a finite description. Keeping only the two private-record marginals would also discard the
conditional pair law in eq. (C.20).

The supplied coupling has a separate role. If the preparation factorizes across (Z0, D0) and (Z1, D1),
its fixed-history likelihood is a product of a function of D0 and a function of D1, even though the
factors use the observed prefix. The common posterior consequently remains a product across the
two agents. After conditioning on its own private record, an agent's own represented-state posterior
cannot change when its peer speaks. It may learn about the peer, but information transfer to its
own target requires a cross-agent relation supplied by the model.

Theorem C.9 (Repeated affine Gaussian closure). Suppose each agent has one presentation,
the joint cue covariance is positive definite, and all result kernels, private sensors, and encoders
are affine Gaussian with positive-definite noise covariances. For every finite protocol history, the
common private-record posterior t is a nondegenerate joint Gaussian. Its mean and full covariance,
together with the fixed Gaussian reconstruction W , determine every posterior and future message
law in theorem C.5.

Proof. After the fixed singleton labels are suppressed, the preparation makes (Z, D) jointly Gaus-
sian and 0 nondegenerate. Completing its quadratic gives W (d, dz) an affine mean in d and a
covariance independent of d. Suppose t = N (mt, St) with St  0. Then W t is jointly Gaussian.
Conditioning its Yj coordinate on Dj = dj gives an affine mean and constant covariance. After
fresh sampling and encoding, the message therefore has a representation

       Ht+1 = bt + AtD + t, t  N (0, Rt), Rt  0,                                                   (C.58)

where At reads only the speaker coordinate and t is independent of D at the fixed prefix. The
coefficients are fixed by the current common state. Multiplying the Gaussian prior density by this
likelihood completes a quadratic with

               St-+11 = St-1 + ATt Rt-1At,                                                         (C.59)
               mt+1 = St+1 St-1mt + ATt Rt-1(ht+1 - bt) .

The precision remains positive definite. Induction gives the claimed closure for every finite stage;
theorem C.5 gives the reconstruction and future-law assertion.

                                                   293
C. Interacting Conditional-Prediction Agents                                                  MAgent Theory 2.0

The retained covariance in this theorem is the joint covariance of (D0, D1). Replacing it by separate-
agent blocks changes the conditional averages in eq. (C.20). The Gaussian family is an exact
special case of the general filter, rather than an assumed closure for multiple presentations.

C.8 Local beliefs do not generally determine the next update

Proposition C.11 (A reachable collision of local-only retention). There is one fixed finite
preparation, a public preparation record, and a posterior-sampling policy with two positive-probability
registered histories having the same pair of complete local recognition laws and private values, but
different receiver updates under the same next message. Thus retaining the local joint laws while
deleting the distinguishing public record and cross-agent dependence does not define an exact
closed assimilation rule.

Proof. Draw X0 fairly and an independent bit B with P (B = 0) = , 0 <  < 1, and set X1 = X0 B.
Conditional on the cues, generate presentations and results as in eq. (C.34). Each local bank is
unchanged. Register the deterministic public preparation readout

                                 C = X0  X1 = B.                                                          (C.64)

Let D0 =  be uninformative and let P (D1 = X1 | X1) = 3/4, with independent sensor noise. Both
parity records occur with positive probability. Given either parity, each individual cue remains fair.
The local laws of (Ai, Xi, Yi) are consequently identical under C = 0 and C = 1. The entire local
law of (A1, X1, Y1, D1) is independent of C, so the sender's local posterior at either fixed value
D1 = d is also identical. Agent 0's local posterior and the actual private values are the same in
these two histories as well.

Let T retain the pair of local joint recognition laws, fixed local banks, private values, and schedule,
while deleting C and the corresponding cross-agent dependence. The two histories have equal T .
Their exact updates after the same admissible message have different T by eqs. (C.66) and (C.67).
They therefore violate the retained-fiber condition of proposition 6.2, which is necessary for an
update defined solely on T .

Keeping C resolves this particular collision. In the private-record representation, one may first
condition the preparation on C and retain WC = P (Z  · | D, C) together with P (D  · | C, H).
Alternatively, one may include the preparation record among the retained coordinates. A complete
common posterior also preserves its effect. The counterexample proves neither minimality of that
posterior nor failure for every fixed initialization; it gives two reachable histories of the specified
preparation. It uses exact local label/content laws throughout, so its lost information is cross-agent
and historical even before any moment projection.

For comparison, if a local label/result posterior A,Y has label marginal w, finite second moments

with nondegenerate covariance, and Gaussian result moment match qG, then, whenever the relative

entropies are finite,

                       DKL(A,Y w  qG) = I(A; Y ) + DKL(Y qG).  (C.68)

Insert w  Y into the logarithmic density ratio and integrate to obtain the identity. This separates
local label/result dependence from non-Gaussian result information, as in proposition B.5. It
does not supply the additional private-evidence conditional in eq. (C.14). An approximation to the
common state must specify that reconstruction as well. A Gaussian output stored alongside a
complete reconstructible transcript is a different retention from one that deletes the distinguishing
information.

Open problem C.12 (Smaller sufficient states and changing preparations). For multiple
presentations, determine a smaller protocol-specific state that preserves every admitted future
message law and receiver update, or specify an approximation together with the conditional recon-
struction it changes. The exact joint-private-record representation does not establish minimality
or finite descriptive complexity on continuous spaces. New private observations, adaptation of
the shared model, differing agent models, or unknown transmission policies require their own
normalized mechanisms. These extensions, and any inherited recursive formation, are separate
from the fixed-preparation communication theorem proved here.

Appendix D

Connections in a Moving Presentation

Links between agents at a single context do not determine transport between neighboring contexts.
A connection requires a smooth dependence on the direction and size of a base displacement. This
appendix records, in matrix form, the transformation law of connection data supplied in a moving
presentation: given a presentation Ui and a one-form ai, it computes the displayed connection
and curvature and their behavior under changes of coordinates. The one-form ai is supplied for
the transformation calculation in this appendix. Chapter 17 separately constructs it from regular
contextual laws, interfaces, and links. The remaining selection and continuation questions are open
problem D.4. Collective least-squares selection in proposition 3.9 is a separate construction. The
context-local and formation flows use it diagnostically. The added energy in chapter 16 instead
makes collective alignment enter the law velocity through a contextual force.

Fix one sector and one agent, suppressing the sector superscript. On a coordinate neighborhood
of C, let Ui(c) be a twice continuously differentiable invertible presentation and let ai = ai,µ(c)dcµ
be a continuously differentiable matrix-valued one-form. For a principal G-connection its values
must lie in the represented Lie algebra. General endomorphism-valued forms instead describe
connections for the extended general linear frame bundle.

Definition D.1 (Infinitesimal directional transport). The proposed transport family has first-order

behavior

          i(c + c, c) = Ui(c + c) exp[-ai,µ(c)cµ]Ui(c)-1 + O(|c|2).            (D.1)

The first-order generator is linear in the tangent displacement. A single finite matrix at c supplies
neither this linear dependence nor the identity value at zero displacement.

Proposition D.2 (Connection and curvature). With the convention Di = d + Bi, eq. (D.1) has
connection and curvature

          Bi = UiaiUi-1 - dUiUi-1,  Fi = Ui(dai + ai  ai)Ui-1.                 (D.2)

Proof. Expanding the two factors at c gives i = I + (dUiUi-1 - UiaiUi-1)(c) + O(|c|2), which
identifies Bi. Acting on a vector-valued function gives the operator identity d + Bi = Ui(d + ai)Ui-1.
Squaring it yields (d + Bi)2 = Ui(d + ai)2Ui-1, and the squares act by the curvature two-forms in
eq. (D.2).

For an explicit curved example, take Ui = I over an open subset of R2 and set

          ai,x = E12,                    ai,y = E21.                           (D.3)

                                    297
D. Connections in a Moving Presentation                        MAgent Theory 2.0

Both are supplied rank-one receiving­sending products, while their derivatives vanish. Neverthe-

less,

                                       10                      (D.4)
          Fi,xy = [E12, E21] = 0 -1 = 0.

Thus even constant directional interfaces can give curvature through noncommutativity. By contrast,
replacing a finite pointwise map by a new frame V (c) and setting B = -dV V -1 gives zero curvature:
it is the case a = 0 of eq. (D.2).

Finite paths use the solution of

          d                                   Ti(0) = I.       (D.5)
          dt Ti(t) = -Bi( (t))Ti(t),

Uniqueness of this linear equation gives composition under concatenation and inversion under path
reversal. The solution is the path-ordered exponential; the usual link and Wilson-line constructions
use this ordering [137]. Independently declared opposite attending edges are not two orientations
of this same path and need not be inverses.

Proposition D.3 (Compatibility under re-expression). Under an agent-coordinate change Ui =
giUi with the same reference form,

          Bi = giBigi-1 - dgigi-1.                             (D.6)

Under a change of reference presentation Ui = Uih, keeping the same intrinsic transport instead

requires

                                         ai = h-1aih + h-1dh.  (D.7)

Proof. Insert giUi into eq. (D.2) and apply the product rule. Inserting Uih and eq. (D.7) cancels the
two terms containing dh, leaving the original Bi.

The same affine law must hold between overlapping coordinate patches. A directional interface
product transforming only by conjugation is a tensorial one-form. It can describe the difference
between two connections, but it is not by itself the full affine connection data. Constructing
displacement links with the endpoint transformation law and then differentiating them is one way to
obtain the required inhomogeneous term.

If patch coordinates satisfy v = gv, their transition functions must obey gg = g on triple
overlaps. The displayed affine law then makes the local connections compatible. A nontrivial bundle
need not admit a single global presentation Ui. Even on a trivial bundle, zero curvature does not
imply path independence: the scalar connection B = bd on the circle is flat but has holonomy
e-2b, which differs from one for real b = 0. Global path independence requires trivial holonomy as
well as local flatness.

Different agents may be assigned different connection data in their own presentations. Since all
agents are sections of one associated bundle, these data define one connection on P only when,
after re-expression in a common frame, their local forms agree and satisfy its overlap relations;
otherwise they are several connections on the same bundle, each used by one agent. Neither case
requires an averaging construction.

                                         298
D. Connections in a Moving Presentation       MAgent Theory 2.0

Open problem D.4 (Selecting and continuing interaction-derived transport). The full-rank
construction in theorems 17.3 and 17.5 supplies displacement identity, a linear first jet, compatible
endpoint laws, and path transport from contextual law and link messages. The regular alignment
construction in proposition 17.8 gives another selector, and its reciprocal-link example has nonzero
curvature. Both require a declared comparison rule. The directed backtrack sector can enter the
data and is not identified with the reversal of a contextual path.

The remaining problem is to select the message labels, column weights, or augmented comparison
metric from a stated agent model, and to establish continuation when rank or infinitesimal identifia-
bility fails. Link-only data cannot identify a continuous gauge subgroup that fixes every input, as
proposition 17.9 proves. A selector also needs new dynamical analysis before it can replace the
law-Fisher auxiliary field in chapter 16: its full constitutive derivative must enter the energy variation.
Neither construction derives the contextual base, its topology, or its dimension.

A Conditional Determinant Geometry

The collective construction of proposition 3.9 does not require a Lorentzian target. This appendix
gives one additional choice for a complex rank-two representation. Its indefinite form is supplied by
a determinant; the Fisher metric used to choose the connection remains positive.

the real rank-four bundle Herm(W ) with Hermitian matrices transforming by H = gHg. Suppose

smooth on the admitted regular families. With the same declared positive weights as in the collective
metric, set

Proposition E.2 (Rank of the aggregate jet for proper complex Gaussian targets). Let pi be

centered proper complex Gaussian laws with positive-definite covariances Mi, i = 1, . . . , n, with
the collective metric i wi tr(Mi-1hiMi-1ki) and the action M  gM g. Then

                  H = (hi)i :           wiMi-1hi = 0 ,  dM(h) = wihi.             (E.7)

                                     i                                      i

dM|H is at most three, so e cannot be an isomorphism on a four-dimensional base there. For n = 4,

at M1 = I, M2 = 2I, M3 = diag(1, 2), M4 =  21           with unit weights, the orbit has dimension

Proof. An orbit direction is (Mi + Mi)i for   gl(2, C). By cyclicity of the trace its pairing
with (hi)i is 2 Re tr(B) with B = i wihiMi-1. This vanishes for all  exactly when B = 0,
equivalently when B = i wiMi-1hi = 0; this proves eq. (E.7). For n = 1 it forces h1 = 0. Put
ki = wihi. For n = 3, dim H = 12 - 7 = 5, and the rank of dM|H is 5 minus the dimension of
{k : i ki = 0, i Mi-1ki = 0}. Eliminating k3 leaves Ak1 + Bk2 = 0 with A = M1-1 - M3-1 and
B = M2-1 - M3-1. When A, B are invertible, (k1, k2) = (A-1, -B-1) and (A-1BA-1, -A-1) are
Hermitian solutions, independent unless B is a multiple of A. So the rank is at most three on

the complement of a proper real-algebraic subset, which is dense in the open set of triples with

seven-dimensional orbits. The rank of a smoothly varying linear map is lower semicontinuous,

so the set where it is at least four is open; being disjoint from a dense set, it is empty. For the

four-agent tuple, a unitary g fixing diag(1, 2) is diagonal, and a diagonal unitary fixing M4 is scalar,

so the stabilizer is the central circle and the orbit has dimension seven. Given a Hermitian S, the
choice k1 = -S, k2 = 2S, k3 = k4 = 0 satisfies i Mi-1ki = 0 and i ki = S.

The bound for three agents holds only on the stratum of maximal orbit dimension. Off it the horizontal
space grows: two agents with proportional covariances M and 2M have a four-dimensional orbit, H
of dimension four, and dM|H surjective by the same choice of k. A section supplying an invertible e
is still required; the proposition shows only where one can exist. For improper complex laws the
central phase acts nontrivially on the pseudo-covariance E[zzT ], which transforms as gP gT , so the
normal equation can then determine the phase component of the connection; we do not develop
that case. Surjectivity of the horizontal differential of M establishes the availability of such a jet
at a law tuple, but does not select a section or prove persistence under inference. If the base has
dimension greater than four and e is surjective, the same formula gives a nondegenerate form on
the quotient vector bundle by ker e. A quotient-manifold interpretation still requires a regular leaf
quotient and basicness, as in proposition 3.6.

Proposition E.3 (Circle completion). Let Qdet  U be the unit circle bundle of det W for the line
metric whose local coefficient is d-e1t. Write det for its projection. Supply a real principal circle
connection det normalized to one on the vertical generator of period 2, and a smooth positive

GKK = det + (rdet  det)2det  det                                        (E.8)

Proof. The connection splits each total tangent space into its horizontal subspace and the one-

positive because rdet > 0. The two subspaces are orthogonal. The base pullback, radius, and
principal connection are invariant under the circle action, proving invariance of the total metric.

A supplied global GL(2, C) connection A gives the local expression det = ddet + Im tr A on this
circle bundle. The coordinate transformation d et = det + arg det g cancels Im tr A = Im tr A -
d arg det g. When the collective minimization determines only a class, its lift to a full connection is
further data. For instance, central phase rotations act trivially on centered proper complex Gaussian
laws and their covariance matrices, so that family cannot fix the corresponding phase connection
from its Fisher normal equations. Neither the positive circle radius nor equations of motion for 
follow from the construction. The determinant and circle choices give this conditional geometric
example without identifying it with physical spacetime dynamics.
